shelves.title: Feeding hospitalized patients Deposit #14 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: Does feeding hospitalized patients — on the wards and around surgery — help them live longer?
shelves.balance: On the medical wards and around surgery, feeding works: individualized nutritional support cut 30-day mortality in EFFORT ( 7% vs 10% , aOR 0.65 ; card on Shelf #99), a specialized supplement halved 90-day mortality in NOURISH (RR 0.49 , a secondary endpoint; card on Shelf #99), and perioperative nutrition cut hospital deaths in malnourished GI-cancer patients (Wu 2006, 2.1% vs 6.0% ). The founding caution stands: the thin and recent-weight-loss subgroups are almost never reported separately.

cards.headline: Perioperative TPN in weight-losing GI cancer patients
cards.summary: Single-center RCT, 90 analyzed — in-hospital deaths 0/43 with TPN vs 5/47 control (P=.05); complications 37% vs 57% ; 17 patients excluded after randomization.
cards.type: Single-center randomized controlled trial, JPEN 2000
cards.people: Gastric or colorectal cancer surgical patients with at least 10% weight loss; 107 randomized, 90 analyzed (43 TPN, 47 control)
cards.result: In-hospital deaths 0/43 with TPN vs 5/47 control (P=.05); complications 37% vs 57%
cards.watchOut: 17 patients excluded after randomization, and the small number of deaths limit confidence in the apparent survival benefit
cards.source: Bozzetti et al., JPEN 2000; PMID 10638466
cards.search: bozzetti perioperative tpn parenteral nutrition weight loss gastrointestinal cancer randomized trial jpen 2000 in-hospital deaths complications pmid 10638466

cards.headline: Preoperative nutrition support in depleted surgical patients
cards.summary: RCT, three randomized arms — mortality 3.9% (TPN), 8.0% (enteral), 4.0% (depleted control), 2.0% (non-depleted reference); not significant.
cards.type: Randomized comparison of TPN, enteral nutrition and depleted control, with a nonrandomized non-depleted reference group, Clin Nutr 1992
cards.people: Randomized groups: TPN n=51, enteral nutrition n=50, depleted control n=50; nonrandomized reference n=49
cards.result: Mortality 3.9% (TPN), 8.0% (enteral), 4.0% (depleted control), 2.0% (non-depleted reference); the comparison was not significant
cards.watchOut: Overall mortality cannot be substituted for mortality among patients with more than 10% prior weight loss, which is not separately reported
cards.source: von Meyenfeldt et al., Clin Nutr 1992; PMID 16839996
cards.search: von meyenfeldt preoperative nutrition support depleted surgical patients tpn enteral randomized trial clinical nutrition 1992 mortality pmid 16839996

cards.headline: Perioperative nutrition in malnourished GI cancer patients
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 468 patients (235 nutrition, 233 control) — hospital mortality 2.1% vs 6.0% (P=0.003; deaths 5 vs 14 ); complications 43 events in 31 patients vs 78 in 64 (P=0.012).
cards.type: Randomized trial, single center (Shanghai), 2000–2004; SGA-defined moderate/severe malnutrition, World J Gastroenterol 2006
cards.people: 512 consented; 28 not randomized after surgery (unresectability); 468 randomized — nutrition (PN+EN) n=235, control n=233
cards.result: Hospital mortality 2.1% (nutrition) vs 6.0% (control), P=0.003 (deaths 5 vs 14 ). Total complications 43 events in 31 patients vs 78 in 64, P=0.012. Hospital stay shorter with nutrition (P<0.001 as printed)
cards.watchOut: Single-center, surgery-era 2000–2004, PN-heavy regimen; outcomes are reported for the whole malnourished cohort — the paper reports no separate mortality by weight-loss stratum
cards.source: Wu et al., World J Gastroenterol 2006; PMID 16688841
cards.search: wu 2006 perioperative nutrition malnourished gastrointestinal cancer randomized trial shanghai hospital mortality complications world journal gastroenterology pmid 16688841 sga parenteral enteral

shelves.title: Immune-modulating nutrition (the AIM shelf) Deposit #15 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: Do immune-modulating feeds and nutrients — arginine, fish oil, RNA, antioxidants, vitamin A — change outcomes in critically ill and septic patients?
shelves.balance: Thirty years of immunonutrition in one shelf, and it argues with itself: the early surgical and trauma trials were positive (Kudsk — pneumonia 11.8% vs 31% with enteral feeding; Daly — complications 11% vs 37% ), and Galbán’s septic-patient trial cut mortality — yet the one severe-sepsis immunonutrition trial was stopped for harm (ICU mortality 44.4% vs 14.3% ), and the nitric-oxide lesson looms over the whole arginine idea (blocking NO in septic shock raised mortality, 59% vs 49% ). Fish oil pools positive (RR 0.74 ) but leans on small heterogeneous trials, the developer’s own vitamin A trial was negative, and two physiology cards explain why the field keeps trying: muscle ATP collapses within a week of critical illness, and septic hypoalbuminemia is a distribution problem, not a synthesis problem.

cards.headline: Puthucheary 2018: muscle ATP falls in the first week of critical illness
cards.summary: Prospective cohort, 63 ICU patients — muscle ATP 17.7 vs 21.7 mmol/kg dry weight on day 1 (p<0.001); day-1-to-7 change −4.8 (p=0.001).
cards.type: Prospective observational mechanistic cohort
cards.people: 63 intensive-care patients; vastus lateralis biopsies and serum samples were obtained on study days 1 and 7
cards.result: Intramuscular ATP content on day 1 was 17.7 mmol/kg dry weight (95% CI 15.3–20.0) , compared with 21.7 mmol/kg dry weight (95% CI 20.4–22.9) in controls (p<0.001). Among 33 patients with serial measurements, the day-1-to-day-7 ATP change was −4.8 mmol/kg dry weight (IQR −8.0 to −1.2; p=0.001)
cards.watchOut: This selected biopsy cohort did not test a randomized nutritional intervention
cards.source: Puthucheary ZA et al., Thorax 2018;73:926–935, DOI 10.1136/thoraxjnl-2017-211073, PMID 29980655
cards.search: puthucheary 2018 skeletal muscle bioenergetics atp critical illness vastus lateralis biopsy thorax prospective observational cohort pmid 29980655

cards.headline: Kudsk 1992: enteral feeding beats parenteral after abdominal trauma
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 98 abdominal trauma patients — pneumonia 11.8% vs 31.0% , intra-abdominal abscess 1.9% vs 13.3% , line sepsis 1.9% vs 13.3% with early enteral feeding.
cards.type: Prospective randomized controlled trial
cards.people: 98 patients with blunt or penetrating abdominal trauma and an abdominal trauma index of at least 15; feeding was assigned within 24 hours of injury
cards.result: Enteral feeding reduced pneumonia ( 11.8% vs 31.0% ; p<0.02), intra-abdominal abscess ( 1.9% vs 13.3% ; p<0.04), and line sepsis ( 1.9% vs 13.3% ; p<0.04) compared with total parenteral nutrition
cards.watchOut: This was a single-center trauma trial conducted under feeding and infection-control practices from the early 1990s
cards.search: kudsk 1992 enteral parenteral feeding abdominal trauma pneumonia abscess line sepsis randomized trial annals of surgery pmid 1616387

cards.headline: Daly 1992: immune-enhancing diet after cancer surgery
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 85 randomized, 77 analyzed — complications 11% vs 37% (p=0.02); hospital stay 15.8 vs 20.2 days (p=0.01).
cards.type: Randomized controlled clinical trial
cards.people: 85 postoperative patients were randomized; 77 were eligible for the reported clinical-complication analysis
cards.result: Infectious and wound complications occurred in 11% of patients receiving the supplemented formula versus 37% receiving the standard formula (p=0.02). Hospital stay was 15.8±5.1 versus 20.2±9.4 days , respectively (p=0.01)
cards.watchOut: The intervention combined several nutrients, and the clinical analysis excluded 8 randomized patients
cards.source: Daly JM et al., Surgery 1992;112:56–67, PMID 1377838
cards.search: daly 1992 arginine rna omega-3 immune enhancing enteral diet cancer surgery complications randomized trial surgery pmid 1377838

cards.headline: Galbán 2000: immune-enhancing formula in septic ICU patients
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 181 septic ICU patients, 176 in the ITT analysis — mortality 17/89 vs 28/87 (p<0.05); bacteremia 7/89 vs 19/87 (p=0.01).
cards.type: Prospective randomized multicenter trial
cards.people: 181 septic ICU patients were enrolled; 176 were eligible for intention-to-treat analysis, including 89 assigned to the enriched formula and 87 to control
cards.result: Mortality was 17/89 with the enriched formula versus 28/87 with control (p<0.05). Bacteremia occurred in 7/89 versus 19/87 (p=0.01), and more than one nosocomial infection occurred in 5/89 versus 17/87 (p=0.01)
cards.watchOut: This multinutrient formula cannot identify which ingredient produced the observed benefit
cards.search: galban 2000 immune enhancing enteral nutrition sepsis icu mortality bacteremia nosocomial infection randomized multicenter critical care medicine pmid 10752808

cards.headline: Bertolini 2003: immunonutrition harm signal in severe sepsis
cards.summary: Randomized subgroup, 39 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock — ICU mortality 44.4% vs 14.3% (p=0.039); recruitment stopped.
cards.type: Randomized multicenter unblinded controlled trial; planned interim subgroup analysis
cards.people: 39 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock from a larger 237-patient trial; 18 received enteral immunonutrition and 21 received parenteral nutrition
cards.result: ICU mortality was 44.4% with enteral immunonutrition versus 14.3% with parenteral nutrition (p=0.039). Death while severe sepsis was still present occurred in 38.9% versus 9.5% , respectively (p=0.055). Recruitment of patients with severe sepsis was stopped
cards.watchOut: The subgroup was small, unblinded, and differed in both feeding route and nutrient composition
cards.source: Bertolini G et al., Intensive Care Med 2003;29:834–840, DOI 10.1007/s00134-003-1711-5, PMID 12684745
cards.search: bertolini 2003 early immunonutrition severe sepsis septic shock enteral parenteral icu mortality stopped intensive care medicine pmid 12684745

cards.headline: López 2004: nitric-oxide synthase inhibition in septic shock
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 797 patients with septic shock in 124 ICUs — day-28 mortality 259/439 (59%) vs 174/358 (49%) (p<0.001); stopped early.
cards.type: Multicenter randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 797 patients with septic shock enrolled at 124 intensive-care units; 439 received 546C88 and 358 received placebo
cards.result: Day-28 mortality was 259/439 (59%) with 546C88 versus 174/358 (49%) with placebo (p<0.001). The trial was stopped early after the data-monitoring committee identified increased mortality
cards.watchOut: This trial tested nitric-oxide synthase inhibition, not arginine supplementation or enteral immunonutrition
cards.search: lopez 2004 nitric oxide synthase inhibition 546c88 septic shock mortality stopped early multicenter randomized double blind critical care medicine pmid 14707556

cards.headline: Gadek 1999: EPA/GLA formula in ARDS
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 146 ARDS patients enrolled, 98 evaluable — ventilator days 11.0 vs 16.3 (p=0.011); ICU stay 12.8 vs 17.5 days; new organ failure 8% vs 28% .
cards.type: Prospective multicenter double-blind randomized controlled trial
cards.people: 146 patients with ARDS were enrolled; 98 were evaluable, including 51 receiving the enriched formula and 47 receiving control
cards.result: The enriched-formula group required 11.0 versus 16.3 days of ventilatory support (p=0.011) and had an ICU stay of 12.8 versus 17.5 days (p=0.016). New organ failure occurred in 4/51 (8%) versus 13/47 (28%; p=0.015)
cards.watchOut: The published efficacy analysis included only 98 of 146 enrolled patients and tested a combined formula
cards.search: gadek 1999 epa gamma linolenic acid antioxidants ards enteral formula ventilator days organ failure randomized double blind critical care medicine pmid 10470743

cards.headline: Wang 2022: fish-oil nutrition in sepsis (meta-analysis)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 25 trials, 1,903 adults with sepsis — mortality RR 0.74 (0.63–0.86) with fish-oil-containing nutrition; parenteral RR 0.68 , enteral RR 0.80 .
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
cards.people: 25 trials involving 1,903 adults with sepsis; 959 received fish-oil-containing nutrition and 944 received control nutrition
cards.result: Overall mortality was lower with fish-oil-containing nutrition ( RR 0.74; 95% CI 0.63–0.86; p<0.0001; I²=0% ). The parenteral subgroup showed lower mortality ( RR 0.68; 95% CI 0.56–0.84 ), whereas the enteral subgroup did not reach statistical significance ( RR 0.80; 95% CI 0.64–1.01; p=0.06 )
cards.watchOut: Route, formulation, trial quality, and patient severity varied, and length-of-stay outcomes had substantial heterogeneity
cards.source: Wang H et al., Burns Trauma 2022;10:tkac012, DOI 10.1093/burnst/tkac012, PMID 35702267
cards.search: wang 2022 fish oil nutrition sepsis mortality meta-analysis randomized trials burns trauma parenteral enteral pmid 35702267

cards.headline: Omiya 2021: albumin synthesis is preserved in sepsis
cards.summary: Tracer study, 24 septic ventilated patients and 14 controls — albumin 26.8 vs 38.0 g/L (p<0.001), but synthesis 244.3 vs 253.4 mg/kg/day (p=0.87).
cards.type: Prospective observational stable-isotope tracer study
cards.people: 24 mechanically ventilated patients with sepsis and 14 nonseptic patients studied before elective coronary-artery bypass grafting
cards.result: Plasma albumin was 26.8±3.1 g/L in sepsis versus 38.0±3.9 g/L in nonseptic controls (p<0.001), but albumin absolute synthesis rates were similar: 244.3±106.2 versus 253.4±89.8 mg/kg/day (p=0.87)
cards.watchOut: The study was small, observational, used nonhealthy cardiac controls, and did not directly measure albumin clearance
cards.search: omiya 2021 albumin synthesis sepsis hypoalbuminemia stable isotope tracer critical care pmid 34920728

cards.headline: Cherukuri & Tayek 2019: high-dose vitamin A in sepsis
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 64 adults with severe sepsis or septic shock — 28-day mortality 34% vs 28% with vitamin A 100,000 IU IM daily for 7 days; no significant benefit.
cards.type: Prospective randomized double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial
cards.people: 64 adults with severe sepsis or septic shock; 32 received vitamin A and 32 received placebo
cards.result: Patients received 100,000 IU of vitamin A intramuscularly each day for 7 days. Twenty-eight-day mortality was 34% with vitamin A versus 28% with placebo, with no significant mortality benefit; ventilator days and vasopressor days were also similar
cards.watchOut: This small single-center trial was not powered to exclude clinically important benefit or harm
cards.source: Cherukuri L et al., Clin Nutr ESPEN 2019;29:49–51, DOI 10.1016/j.clnesp.2018.10.011, PMID 30661700
cards.search: cherukuri tayek 2019 high dose vitamin a sepsis septic shock intramuscular randomized double blind clinical nutrition espen pmid 30661700

shelves.title: Feeding more in the ICU
shelves.question: In the ICU, does feeding more — more energy, more protein, earlier — help patients live longer?
shelves.balance: In the ICU, every large trial of more is neutral: energy-dense formula (RR 1.05 ), higher protein (RR 1.08 ), augmented protein (RR 0.99 alive), full vs trophic feeding, permissive underfeeding (RR 0.94 ) and early restriction in shock all cross no-difference. Whether thin patients are the exception is untested — none of these trials isolated them.

cards.headline: TARGET — energy-dense formula in the ICU
cards.summary: Double-blind RCT, ~ 3,900 patients — 90-day mortality 26.8% vs 25.7% (RR 1.05 , 0.94–1.16); no benefit from more energy.
cards.type: Multicenter double-blind randomized controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: Mechanically ventilated critically ill adults; mortality reported for 1,948 assigned energy-dense formula and 1,966 assigned routine formula
cards.result: By day 90, 26.8% with energy-dense feeding vs 25.7% with routine feeding died; RR 1.05 (95% CI 0.94–1.16)
cards.watchOut: An overall ICU result does not establish the treatment effect in underweight patients or those with documented recent weight loss
cards.source: Chapman et al., NEJM 2018; PMID 30346225
cards.search: target energy dense formula icu chapman new england journal medicine 2018 double blind randomized trial enteral feeding 90-day mortality pmid 30346225

cards.headline: EFFORT Protein — higher protein in the ICU
cards.summary: Pragmatic RCT — 60-day mortality 34.6% vs 32.1% (RR 1.08 , 0.92–1.26); no benefit.
cards.type: International multicenter pragmatic registry-based randomized trial, Lancet 2023
cards.people: Critically ill adults at high nutritional risk; mortality analysis includes 642 higher-dose and 648 usual-dose participants
cards.result: Mortality at 60 days was 34.6% with higher protein vs 32.1% with usual protein; RR 1.08 (95% CI 0.92–1.26)
cards.watchOut: These mortality denominators are outcome-specific and must not be mistaken for the full randomized population or an underweight subgroup
cards.source: Heyland et al., Lancet 2023; PMID 36708732
cards.search: effort protein higher protein icu heyland lancet 2023 pragmatic randomized trial nutritional risk 60-day mortality pmid 36708732

cards.headline: NUTRIREA-3 — early restriction in shock
cards.summary: Open-label RCT, 3,044 patients — day-90 deaths 41.3% vs 42.8% (difference −1.5 points, NS); patients on low targets were ready for ICU discharge sooner (HR 1.12 ).
cards.type: Multicenter open-label randomized controlled trial, Lancet Respir Med 2023
cards.people: Ventilated adults receiving vasopressors for shock; 3,044 randomized
cards.result: Day-90 deaths were 41.3% vs 42.8% ; absolute difference −1.5 percentage points, not significant. Median time to readiness for ICU discharge was 8.0 vs 9.0 days; HR 1.12 (95% CI 1.02–1.22)
cards.watchOut: Calories and protein were changed together, so their separate contributions cannot be identified
cards.source: Reignier et al., Lancet Respir Med 2023; PMID 36958363
cards.search: nutrirea-3 early restriction shock reignier lancet respiratory medicine 2023 open label randomized trial low calorie protein day-90 mortality icu discharge pmid 36958363

cards.headline: TARGET Protein — more protein, same calories
cards.summary: Cluster crossover trial, 3,397 patients — alive at day 90: 72.6% vs 74.0% (RR 0.99 ); no benefit.
cards.type: Cluster randomized crossover open-label trial, JAMA 2025
cards.people: Critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition; n=3,397 (1,681 augmented protein, 1,716 usual protein)
cards.result: At day 90, 72.6% vs 74.0% were alive; reported RR 0.99 (95% CI 0.95–1.03)
cards.watchOut: Cluster allocation and crossover require the reported adjusted analysis rather than a simple unadjusted comparison of the raw survival proportions
cards.source: Summers et al., JAMA 2025; PMID 40495743
cards.search: target protein augmented protein same calories summers jama 2025 cluster crossover trial enteral nutrition alive day 90 pmid 40495743

cards.headline: PermiT — permissive underfeeding
cards.summary: RCT, 894 patients — day-90 deaths 27.2% vs 28.9% (RR 0.94 , 0.76–1.16); feeding less did not cost lives.
cards.type: Multicenter randomized controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2015
cards.people: Critically ill medical, surgical or trauma adults; 894 randomized
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval permits clinically relevant benefit or harm, and this overall comparison is not specific to patients with recent weight loss
cards.source: Arabi et al., NEJM 2015; PMID 25992505
cards.search: permit permissive underfeeding arabi new england journal medicine 2015 randomized trial critically ill day-90 deaths nonprotein calories pmid 25992505

cards.headline: EDEN — trophic vs full feeding in lung injury
cards.summary: RCT, 1,000 patients — 60-day mortality 23.2% vs 22.2% (difference 1.0 point, NS); starting small cost nothing.
cards.type: Multicenter randomized controlled trial, JAMA 2012
cards.people: Acute lung injury patients requiring mechanical ventilation; trophic feeding n=508, full feeding n=492
cards.result: Mortality at 60 days was 23.2% vs 22.2% ; reported difference 1.0 percentage point, not significant. Ventilator-free days were 14.9 vs 15.0
cards.watchOut: A strategy tested in acute lung injury cannot establish the effect of feeding in severely underweight or recent-weight-loss patients
cards.source: Rice et al., JAMA 2012; PMID 22307571
cards.search: eden trophic full feeding acute lung injury rice jama 2012 randomized trial enteral nutrition 60-day mortality ventilator free days pmid 22307571

shelves.title: AIONID: anti-inflammatory nutrition in hypoalbuminemic dialysis patients
shelves.question: Can an anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative oral nutrition supplement raise serum albumin in hypoalbuminemic maintenance hemodialysis patients?
shelves.balance: Supplements reliably raise albumin a little ( +0.19 to +0.23 g/dL across the syntheses; +0.21 in AIONID), an anti-inflammatory drug alone does the same with CRP falling (Pakfetrat), and the one large trial with a mortality endpoint (FINE) found no survival gain from intensifying nutrition — patients whose prealbumin rose did better, but raising the number has never been shown to be what saves them. Albumin here is a marker that moves, not yet a lever proven to change outcomes.

cards.headline: High-protein anti-inflammatory supplement: albumin +0.21 g/dL in 16 weeks — but pentoxifylline alone did nearly as well.
cards.summary: Albumin change at 16 weeks: supplement +0.21 g/dL , pentoxifylline +0.14 , both +0.18 , placebo +0.03 — 84 hypoalbuminemic hemodialysis patients.
cards.type: Pilot-feasibility, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (2 × 2 factorial).
cards.people: 84 adult hypoalbuminemic (albumin <4.0 g/dL) maintenance hemodialysis outpatients, Jan 2008–Jun 2010; mean age 59 ± 12 years; dialysis vintage 34 ± 34 months; 32% Black, 54% female, 68% diabetic. Randomized to 16 weeks of ONS, pentoxifylline (PTX), ONS + PTX, or placebos.
cards.result: Average change in serum albumin: ONS +0.21 g/dL (P=0.004), PTX +0.14 (P=0.008), ONS + PTX +0.18 (P=0.001), placebo +0.03 (P=0.59). In the predetermined intention-to-treat regression (post-trial albumin vs pre-trial albumin and intervention, placebo as reference), only ONS without PTX was significantly associated with an albumin rise (+0.17 ± 0.07 g/dL, P=0.018). No related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Pilot-feasibility trial with a surrogate endpoint — albumin, not survival, hospitalization, or function. The combination arm did no better than either alone, and PTX alone also raised albumin, so the supplement's specific contribution is not clean. Larger, long-term trials for hard outcomes are still needed.
cards.source: Rattanasompattikul M, Molnar MZ, Lee ML, et al. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle. 2013;4(4):247–257. DOI 10.1007/s13539-013-0115-9. PMID 24052226. PMCID PMC3830006.
cards.search: aionid rattanasompattikul 2013 anti-inflammatory anti-oxidative oral nutrition supplement ons albumin hypoalbuminemic hemodialysis dialysis pentoxifylline ptx factorial randomized placebo-controlled pilot feasibility journal cachexia sarcopenia muscle pmid 24052226 pmcid pmc3830006 doi 10.1007/s13539-013-0115-9

cards.headline: Pakfetrat 2023: pentoxifylline alone raised albumin and lowered CRP in hemodialysis patients
cards.summary: Double-blind RCT, 57 hemodialysis patients — albumin 3.9 → 4.1 g/dL in the pentoxifylline arm only (p = 0.031); CRP fell 22.8 → 16.5 (p = 0.005); erythropoietin dose fell 11,000 → 9,100 IU (p = 0.018).
cards.type: Double-blind randomized controlled trial, J Exp Nephrol 2023
cards.people: 57 hemodialysis patients: 27 pentoxifylline, 30 control
cards.result: Albumin rose 3.9 ± 0.4 → 4.1 ± 0.3 g/dL in the pentoxifylline arm only (p = 0.031; control not significant, p = 0.062); CRP fell 22.8 ± 15.3 → 16.5 ± 9.5 (p = 0.005, pentoxifylline only); erythropoietin dose fell 11,000 → 9,100 IU (p = 0.018)
cards.watchOut: Small trial in a lower-tier journal; supports the hypothesis that blocking inflammation — not feeding — raises albumin
cards.source: Pakfetrat M et al., J Exp Nephrol 2023;4(1):1–5
cards.search: pakfetrat 2023 pentoxifylline hemodialysis albumin crp erythropoietin double-blind randomized trial journal experimental nephrology inflammation

cards.headline: Stratton 2005: enteral nutrition support in dialysis raised albumin by 0.23 g/dL
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 18 studies (5 RCTs, 13 non-RCTs) — enteral multinutrient support raised serum albumin by 0.23 g/dL (0.037–0.418) and increased energy and protein intake; clinical-outcome data insufficient.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, Am J Kidney Dis 2005
cards.people: 18 studies in maintenance dialysis patients: 5 randomized and 13 non-randomized trials of enteral multinutrient support
cards.result: Serum albumin increased by 0.23 g/dL (95% CI 0.037–0.418); total energy and protein intake rose; little effect on phosphate or potassium; data on clinical outcomes insufficient
cards.watchOut: Most included studies were not randomized, so the pooled estimate cannot support claims about survival or other clinical outcomes
cards.source: Stratton RJ et al., Am J Kidney Dis 2005;46:387–405. DOI 10.1053/j.ajkd.2005.04.036
cards.search: stratton 2005 enteral nutrition support dialysis systematic review meta-analysis albumin american journal kidney diseases doi 10.1053/j.ajkd.2005.04.036

cards.headline: Mah 2020 (Cochrane): oral protein supplements raised albumin by 0.19 g/dL in dialysis patients
cards.summary: Cochrane review, 22 studies , 1,278 participants — oral protein supplements vs control: mean albumin change +0.19 g/dL (0.05–0.33) , moderate-certainty evidence, I² = 84%; mortality data insufficient.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020
cards.people: 22 studies, 1,278 participants with chronic kidney disease requiring dialysis
cards.result: Mean change in serum albumin +0.19 g/dL (95% CI 0.05–0.33; moderate-certainty evidence; heterogeneity I² = 84%); hemodialysis subgroup +0.28 (0.11–0.46); malnourished subgroup +0.31 (0.10–0.52); insufficient data for mortality
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity was high (I² = 84%), and the review could not answer whether supplements change survival
cards.source: Mah JY et al. Oral protein-based supplements for people with chronic kidney disease requiring dialysis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020
cards.search: mah 2020 cochrane oral protein-based supplements chronic kidney disease dialysis albumin systematic review moderate certainty

cards.headline: Cano 2007 (FINE): adding parenteral nutrition did not improve survival in malnourished hemodialysis patients
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 186 malnourished hemodialysis patients, 1 year — intradialytic parenteral nutrition plus oral supplements vs oral supplements alone: 2-year mortality 43% vs 39% , no difference. Rising prealbumin tracked better outcomes; the route did not.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (FINE study), J Am Soc Nephrol 2007
cards.people: 186 malnourished hemodialysis patients randomized to 1 year of intradialytic parenteral nutrition plus oral supplements vs oral supplements alone
cards.result: 2-year mortality did not differ: 43% vs 39% . Improvement in prealbumin during nutritional therapy was prospectively associated with lower morbidity and mortality — response to feeding tracked outcome, the route did not
cards.watchOut: A null result for the intensified route, not for nutrition itself — both arms received oral supplements
cards.source: Cano NJM et al., J Am Soc Nephrol 2007;18:2583–2591. DOI 10.1681/ASN.2007020184. PMID 17656473
cards.search: cano 2007 fine study intradialytic parenteral nutrition idpn hemodialysis mortality prealbumin journal american society nephrology pmid 17656473 doi 10.1681/asn.2007020184

shelves.title: The Mediterranean diet trials
shelves.question: Tested the way drugs are tested — randomised, with heart attacks, strokes, and deaths as the endpoints — does a Mediterranean dietary pattern actually prevent cardiovascular events, in people who have never had one and in people who already have?
shelves.balance: Three randomized trials, three decades: Lyon showed a Mediterranean-type diet could prevent second events after infarction but was small and pre-statin; PREDIMED tested the pattern at scale in primary prevention and cut major events by about 30% — and its retraction and republication over randomization lapses is stated on its card, because the shelf keeps the correction with the claim; CORDIOPREV then showed the pattern beats a low-fat diet in patients with established coronary disease (HR 0.73). No drug-style effect size is claimed: the pattern is the intervention. (Panel positions: AHA dietary guidance and ASN statements endorse Mediterranean-style patterns — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: PREDIMED: olive oil or nuts on a Mediterranean diet cut major events by about 30% — and this card keeps the retraction with the result.
cards.summary: PREDIMED 2018 (corrected republication) — primary endpoint (MI, stroke, or cardiovascular death) in 288 participants : 3.8% on Mediterranean diet + extra-virgin olive oil (HR 0.69 ), 3.4% on Mediterranean diet + nuts (HR 0.72 ), vs 4.4% on the control diet (reduced-fat advice) — 7,447 people at high cardiovascular risk with no cardiovascular disease at baseline; median follow-up 4.8 years.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial, N Engl J Med 2018 — corrected and republished; the 2013 original was retracted (see Watch out)
cards.people: 7,447 participants in Spain, aged 55 to 80 years (57% women), at high cardiovascular risk but with no cardiovascular disease at enrollment; Mediterranean diet + extra-virgin olive oil (2,543), Mediterranean diet + mixed nuts (2,454), or control diet (2,450); quarterly individual and group educational sessions, with free olive oil or nuts provided; the trial was stopped after a median follow-up of 4.8 years on the basis of a prespecified interim analysis
cards.result: A primary end-point event occurred in 288 participants : 96 events (3.8%) in the group assigned to a Mediterranean diet with extra-virgin olive oil, 83 (3.4%) in the group assigned to a Mediterranean diet with nuts, and 109 (4.4%) in the control group. In the intention-to-treat analysis adjusting for baseline characteristics and propensity scores, the hazard ratio was 0.69 (95% CI 0.53–0.91) for the Mediterranean diet with extra-virgin olive oil and 0.72 (95% CI 0.54–0.95) for the Mediterranean diet with nuts, as compared with the control diet
cards.watchOut: The correction is part of this card: the original 2013 paper was retracted and republished in 2018 after protocol deviations were identified — enrollment of household members without randomization, assignment to a study group without randomization of some participants at 1 of the 11 study sites, and apparent inconsistent use of randomization tables at another site. The investigators withdrew the 2013 report and re-estimated the effects with analyses that do not rely on the assumption that all participants were randomly assigned; the revised estimates were essentially unchanged, and results were similar after the omission of the 1,588 participants whose study-group assignments were known or suspected to have departed from the protocol
cards.source: Estruch R, Ros E, Salas-Salvadó J, et al; PREDIMED Study Investigators. Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease with a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(25):e34. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1800389. PMID 29897866. (Corrected and republished from the retracted 2013 report, N Engl J Med. 2013;368(14):1279–1290.)
cards.search: predimed estruch 2018 nejm mediterranean diet extra-virgin olive oil nuts primary prevention cardiovascular retracted republished randomization pmid 29897866

cards.headline: CORDIOPREV: in patients who already have coronary disease, the Mediterranean diet beat the low-fat diet over 7 years.
cards.summary: CORDIOPREV 2022 — primary composite (myocardial infarction, revascularisation, ischaemic stroke, peripheral artery disease, or cardiovascular death) in 87 vs 111 patients (28.1 vs 37.7 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.73 ) — 1,002 patients with established coronary heart disease in Córdoba, Spain; follow-up of 7 years.
cards.type: Single-centre randomised controlled trial, Lancet 2022
cards.people: 1,002 patients with established coronary heart disease (aged 20–75 years) at the Reina Sofia University Hospital in Córdoba, Spain; 502 randomly assigned to a Mediterranean diet and 500 to a low-fat diet; mean age 59.5 years and 82.5% men; clinical investigators were masked to treatment assignment, participants were not; dietitian teams delivered both interventions, with a follow-up of 7 years
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 198 participants: 87 in the Mediterranean diet group and 111 in the low-fat group — crude rates 28.1 vs 37.7 per 1,000 person-years (log-rank P=0.039). Multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios across the different models ranged from 0.72 (95% CI 0.54–0.96) to 0.75 (0.57–1.00) in favour of the Mediterranean diet, the headline estimate being HR 0.73 (0.55–0.97) . Component events: nonfatal myocardial infarction 19 vs 24, revascularisation 64 vs 77, ischaemic stroke 8 vs 15, peripheral artery disease 11 vs 17, cardiovascular death 11 vs 20
cards.watchOut: No individual component of the composite differed significantly between the diets, despite all five numerically favouring the Mediterranean diet. The effect was also uneven by sex: in men the primary endpoint occurred in 16.2% vs 22.8% (multiadjusted HR 0.67 ), while among the 175 women no difference was found between groups — the trial was not powered to settle the question in women. And it was one centre in one Spanish city, with intensive dietitian support
cards.source: Delgado-Lista J, Alcala-Diaz JF, Torres-Peña JD, et al; CORDIOPREV Investigators. Long-term secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease with a Mediterranean diet and a low-fat diet (CORDIOPREV): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2022;399(10338):1876–1885. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(22)00122-2. PMID 35525255.
cards.search: cordioprev delgado-lista 2022 lancet mediterranean diet low-fat diet secondary prevention coronary heart disease randomised controlled trial pmid 35525255

cards.headline: Lyon 1999: after a first heart attack, a Mediterranean-type diet cut cardiac death and repeat infarction from 44 events to 14.
cards.summary: Lyon Diet Heart Study 1999 — cardiac death and nonfatal myocardial infarction (first composite outcome): 14 events vs 44 (P=0.0001); adjusted risk ratios across the trial’s three composite outcomes ranged from 0.28 to 0.53 — 605 patients after a first myocardial infarction; mean follow-up 46 months.
cards.type: Randomised, single-blind secondary prevention trial, Circulation 1999 (final report)
cards.people: 605 patients after a first myocardial infarction, in France; a Mediterranean-type diet rich in alpha-linolenic acid vs a prudent Western-type diet; this final report covers an extended follow-up with a mean of 46 months per patient
cards.result: The first composite outcome (cardiac death and nonfatal myocardial infarction) was reduced in the Mediterranean diet group — 14 events vs 44 in the prudent Western-type diet group (P=0.0001) — as were the second composite (adding unstable angina, stroke, heart failure, and embolism: 27 vs 90 events , P=0.0001) and the third (adding minor events requiring hospital admission: 95 vs 180 , P=0.0002). Adjusted risk ratios ranged from 0.28 to 0.53 , and the protective effect of the Mediterranean dietary pattern was maintained up to 4 years after the first infarction
cards.watchOut: The limits, stated plainly: this was a small trial (605 patients) at a single centre ; it was stopped early after an intermediate analysis at 27 months showed a striking protective effect — early stopping tends to exaggerate effect sizes; and it belongs to the pre-statin era , before modern secondary-prevention drug therapy existed to compare against or add to. The experimental diet drew its alpha-linolenic acid largely from a canola-oil-based margarine rather than olive oil, so the trial tests a Mediterranean-type pattern, not the olive-oil diet of PREDIMED
cards.source: de Lorgeril M, Salen P, Martin JL, Monjaud I, Delaye J, Mamelle N. Mediterranean diet, traditional risk factors, and the rate of cardiovascular complications after myocardial infarction: final report of the Lyon Diet Heart Study. Circulation. 1999;99(6):779–785. DOI 10.1161/01.CIR.99.6.779. PMID 9989963.
cards.search: lyon diet heart study de lorgeril 1999 circulation mediterranean diet alpha-linolenic acid myocardial infarction secondary prevention pmid 9989963

shelves.title: Feeding acute pancreatitis early
shelves.question: For decades the inflamed pancreas was “rested” by starvation. When should feeding start, by what route — and what happened the one time a trial added something extra?
shelves.balance: Feed early, by mouth when the patient can. The older pooled trials say starting enteral feeding early — within 24 hours where possible — beats feeding through a vein or waiting, on mortality, pancreatic infection, and organ failure (Reference 2); the newest network ranking puts early oral feeding first of all strategies (Reference 3). But the one large modern trial found that forcing a tube in within 24 hours did not beat simply offering food at 72 hours and tubing only those who could not eat (Reference 1) — and in mild disease, eating immediately was safe and sent patients home sooner (Reference 4). Timing matters more than the tube’s tip: a gastric tube performed like a jejunal one (Reference 5). And more intervention is not more care — the one attempt to add something extra to early feeding in this disease killed people (PROPATRIA, Card 6).

cards.headline: PYTHON 2014: forcing a feeding tube in within 24 hours did not beat letting patients eat at 72 hours — major infection or death 30% vs 27%, not significant.
cards.summary: PYTHON 2014 — in 208 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis at 19 Dutch hospitals, early nasoenteric tube feeding within 24 hours of randomization vs an on-demand strategy (oral diet started at 72 hours, tube feeding only if the oral diet was not tolerated): the primary composite of major infection or death over 6 months occurred in 30 of 101 patients ( 30% ) vs 28 of 104 ( 27% ) — risk ratio 1.07 , P=0.76. Death alone: 11% vs 7%. And in the on-demand group, 72 patients ( 69% ) tolerated the oral diet and never needed a tube at all.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (PYTHON), N Engl J Med 2014
cards.people: 208 patients enrolled at 19 Dutch hospitals, at high risk for complications on the basis of an APACHE II score of 8 or higher, an Imrie or modified Glasgow score of 3 or higher, or a serum C-reactive protein level of more than 150 mg/L. Early group: nasoenteric tube feeding within 24 hours after randomization. On-demand group: an oral diet initiated 72 hours after presentation, with tube feeding provided if the oral diet was not tolerated. The primary end point was assessed during 6 months of follow-up
cards.result: The primary end point — a composite of major infection (infected pancreatic necrosis, bacteremia, or pneumonia) or death — occurred in 30 of 101 patients ( 30% ) in the early group and 28 of 104 ( 27% ) in the on-demand group (risk ratio 1.07 ; 95% CI 0.79–1.44; P=0.76). There were no significant differences between the groups in the rate of major infection (25% and 26%, respectively; P=0.87) or death (11% and 7%, respectively; P=0.33). In the on-demand group, 72 patients ( 69% ) tolerated an oral diet and did not require tube feeding. The authors’ conclusion: the trial did not show the superiority of early nasoenteric tube feeding, as compared with an oral diet after 72 hours, in reducing the rate of infection or death
cards.watchOut: A superiority trial that found none — the confidence interval (0.79–1.44) cannot exclude a moderate benefit, or a moderate harm, of the early tube, so this card files the result as “no advantage shown,” not proof the two strategies are identical. The on-demand arm was not “no feeding”: seven in ten patients ate successfully and the rest received tubes. The trial compared forced-early against feed-when-ready — not feeding against starvation
cards.source: Bakker OJ, van Brunschot S, van Santvoort HC, et al; Dutch Pancreatitis Study Group. Early versus on-demand nasoenteric tube feeding in acute pancreatitis. N Engl J Med. 2014;371(21):1983–1993. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1404393. PMID 25409371.
cards.search: python bakker early versus on-demand nasoenteric tube feeding acute pancreatitis nejm 2014 pmid 25409371 doi 10.1056/nejmoa1404393 predicted severe infection death oral diet 72 hours

cards.headline: Twelve RCTs pooled (2014): early enteral feeding beat parenteral or delayed feeding on mortality (RR 0.51), pancreatic infection (0.44), organ failure (0.59) and catheter sepsis (0.29) — and a start within 24 hours beat 24–72 hours on mortality.
cards.summary: Li 2014 — pooling 12 randomized trials (625 patients with severe or predicted severe acute pancreatitis), early enteral nutrition vs total parenteral nutrition or delayed enteral nutrition was associated with lower mortality (RR 0.51 ), pancreatic infection (RR 0.44 ), organ failure (RR 0.59 ), hyperglycemia (RR 0.38 ), and catheter-related septic complications (RR 0.29 ). Split by start time, enteral feeding begun within 24 hours of admission carried lower mortality (RR 0.27 ) than feeding begun at 24–72 hours (RR 0.67, not significant) — mortality was the one outcome on which the under-24-hour start separated from the later start.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of 12 randomised controlled trials, Med Sci Monit 2014 (open access)
cards.people: 625 participants across the 12 trials (301 early enteral nutrition, 324 control). The control group received total parenteral nutrition in 10 trials and delayed enteral nutrition in 2. Four trials started enteral feeding within 24 hours of admission and eight at 24–72 hours; all but one fed by the nasojejunal route
cards.result: Pooled risk ratios, early enteral nutrition vs control: pancreatic infection 0.44 (95% CI 0.28–0.69; p=0.0004); mortality 0.51 (0.30–0.86; p=0.01); organ failure 0.59 (0.44–0.79; p=0.0003); hyperglycemia 0.38 (0.24–0.59; p<0.0001); catheter-related septic complications 0.29 (0.13–0.64; p=0.002). Mortality by start time: within 24 hours RR 0.27 (0.10–0.78; p=0.02); 24–72 hours RR 0.67 (0.36–1.25; p=0.29). No significant subgroup difference between the two start times was observed for pancreatic infection, organ failure, hyperglycemia, or catheter-related septic complications
cards.watchOut: The component trials are small and old — several from the 1990s, most with parenteral nutrition as the comparator — so part of the “early enteral” advantage is the harm of the parenteral control (catheter sepsis, hyperglycemia) rather than a benefit of the tube itself. The under-24-hour mortality signal rests on four small trials, and the one large modern trial, PYTHON (Reference 1), found no advantage in forcing feeding earlier than the patient’s own readiness
cards.source: Li X, Ma F, Jia K. Early enteral nutrition within 24 hours or between 24 and 72 hours for acute pancreatitis: evidence based on 12 RCTs. Med Sci Monit. 2014;20:2327–2335. PMID 25399541. PMCID: PMC4247233 (open access).
cards.search: li ma jia early enteral nutrition within 24 hours 24 72 hours acute pancreatitis meta-analysis 12 rcts medical science monitor 2014 pmid 25399541 pmc4247233 mortality pancreatic infection organ failure catheter sepsis

cards.headline: Network meta-analysis, 23 RCTs and 2,095 patients: early oral feeding ranked first for survival (mortality RR 0.06 vs parenteral nutrition; SUCRA 92%) — the mouth beat every tube and the vein.
cards.summary: Elhady 2026 — across 23 randomized trials involving 2,095 patients with acute pancreatitis, early oral feeding showed the most significant mortality reduction compared with parenteral nutrition (RR 0.06 , 95% CI 0.00–0.68) and ranked best (SUCRA 92% ). Delayed oral feeding (RR 0.19) and early enteral nutrition (RR 0.31) also reduced mortality vs parenteral nutrition. Very-early oral feeding shortened hospital stay (mean difference −4.3 days ) and lowered C-reactive protein. No intervention significantly affected sepsis, necrosis, or overall complications.
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials, Pancreatology 2026 (databases searched to July 2025)
cards.people: 23 RCTs involving 2,095 patients with acute pancreatitis. Strategies compared: very early oral feeding, early oral feeding, delayed oral feeding, early enteral nutrition, delayed enteral nutrition, and parenteral nutrition. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane RoB 2 tool; the review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251152683)
cards.result: Mortality, each strategy vs parenteral nutrition: early oral feeding RR 0.06 (95% CI 0.00–0.68; SUCRA 92% , ranked best); delayed oral feeding RR 0.19 (0.06–0.58); early enteral nutrition RR 0.31 (0.17–0.58). Multiple organ failure risk was significantly reduced with delayed oral feeding (RR 0.25, 0.08–0.79) and early enteral nutrition (RR 0.32, 0.20–0.51). Very-early oral feeding reduced C-reactive protein (mean difference −47.3 mg/L, −89.8 to −4.8) and length of hospital stay (mean difference −4.3 days , −8.1 to −0.4). No intervention significantly affected sepsis, necrosis, or overall complications
cards.watchOut: Network rankings lean on indirect comparisons — few of these strategies have ever met head-to-head — and the headline mortality ratio of 0.06 carries a confidence interval running from 0.00 to 0.68, the signature of few events in small trials. A SUCRA rank says “most likely best within this network,” not “proven better in a trial”; PYTHON (Reference 1) remains the one large direct test of forcing early feeding, and it was null
cards.source: Elhady MM, Rifai M, Nada EA, et al. Optimizing nutritional support in acute pancreatitis: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of timing and route of feeding. Pancreatology. 2026;26(4):539–551. DOI 10.1016/j.pan.2026.04.004. PMID 42062193.
cards.search: elhady network meta-analysis timing route feeding acute pancreatitis pancreatology 23 rcts 2095 patients early oral feeding mortality sucra parenteral nutrition pmid 42062193

cards.headline: Eckerwall 2007: in mild pancreatitis, eating immediately was as safe as fasting — no more pain or gastrointestinal symptoms — and patients went home two days sooner (stay 4 vs 6 days).
cards.summary: Eckerwall 2007 — 60 patients with mild acute pancreatitis were randomised to immediate oral feeding or to traditional fasting with stepwise reintroduction of oral intake. No significant differences were seen between the groups concerning levels of amylase, C-reactive protein, or leukocytes, abdominal pain, or the number of gastrointestinal symptoms — and length of hospital stay was significantly shorter in the oral feeding group ( 4 vs 6 days ; p<0.05). No signs of exacerbation of the disease process were seen.
cards.type: Randomised clinical study, Clin Nutr 2007 (Sweden)
cards.people: 60 patients with mild acute pancreatitis, randomised to immediate oral feeding or fasting. Inclusion criteria: pancreas-specific amylase at least 3 times above normal, onset of abdominal pain within 48 hours, APACHE score <8, and C-reactive protein <150 mg/L. In the control group, oral fluids and diet were reintroduced in the traditional stepwise manner
cards.result: The groups were comparable with respect to age, sex, etiology, APACHE score, time from onset of pain, and amylase at admission. No significant differences were seen between the groups concerning levels of amylase, CRP, or leukocytes, abdominal pain, or number of gastrointestinal symptoms. Length of hospital stay was significantly shorter in the oral feeding group ( 4 vs 6 days ; p<0.05). The authors’ conclusion: in mild acute pancreatitis, immediate oral feeding was feasible and safe and may accelerate recovery, without adverse gastrointestinal events
cards.watchOut: Mild disease only — an APACHE score under 8 and CRP under 150 mg/L were entry tickets, so nothing on this card licenses immediate eating in predicted severe pancreatitis; that is PYTHON’s and PROPATRIA’s territory (Cards 1 and 6). A single-centre trial of 60 patients can show feasibility and a two-day stay difference; it cannot see uncommon harms
cards.source: Eckerwall GE, Tingstedt BB, Bergenzaun PE, Andersson RG. Immediate oral feeding in patients with mild acute pancreatitis is safe and may accelerate recovery — a randomized clinical study. Clin Nutr. 2007;26(6):758–763. DOI 10.1016/j.clnu.2007.04.007. PMID 17719703.
cards.search: eckerwall immediate oral feeding mild acute pancreatitis randomized clinical nutrition 2007 pmid 17719703 length of hospital stay 4 vs 6 days fasting gastrointestinal symptoms

cards.headline: Eatock 2005: nasogastric feeding matched nasojejunal feeding in severe pancreatitis — no significant difference in pain, analgesic use, inflammation markers, or clinical outcome. The simpler route lost nothing.
cards.summary: Eatock 2005 — 50 consecutive patients with objectively graded severe acute pancreatitis were randomised to early nasogastric or nasojejunal feeding via a fine-bore tube. No significant differences were found between the groups in APACHE II score, C-reactive protein measurement, pain (visual analogue score), or analgesic requirement, and clinical differences between the two groups were not significant. Overall mortality was 24.5% , with five deaths in the nasogastric group and seven in the nasojejunal group.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, Am J Gastroenterol 2005 (Glasgow, Scotland)
cards.people: 50 consecutive patients with objectively graded severe acute pancreatitis, randomised to nasogastric feeding (27 patients) or nasojejunal feeding (23 patients) via a fine-bore feeding tube. One patient in the nasojejunal group had a false diagnosis, reducing that group to 22 — 49 patients analysed. End points were APACHE II scores and C-reactive protein measurements, pain patterns by visual analogue score and analgesic requirements, complications, and total hospital and intensive-care stays
cards.result: Demographics were similar between the groups, and no significant differences were found between the groups in APACHE II score, CRP measurement, visual analogue pain score, or analgesic requirement. Clinical differences between the two groups were not significant. Overall mortality was 24.5% , with five deaths in the nasogastric group and seven in the nasojejunal group. The authors’ conclusion: the simpler, cheaper, and more easily used nasogastric feeding is as good as nasojejunal feeding in patients with objectively graded severe acute pancreatitis
cards.watchOut: Forty-nine analysed patients cannot prove equivalence — “no significant difference” in a trial this size is compatible with a real advantage either way, and the mortality split (five vs seven deaths) is reported for completeness, not as a verdict. What the trial does establish is feasibility, and the absence of the feared harm: feeding into the stomach did not worsen pain or the acute-phase response
cards.source: Eatock FC, Chong P, Menezes N, Murray L, McKay CJ, Carter CR, Imrie CW. A randomized study of early nasogastric versus nasojejunal feeding in severe acute pancreatitis. Am J Gastroenterol. 2005;100(2):432–439. DOI 10.1111/j.1572-0241.2005.40587.x. PMID 15667504.
cards.search: eatock nasogastric nasojejunal feeding severe acute pancreatitis randomized american journal of gastroenterology 2005 pmid 15667504 pain analgesia apache crp

cards.headline: PROPATRIA 2008 — the harm card: adding probiotics to early feeding in predicted severe pancreatitis did not prevent infection and doubled mortality (16% vs 6%; RR 2.53), with fatal bowel ischaemia (9 cases vs 0).
cards.summary: PROPATRIA 2008 — in 298 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis, a multispecies probiotic preparation given enterally twice daily for 28 days did not reduce infectious complications (46 patients, 30%, vs 41, 28%) — and mortality was higher on probiotics: 24 of 152 patients ( 16% ) vs 9 of 144 ( 6% ) on placebo (relative risk 2.53 ). Nine patients in the probiotics group developed bowel ischaemia — eight with fatal outcome — compared with none in the placebo group (p=0.004). The authors’ instruction: probiotic prophylaxis should not be administered in this category of patients.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (PROPATRIA), Lancet 2008 (Netherlands)
cards.people: 298 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis (APACHE II score ≥8, Imrie score ≥3, or C-reactive protein >150 mg/L), randomly assigned within 72 hours of onset of symptoms to a multispecies probiotic preparation (153 patients) or placebo (145), administered enterally twice daily for 28 days. One person in each group was excluded from analyses because of an incorrect diagnosis of pancreatitis, leaving 152 individuals in the probiotics group and 144 in the placebo group analysed
cards.result: Infectious complications — the primary end point, a composite of infected pancreatic necrosis, bacteraemia, pneumonia, urosepsis, or infected ascites during admission and 90-day follow-up — occurred in 46 ( 30% ) patients in the probiotics group and 41 ( 28% ) in the placebo group (relative risk 1.06; 95% CI 0.75–1.51): no benefit. Mortality: 24 ( 16% ) patients in the probiotics group died, compared with nine ( 6% ) in the placebo group (relative risk 2.53 ; 95% CI 1.22–5.25). Nine patients in the probiotics group developed bowel ischaemia (eight with fatal outcome), compared with none in the placebo group (p=0.004)
cards.watchOut: The harm belongs to this preparation, this dose, and this disease — a multispecies product given enterally for 28 days to patients whose gut perfusion was already failing; the trial does not convict probiotics in milder illness. But within its indication the signal is not subtle: a doubling of mortality, with a mechanism — bowel ischaemia — visible in the case count. This card is the shelf’s standing warning that “one more additive” is itself an intervention, with an intervention’s risks
cards.source: Besselink MG, van Santvoort HC, Buskens E, et al; Dutch Acute Pancreatitis Study Group. Probiotic prophylaxis in predicted severe acute pancreatitis: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2008;371(9613):651–659. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(08)60207-X. PMID 18279948.
cards.search: propatria besselink probiotic prophylaxis predicted severe acute pancreatitis lancet 2008 pmid 18279948 mortality bowel ischaemia harm ecologic 641

shelves.title: Feeding the undernourished hospital patient
shelves.question: Does feeding hospital patients who are truly undernourished change survival — and how do you know which patients those are?
shelves.balance: Across five decades of trials, the pattern is consistent: feeding helps the genuinely undernourished and does nothing measurable for the well-nourished. One large modern RCT (EFFORT) and two meta-analyses put mortality roughly a quarter to a third lower with nutritional support in malnourished medical inpatients; the biggest null (FOOD) supplemented a population only 8% of whom were undernourished. Potter’s 2001 subgroup result — the shelf’s anchor — agrees with the Cochrane undernourished stratum, but on its own it is a subgroup of an overall-null trial that was powered for weight, not survival. Screen for undernutrition, feed the ones who have it, and deliver the supplement like a medicine — prescribed, scheduled, and observed.

cards.headline: Potter 2001: supplements given like a medicine — overall null, but in the severely undernourished, mortality 14.7% vs 35%
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 381 emergency admissions over 60 — overall mortality 11.3% vs 16.9% (OR 0.62, 0.35–1.13), not significant; in the severely undernourished stratum (n=74): mortality 14.7% (5/34) vs 35% (14/40) , p<.05, OR 0.32 (0.1–1.0).
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial, JPEN 2001 (Glasgow)
cards.people: 381 emergency admissions (age >60) to a Medicine for the Elderly unit, Glasgow, stratified by BMI percentile vs elderly norms. Intervention: 120 mL sip feed (1.5 kcal/mL; 540 kcal, 22.5 g protein/day) at 8am/2pm/6pm, prescribed on the medicine chart and given by nurses in medicine cups at medication rounds (the method now called MEDPass)
cards.result: Overall mortality 11.3% vs 16.9% (OR 0.62 , 0.35–1.13) — NOT significant. In the “severely undernourished” stratum (BMI below the 5th percentile for age; n=74): mortality 14.7% (5/34) vs 35% (14/40) , p<.05, OR 0.32 (0.1–1.0); functional recovery also better (p<.04)
cards.watchOut: The trial was powered for weight change, not mortality — the mortality signal is a subgroup of an overall-null trial
cards.source: Potter JM, Roberts MA, McColl JH, Reilly JJ. Protein energy supplements in unwell elderly patients — a randomized controlled trial. JPEN 2001;25(6):323–329. PMID 11688936.
cards.search: potter 2001 protein energy supplements unwell elderly randomized controlled trial jpen medpass severely undernourished bmi 5th percentile mortality glasgow pmid 11688936

cards.headline: Schuetz 2019 (EFFORT): individualised nutritional support cut 30-day mortality in medical inpatients at nutritional risk (7% vs 10%)
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 2,088 medical inpatients at nutritional risk (NRS-2002 ≥3), 8 Swiss hospitals — 30-day mortality 7% vs 10% (adjusted OR 0.65 , 0.47–0.91, p=0.011); composite adverse outcome 23% vs 27% (adjusted OR 0.79, 0.64–0.97).
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (EFFORT), Lancet 2019 — open-label, pragmatic
cards.people: 2,088 medical inpatients at nutritional risk (NRS-2002 ≥3), 8 Swiss hospitals; dietitian-guided individualized support to protein/calorie goals vs standard hospital food
cards.result: 30-day mortality 7% vs 10% (adjusted OR 0.65 , 0.47–0.91, p=0.011); composite adverse outcome 23% vs 27% (adjusted OR 0.79 , 0.64–0.97)
cards.watchOut: Open-label, pragmatic — patients and staff knew who was receiving the individualized support
cards.source: Schuetz P, et al. Individualised nutritional support in medical inpatients at nutritional risk: a randomised clinical trial (EFFORT). Lancet 2019;393:2312–2321. PMID 31030981.
cards.search: schuetz 2019 effort individualised nutritional support medical inpatients nutritional risk nrs-2002 randomised clinical trial lancet 30-day mortality pmid 31030981

cards.headline: Gomes 2019: across 27 trials, nutritional support lowered mortality — and the effect concentrated in established malnutrition
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 27 trials, 6,803 patients — mortality 8.3% vs 11.0% (OR 0.73 , 0.56–0.97); in established malnutrition OR 0.52 (0.34–0.80), in at-risk patients OR 0.85 (ns); nonelective readmissions RR 0.76 (0.60–0.96).
cards.type: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis, JAMA Network Open 2019
cards.people: 27 trials, 6,803 medical inpatients who were malnourished or at nutritional risk
cards.result: Mortality 8.3% vs 11.0% (OR 0.73 , 0.56–0.97). The effect was larger in established malnutrition (OR 0.52 , 0.34–0.80) than in at-risk patients (OR 0.85, ns), larger in recent trials (OR 0.47), and larger with high protocol adherence (OR 0.67). Nonelective readmissions RR 0.76 (0.60–0.96)
cards.watchOut: The mortality effect is not uniform: it is carried by established malnutrition, recent trials, and high-adherence protocols — in patients merely at risk, it was not significant
cards.source: Gomes F, et al. Association of nutritional support with clinical outcomes among medical inpatients who are malnourished or at nutritional risk: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Network Open 2019;2(11):e1915138. PMID 31747030.
cards.search: gomes 2019 nutritional support malnourished nutritional risk medical inpatients systematic review meta-analysis jama network open mortality readmissions pmid 31747030

cards.headline: Milne 2009 (Cochrane): no overall mortality benefit — but RR 0.79 in trials of the undernourished
cards.summary: Cochrane review, 62 trials, 10,187 older participants — mortality overall RR 0.92 (0.81–1.04), not significant; limited to trials in undernourished participants (n=2,461): mortality RR 0.79 (0.64–0.97); complications RR 0.86 (0.75–0.99).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009
cards.people: 62 trials, 10,187 older participants at risk from malnutrition
cards.result: Mortality overall RR 0.92 (0.81–1.04) — not significant. Limited to trials in undernourished participants (n=2,461): mortality RR 0.79 (0.64–0.97). Complications RR 0.86 (0.75–0.99); weight gain +2.2%; length of stay −0.8 days (ns)
cards.watchOut: Most included trials were of poor quality. (Potter, the Card 1 trialist, is a co-author of this review)

shelves.title: Sleeve gastrectomy versus Roux-en-Y gastric bypass: SLEEVEPASS and SM-BOSS
shelves.question: In severe obesity, how do sleeve gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass compare on durable weight loss, diabetes remission, and reflux — at five years and at ten?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/surgery · Esophagitis/etiology,surgery · Gastrectomy/methods · Gastric Bypass/adverse effects · Gastroesophageal Reflux/epidemiology,etiology,surgery · Laparoscopy · Obesity/complications,epidemiology,surgery
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — bypass gives modestly more durable weight loss · LIKELY — reflux is worse after sleeve. On weight: SM-BOSS at 5 years found excess BMI loss 61.1% (sleeve) versus 68.3% (bypass), a difference that was not significant after adjustment (P=.22); SLEEVEPASS at 10 years found percentage excess weight loss not equivalent and 8.4 points higher after bypass (median 43.5% vs 50.7%). Diabetes remission did not differ significantly in SLEEVEPASS at 10 years (26% vs 33%; P=.63); hypertension remission favoured bypass (8% vs 24%; P=.04). On reflux the trials agree and the differences are large: reflux remission 60.4% after bypass versus 25.0% after sleeve and worsening in 31.8% versus 6.3% (SM-BOSS); oesophagitis 31% versus 7% at 10 years (SLEEVEPASS). Metabolic surgery versus medical therapy is a different question and stays home on Shelf #288.

cards.headline: Salminen 2022 (SLEEVEPASS, 10 years): excess weight loss 43.5% after sleeve vs 50.7% after bypass (not equivalent; 8.4 points higher with bypass), oesophagitis 31% vs 7%
cards.summary: SLEEVEPASS (2022, 10 years): excess weight loss 43.5% after sleeve vs 50.7% after bypass — not equivalent; 8.4 points higher with bypass.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, equivalence trial with 10-year follow-up
cards.people: 240 patients aged 18 to 60 with severe obesity (mean age 48.4 [SD 9.4] years; 167 women [69.6%]; mean baseline BMI 45.9 [6.0]), randomised to sleeve gastrectomy (121) or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (119) in Finland; 193 of 228 surviving operated patients (85%) completed 10-year follow-up and 176 (77%) had gastroscopy.
cards.result: Median percentage excess weight loss at 10 years was 43.5% (range 2.1%-109.2%) after sleeve and 50.7% (1.7%-111.7%) after bypass; the mean estimate was not equivalent between procedures and was 8.4 points (95% CI 3.1 to 13.6) higher after bypass. Type 2 diabetes remission (26% vs 33%; P=.63), dyslipidaemia remission (19% vs 35%; P=.23) and sleep apnoea remission (16% vs 31%; P=.30) did not differ significantly; hypertension remission was superior after bypass (8% vs 24%; P=.04). Oesophagitis was more prevalent after sleeve (31% vs 7%; P<.001) with no significant difference in Barrett oesophagus (4% vs 4%). Reoperation rates were 15.7% versus 18.5% (P=.57).
cards.watchOut: An equivalence trial that found non-equivalence on its own primary measure at 10 years, with 15% lost to weight follow-up — the direction (bypass ahead) is consistent with SM-BOSS, the size is an estimate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: both operations work durably; bypass is modestly ahead on weight and clearly ahead on reflux — split stamp
cards.summary: Both operations work durably; bypass is modestly ahead on weight and clearly ahead on reflux — Split: POSSIBLE (weight) · LIKELY (reflux).

shelves.title: Alternate-day fasting versus daily calorie restriction (Trepanowski, HELENA)
shelves.question: Does alternate-day fasting (or 5:2 intermittent restriction) produce more weight loss, better weight maintenance, or better cardiometabolic risk markers than daily calorie restriction at one year (Trepanowski; HELENA)?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis,metabolism · Caloric Restriction/methods · Cardiovascular Diseases/metabolism,prevention & control · Diet Therapy/methods · Fasting/physiology,psychology · Feeding Behavior/physiology · Insulin/analysis,blood
shelves.balance: LIKELY (equivalence, not superiority): Two randomised trials with matched energy deficits agree that intermittent schedules lose no more weight than daily restriction. Trepanowski (100 metabolically healthy obese adults, 1 year) found identical month-6 weight loss (−6.8% in both the alternate-day-fasting and daily-restriction groups) and similar month-12 loss (−6.0% versus −5.3%), with the highest dropout in the fasting group (38% versus 29%) and LDL cholesterol significantly higher on fasting by month 12 (between-group difference 11.5 mg/dL, 95% CI 1.9 to 21.1). HELENA (150 overweight/obese adults, 50 weeks) found week-50 weight loss of −5.2% (intermittent 5:2) versus −4.9% (continuous) (P for the comparison = 0.89) and no differences in adipose-tissue gene expression or circulating metabolic biomarkers. The claim stamped LIKELY is the negative one: intermittent fasting is not superior to the daily restriction it replaces.

cards.headline: Trepanowski 2017: alternate-day fasting lost exactly the same weight as daily restriction at 6 months (−6.8% both) — with more dropouts and higher LDL at 12 months
cards.summary: Trepanowski 2017: alternate-day fasting lost exactly the same weight as daily restriction at 6 months ( −6.8% both ) — with more dropouts and a month-12 LDL signal, both printed on the card.
cards.type: Single-centre randomised clinical trial (6-month weight-loss phase, 6-month maintenance phase)
cards.people: 100 metabolically healthy obese adults (86 women, 14 men; mean age 44 years, SD 11; mean BMI 34), randomised to alternate-day fasting (34), daily calorie restriction (35) or no-intervention control (31) for 1 year. Fasting meant 25% of energy needs on fast days and 125% on feast days; restriction meant 75% of needs daily.
cards.result: Mean weight loss versus control was identical at month 6 (−6.8% [95% CI −9.1 to −4.5] fasting versus −6.8% [−9.1 to −4.6] restriction) and similar at month 12 (−6.0% [−8.5 to −3.6] versus −5.3% [−7.6 to −3.0]). Dropout was highest on fasting (13 of 34, 38%) versus restriction (10 of 35, 29%) and control (8 of 31, 26%); fasting participants ate more than prescribed on fast days and less on feast days. There were no significant between-group differences in blood pressure, heart rate, triglycerides, fasting glucose, insulin, insulin resistance, C-reactive protein or homocysteine at month 6 or 12. HDL cholesterol rose more on fasting at month 6 (6.2 mg/dL [0.1 to 12.4]) but not month 12; LDL cholesterol was significantly higher on fasting at month 12 (difference 11.5 mg/dL [1.9 to 21.1]) versus restriction.
cards.watchOut: One hundred participants at one centre, with adherence on fasting drifting toward ordinary daily eating — the trial tests the prescription as actually followed, and its LDL signal at 12 months is a caution, not a rounding error.
cards.source: Trepanowski JF et al. Effect of Alternate-Day Fasting on Weight Loss, Weight Maintenance, and Cardioprotection Among Metabolically Healthy Obese Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2017;177(7):930-938. PMID: 28459931. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00960505, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: HELENA 2018: 5:2 intermittent restriction and daily restriction ended 50 weeks within 0.3 points of each other (−5.2% vs −4.9%).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (12-week intervention, 12-week maintenance, 26-week follow-up)

cards.headline: Synthesis: intermittent schedules match daily restriction; they do not beat it — LIKELY
cards.summary: Intermittent schedules match daily restriction; they do not beat it — LIKELY.
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Trepanowski (100 adults, alternate-day fasting) and HELENA (150 adults, 5:2 intermittent restriction).

shelves.title: Caloric restriction during refeeding syndrome in critical illness (Doig)
shelves.question: In critically ill adults who develop refeeding syndrome, does protocolised caloric restriction (with electrolyte replacement) improve survival and outcomes versus continuing standard caloric intake?
shelves.mesh: Critical Illness · Energy Intake · Refeeding Syndrome/diet therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C at build: the shelf face carries a day-60 survival benefit, a mortality claim, even though it comes from a component of the trial's composite primary outcome). In Doig's multicentre trial (339 patients), the primary outcome — days alive after ICU discharge at 60 days — did not differ significantly (44.8 versus 39.9 days; difference 4.9, 95% CI −2.3 to 13.6; P=0.19), while its survival components did: 91% versus 78% alive at day 60 (P=0.002) and longer overall survival time (P=0.002). A null primary with positive survival components, in a single trial: POSSIBLE, and the developer rules personally on the mortality reading. Where this shelf touches albumin at all, it is read as an inflammation/injury marker, never as a diet effect, per standing rule.

cards.headline: Doig 2015: caloric restriction did not significantly improve days alive after ICU discharge (P=0.19), but more patients were alive at day 60 (91% vs 78%; P=0.002)
cards.summary: Doig 2015: caloric restriction did not significantly improve days alive after ICU discharge (P=0.19), but more patients were alive at day 60 ( 91% vs 78% ; P=0.002).
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre, single-blind clinical trial (13 ICUs, Australia and New Zealand)
cards.people: 339 critically ill adults who developed refeeding syndrome within 72 hours of commencing nutritional support in the ICU, allocated to continued standard nutritional support (170) or protocolised caloric restriction (169), with randomisation stratified by enrolment serum phosphate and body-mass index; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — mean days alive after ICU discharge over 60 days, in the modified intention-to-treat population — was 44.8 days (95% CI 40.9 to 49.1) in 166 assessable patients in the caloric-restriction group versus 39.9 days (36.4 to 43.7) in 165 in the standard-care group (difference 4.9 days, 95% CI −2.3 to 13.6; P=0.19) — not significant. Individual components of the primary outcome favoured restriction: more patients were alive at day 60 (149 of 164 [91%] versus 128 of 163 [78%]; P=0.002) and overall survival time was increased (53.65 [SD 0.97] versus 48.9 [1.46] days; log-rank P=0.002). The authors conclude protocolised caloric restriction is a suitable therapeutic option in this setting and identify no safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: The honest reading is two-handed: the composite primary outcome was null, and the survival difference is a component analysis of that composite in a single trial — exactly the pattern that over-reads. The Tier C flag exists because the survival figures sit on this shelf's face.
cards.source: Doig GS et al. Restricted versus continued standard caloric intake during the management of refeeding syndrome in critically ill adults: a randomised, parallel-group, multicentre, single-blind controlled trial. Lancet Respir Med. 2015;3(12):943-952. PMID: 26597128. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record's abstract states the trial was registered with the Australian and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, ANZCTR 12609001043224.

shelves.title: The dietary portfolio of cholesterol-lowering foods (Jenkins)
shelves.question: In people with hyperlipidaemia, does a dietary portfolio (plant sterols, soy protein, viscous fibres, nuts) lower LDL cholesterol versus a low-saturated-fat control diet?
shelves.mesh: Cholesterol, LDL · Counseling · Diet · Dietary Fats · Dietary Fiber · Female · Humans · Hyperlipidemias · Male · Middle Aged · Nuts · Patient Compliance · Phytosterols · Soybean Proteins
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials from the same Toronto programme point the same way. In the definitive self-selected-diet trial (351 adults with hyperlipidaemia, 6 months), the portfolio lowered LDL cholesterol by 13.8% with intensive counselling and 13.1% with routine counselling, versus 3.0% on a low-saturated-fat therapeutic diet (P<.001 for each portfolio arm versus control). A decade earlier, under fully controlled feeding for one month, the portfolio lowered LDL by 28.6% — statistically indistinguishable from lovastatin 20 mg (−30.9%) and far more than the control diet (−8.0%). The claim carded here is narrow and is the question asked: the portfolio lowers LDL cholesterol more than standard low-saturated-fat advice. Both trials are unblinded (diet trials cannot be blinded), the endpoint is a surrogate, and no trial tests clinical events. PROPOSED LIKELY for LDL lowering.

cards.headline: Jenkins 2011: dietary portfolio lowered LDL cholesterol ~13–14% over 6 months versus 3% on a low-saturated-fat control diet
cards.summary: Jenkins 2011: dietary portfolio lowered LDL cholesterol ~13–14% over 6 months versus 3% on a low-saturated-fat control diet
cards.type: Randomized trial
cards.people: 351 participants with hyperlipidaemia at 4 Canadian academic centres, randomised to a low-saturated-fat therapeutic diet (control) or a dietary portfolio emphasising plant sterols, soy protein, viscous fibres and nuts, delivered at routine intensity (2 clinic visits over 6 months) or intensive intensity (7 visits). The primary outcome was percentage change in LDL cholesterol; 345 participants contributed to the modified intention-to-treat analysis, and overall attrition did not differ between treatments.
cards.result: From a mean baseline LDL cholesterol of 171 mg/dL, reductions were −13.8% (95% CI −17.2% to −10.3%; −26 mg/dL) for the intensive portfolio, −13.1% (95% CI −16.7% to −9.5%; −24 mg/dL) for the routine portfolio, and −3.0% (95% CI −6.1% to 0.1%; −8 mg/dL) for the control diet. Each portfolio arm lowered LDL significantly more than control (P<.001 for both); the two portfolio intensities did not differ from each other (P=.66). Among portfolio participants, LDL reduction tracked dietary adherence (r=−0.34, P<.001).
cards.watchOut: Unblinded by necessity, run by the group that developed the portfolio, and a cholesterol endpoint only — no cardiovascular events were tested. The control diet's small LDL fall in percentage terms (−3.0%, P=.06) shows the comparison is against competent standard advice, not against nothing.
cards.source: Jenkins DJ et al. Effect of a dietary portfolio of cholesterol-lowering foods given at 2 levels of intensity of dietary advice on serum lipids in hyperlipidemia: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2011. PMID: 21862744. Registry ID: NCT00438425, from the record. cards.headline: Jenkins 2003: under controlled feeding, the portfolio matched lovastatin for one month — LDL down 28.6% versus 30.9% on the statin
cards.summary: Jenkins 2003: under controlled feeding, the portfolio matched lovastatin for one month — LDL down 28.6% versus 30.9% on the statin
cards.type: Randomized trial (controlled feeding)
cards.people: 46 healthy hyperlipidaemic adults (mean age 59 years) randomised for one month to a very-low-saturated-fat control diet, the same diet plus lovastatin 20 mg/day, or a dietary portfolio diet high in plant sterols (1.0 g/1000 kcal), soy protein (21.4 g/1000 kcal), viscous fibres (9.8 g/1000 kcal) and almonds (14 g/1000 kcal). All food was provided under metabolically controlled conditions.
cards.result: Mean LDL cholesterol decreases were 8.0% (SE 2.1%) on the control diet, 30.9% (SE 3.6%) on the statin diet, and 28.6% (SE 3.2%) on the dietary portfolio; the portfolio and statin reductions were each significantly greater than control, with no significant difference in efficacy between the portfolio and lovastatin. C-reactive protein fell 28.2% on the portfolio and 33.3% on the statin versus 10.0% on control.
cards.watchOut: A one-month efficacy study with all meals supplied — it shows what the portfolio can do under ideal adherence, not what free-living patients sustain; the 2011 trial is the effectiveness estimate. The record shows no registry ID (a 2002–03 trial, before routine registration).
cards.source: Jenkins DJ et al. Effects of a dietary portfolio of cholesterol-lowering foods vs lovastatin on serum lipids and C-reactive protein. JAMA. 2003. PMID: 12876093. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: the portfolio beats standard low-fat advice on LDL in both a feeding study and a real-world trial — events untested
