shelves.title: Daily walnuts for two years in healthy elders (WAHA)
shelves.question: In healthy older adults, does eating walnuts daily for two years improve the lipoprotein profile versus a walnut-free control diet?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cholesterol, LDL · Circulating MicroRNA · Female · Humans · Juglans · Male · MicroRNAs · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: The Walnuts and Healthy Aging (WAHA) trial randomised healthy elders to a walnut-supplemented diet (about 15% of daily energy, roughly 30–60 g/day) or to walnut abstinence for two years. The trial's designated two-year lipoprotein-subclass report (Rajaram et al., Circulation 2021) is named in the topic file, but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so no figures can be verified from that record — this shelf cards it for provenance and takes no numbers from it. The figures that can be gate-verified come from a WAHA sub-study with an abstract: at one year, in 330 participants, LDL cholesterol had fallen by 9.07 mg/dL in the walnut group (95% CI −12.87 to −5.73), a change reported as significant versus the control group (p=0.010). A modest, real LDL reduction in a single trial, resting on surrogate endpoints and a sub-study for its verifiable numbers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: WAHA sub-study: one year of walnuts — LDL cholesterol down 9.07 mg/dL versus control-group changes (p=0.010)
cards.summary: WAHA sub-study: one year of walnuts — LDL cholesterol down 9.07 mg/dL versus control-group changes (p=0.010)
cards.type: Randomized trial (sub-study of WAHA)
cards.people: 330 free-living participants aged 63–79 years (68% women) in the Walnuts and Healthy Aging (WAHA) trial, allocated to a control group abstaining from walnuts (n=164) or a walnut group eating walnuts at 15% of daily energy (about 30–60 g/day, n=166), with fasting serum at baseline and one year. This mechanistic sub-study (circulating microRNAs) reports the trial's LDL cholesterol change, and it is the WAHA record from which figures can be verified.
cards.result: Participants in the walnut group showed a one-year decrease in LDL cholesterol of −9.07 mg/dL (95% CI −12.87 to −5.73), reported as p=0.010 versus changes in the control group. The study's microRNA mediation hypothesis was not supported: the change in the validated microRNA (hsa-miR-551a) was unrelated to the LDL decrease, so walnuts lowered LDL independently of the measured microRNA changes.
cards.watchOut: A sub-study, not the trial's primary lipid report: the LDL figure is a secondary element of a microRNA paper, at one year rather than two, in 330 of the trial's participants. The record shows no registry ID. Do not read a ~9 mg/dL LDL change as evidence about cardiovascular events.
cards.source: Gil-Zamorano J et al. Interplay of Walnut Consumption, Changes in Circulating miRNAs and Reduction in LDL-Cholesterol in Elders. Nutrients. 2022. PMID: 35406086. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Cholesterol, LDL · Circulating MicroRNA · Female · Humans · Juglans · Male · MicroRNAs · Middle Aged

shelves.title: Two years of calorie restriction in non-obese adults (CALERIE)
shelves.question: In healthy non-obese adults, does sustained calorie restriction (target 25%, achieved ~12%) improve cardiometabolic risk factors versus ad libitum eating over two years?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Pressure · Caloric Restriction · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol, LDL · Female · Glucose Tolerance Test · Humans · Male · Metabolic Diseases · Middle Aged · Overweight · Prospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss · Young Adult
shelves.balance: CALERIE phase 2 randomised 218 healthy non-obese adults (BMI 22.0–27.9, aged 21–50) 2:1 to a prescribed 25% calorie restriction or ad libitum eating for two years. The restriction group achieved an 11.9% reduction in calorie intake (versus 0.8% in controls) and sustained weight loss of 7.5 kg (versus a 0.1 kg gain), 71% of it fat mass. On exploratory cardiometabolic outcomes, calorie restriction produced persistent, significant improvements versus control in LDL cholesterol, the total-to-HDL cholesterol ratio, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, C-reactive protein, insulin sensitivity and metabolic syndrome score — improvements the authors report as robust after controlling for the weight loss itself. One trial, surrogate endpoints, exploratory analysis set. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CALERIE: two years of ~12% calorie restriction improved every measured cardiometabolic risk factor in non-obese adults
cards.summary: CALERIE: two years of ~12% calorie restriction improved every measured cardiometabolic risk factor in non-obese adults
cards.type: Randomized trial (phase 2, exploratory outcomes)
cards.people: 218 healthy non-obese men and women (aged 21–50 years, BMI 22.0–27.9 kg/m²) at three US centres, randomly assigned 2:1 to a 25% calorie restriction diet (n=143) or an ad libitum control diet (n=75) for two years. Exploratory outcomes were conventional cardiometabolic risk factors (blood pressure, plasma lipids, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, metabolic syndrome score) and glucose homoeostasis measures, analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: The calorie restriction group achieved a mean calorie intake reduction of 11.9% (SE 0.7) versus 0.8% (1.0) in controls, with sustained mean weight loss of 7.5 kg (SE 0.4) versus a 0.1 kg (0.5) gain, 71% of the loss being fat mass. Calorie restriction caused persistent significant reductions versus control in LDL cholesterol (p<0.0001), total cholesterol to HDL cholesterol ratio (p<0.0001), systolic (p<0.0011) and diastolic (p<0.0001) blood pressure, and at two years significant improvements in C-reactive protein (p=0.012), insulin sensitivity index (p<0.0001) and metabolic syndrome score (p<0.0001); a sensitivity analysis found the responses robust after controlling for relative weight loss.
cards.watchOut: These are exploratory outcomes of a trial whose achieved restriction (about 12%) was half the prescribed 25% — the result is about moderate, sustainable restriction, not the target dose. All endpoints are risk-factor surrogates in young, healthy, non-obese volunteers; nothing here measures disease events, and the population excludes the people with most to gain.
cards.source: Kraus WE et al. 2 years of calorie restriction and cardiometabolic risk (CALERIE): exploratory outcomes of a multicentre, phase 2, randomised controlled trial. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2019. PMID: 31303390. Registry ID: NCT00427193, from the record. shelves.title: Ultra-processed versus unprocessed diets, fed ad libitum (Hall)
shelves.question: In adults fed inpatient diets matched for presented calories, macronutrients, fibre, sugar and sodium, does an ultra-processed diet cause greater ad libitum energy intake and weight gain than an unprocessed diet over two weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Composition · Dietary Fiber · Eating · Energy Intake · Energy Metabolism · Female · Humans · Inpatients · Male · Weight Gain
shelves.balance: In the only inpatient randomised crossover test of the question, 20 weight-stable adults lived at the NIH Clinical Center and received ultra-processed and unprocessed diets for two weeks each, in random order, with meals matched for presented calories, energy density, macronutrients, sugar, sodium and fibre, and instructions to eat as much or as little as they wished. On the ultra-processed diet they ate 508 kcal/day more (p=0.0001) — the excess coming from carbohydrate and fat, not protein — gained 0.9 kg, and on the unprocessed diet lost 0.9 kg, with weight change tightly correlated with intake (r=0.8). A large, mechanistically clean effect in a very small, very short, single trial: it shows ultra-processing can drive intake under matched presentation, not what years of free-living eating do. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Hall 2019: ultra-processed diet — 508 kcal/day more eaten, 0.9 kg gained in two weeks; unprocessed — 0.9 kg lost
cards.summary: Hall 2019: ultra-processed diet — 508 kcal/day more eaten, 0.9 kg gained in two weeks; unprocessed — 0.9 kg lost
cards.type: Randomized trial (inpatient crossover, single)
cards.people: 20 weight-stable adults (mean age 31.2 years, BMI 27) admitted to the NIH Clinical Center, randomised to receive either an ultra-processed or an unprocessed diet for two weeks, immediately followed by the alternate diet for two weeks. Meals were designed to be matched for presented calories, energy density, macronutrients, sugar, sodium and fibre; participants were instructed to consume as much or as little as desired. Energy intake was the central measure, with weight change over each two-week period.
cards.result: Energy intake was greater on the ultra-processed diet by 508 ± 106 kcal/day (p=0.0001), driven by carbohydrate (280 ± 54 kcal/day; p<0.0001) and fat (230 ± 53 kcal/day; p=0.0004) but not protein (−2 ± 12 kcal/day; p=0.85). Participants gained 0.9 ± 0.3 kg (p=0.009) during the ultra-processed diet and lost 0.9 ± 0.3 kg (p=0.007) during the unprocessed diet; weight changes were highly correlated with energy intake (r=0.8, p<0.0001). The authors concluded that limiting ultra-processed foods may be an effective obesity strategy.
cards.watchOut: Twenty people, two weeks per diet, one metabolic ward. The matching was for presented nutrients — the diets differed in texture, eating rate and food form by design, which is the point of the question but also why the result identifies the category, not a mechanism. Free-living effects over years are extrapolation, not data.
cards.source: Hall KD et al. Ultra-Processed Diets Cause Excess Calorie Intake and Weight Gain: An Inpatient Randomized Controlled Trial of Ad Libitum Food Intake. Cell Metab. 2019. PMID: 31105044. Registry ID: NCT03407053, from the record. MeSH: Adult · Body Composition · Dietary Fiber · Eating · Energy Intake · Energy Metabolism · Female · Humans · Inpatients · Male · Weight Gain

shelves.title: Eating breakfast versus fasting until noon (Bath Breakfast Project)
shelves.question: In lean adults, does eating breakfast daily for six weeks change body weight, energy intake, and physical-activity energy expenditure versus morning fasting?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Appetite Regulation · Biomarkers · Blood Glucose · Breakfast · Cohort Studies · Energy Intake · Energy Metabolism · Feeding Behavior · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Promotion · Humans · Hyperglycemia · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Activity · Thermogenesis · Up-Regulation · Young Adult
shelves.balance: The Bath Breakfast Project ran the same six-week randomised experiment twice — in lean adults and in adults with obesity — allocating participants to a daily breakfast (≥700 kcal before 11:00) or extended morning fasting (nothing until noon). In neither trial did body weight or adiposity differ between groups, and resting metabolic rate was essentially unchanged in both. What breakfast did change was movement: physical-activity thermogenesis was markedly higher in the morning in both trials (by 442 kcal/day in lean adults; by 188 kcal/day for morning activity in adults with obesity), while energy intake rose in lean adults (+539 kcal/day) and was not significantly different in adults with obesity (+338 kcal/day, 95% CI −313 to 988), who partly compensated later in the day. Breakfast is not a weight lever in these trials — for the weight question, PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), on two concordant trials from one programme.

cards.headline: Bath (lean adults): breakfast raised morning activity and intake, but body mass and adiposity were unchanged after six weeks
cards.summary: Bath (lean adults): breakfast raised morning activity and intake, but body mass and adiposity were unchanged after six weeks
cards.type: Randomized trial
cards.people: 33 lean adults in southwest England (21 women with fat mass index ≤11 kg/m² and 12 men with fat mass index ≤7.5 kg/m², aged 21–60), randomised to daily breakfast (≥700 kcal before 11:00) or extended fasting (0 kcal until 12:00) for six weeks, with free-living measurement of all components of energy balance and 24-hour glycaemic responses.
cards.result: There was no metabolic adaptation to breakfast — resting metabolic rate stayed stable within 11 kcal/day — and appetite suppression was limited: energy intake remained 539 kcal/day greater with breakfast than after fasting (95% CI 157 to 920 kcal/day). Physical activity thermogenesis was markedly higher with breakfast (442 kcal/day; 95% CI 34 to 851 kcal/day). Body mass and adiposity did not differ between treatments, nor did adipose tissue glucose uptake or systemic cardiovascular health indexes; glycaemia was more variable in the afternoon and evening with fasting by the final week.

shelves.title: Immunonutrition around GI cancer surgery: infections cut by roughly a third relative in the largest synthesis — consistently, across 48 trials — with no mortality benefit and timing that matters
shelves.question: Before major gastrointestinal cancer surgery, does perioperative immunonutrition reduce infectious complications?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Bacterial Infections/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · *Enteral Nutrition · Female · *Food, Formulated · Gastrointestinal Neoplasms/immunology/surgery · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · *Postoperative Care · Postoperative Complications/immunology/prevention & control · *Preoperative Care · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: Yes for infections and complications; no for mortality — and the effect is clearest when the formula is given around and after surgery rather than only before it. The founding double-blind phase 3 trial (Braga 1999, PMID: 10199318; 206 GI cancer patients) found postoperative infections in 14% on an arginine-, RNA- and omega-3-enriched formula versus 30% on the identical unenriched feed. The pooled estimates have moderated as the literature grew: Zhang 2012 (PMID: 22317969; 19 trials) gives an infectious-complication risk ratio of 0.44, while the largest and most recent synthesis (Matsui 2024, PMID: 37882375; 48 trials, 4,825 patients, high-certainty) gives 0.71 for infections and 0.78 for total complications — roughly a 29% relative reduction in infections. Osland 2014 (PMID: 23411423) adds the timing lesson: perioperative and postoperative administration carried the benefit, preoperative-only administration showed none, and no timing stratum reduced mortality. Two cautions travel with the stamp: the formulas differ between trials and the records name enrichments rather than brands, so no specific commercial product is endorsed by this shelf; and immunonutrition for the critically ill — a different question with a different and contested record — is shelf #16.

cards.headline: Braga 1999 (phase 3): postoperative infections 14% on perioperative immunonutrition versus 30% on the control formula (P = .009), and 1.8 days shorter stay
cards.summary: Braga 1999 (phase 3): postoperative infections 14% on perioperative immunonutrition versus 30% on the control formula (P = .009), and 1.8 days shorter stay
cards.type: Randomised double-blind phase 3 trial (Braga 1999)
cards.people: 206 patients with colorectal, gastric or pancreatic cancer at one university hospital, randomised double-blind to drink 1 L/day of a control enteral formula (n = 104) or the same formula enriched with arginine, RNA and omega-3 fatty acids (n = 102) for 7 days before surgery, with jejunal infusion of the same formulas from 6 hours after surgery to day 7. The formulas were isoenergetic and isonitrogenous. The record describes the enrichment but names no brand or manufacturer for the formula.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, infectious complications occurred in 14% (14/102) on the enriched formula versus 30% (31/104) on control (P = .009); in the eligible population the rates were 11% (9/85) versus 24% (21/86) (P = .02). Mean postoperative stay was 11.1 ± 4.4 days versus 12.9 ± 4.6 days (P = .01). Groups were comparable for age, sex, weight loss, nutritional status, surgical duration, blood loss and transfusion.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, 1999, and the formula is identified only by its enrichment (arginine, RNA, omega-3 fatty acids): the record names no specific product or brand, so no current commercial preparation can be assumed equivalent to what was tested — products sold today may differ in composition, safety and effectiveness. Surgical and perioperative care have also moved on since 1999, which usually shrinks absolute benefits even when relative effects persist.
cards.source: Braga M et al. Perioperative immunonutrition in patients undergoing cancer surgery: results of a randomized double-blind phase 3 trial. Arch Surg. 1999. PMID: 10199318. cards.headline: Zhang 2012 (meta-analysis, 19 RCTs, 2,331 patients): infectious complications risk ratio 0.44, non-infectious 0.72, stay 2.6 days shorter
cards.summary: Zhang 2012 (meta-analysis, 19 RCTs, 2,331 patients): infectious complications risk ratio 0.44, non-infectious 0.72, stay 2.6 days shorter
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 19 RCTs (Zhang 2012)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials (1995–2011) of perioperative immunonutrition versus standard diet in elective gastrointestinal cancer surgery: 19 trials, 2,331 patients, trial quality assessed against the Cochrane handbook.
cards.result: Perioperative immunonutrition significantly reduced postoperative infectious complications (risk ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.60 — a 56% relative reduction) and non-infectious complications (risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.97), and shortened hospital stay by a weighted mean of 2.62 days (95% CI −3.26 to −1.97). The authors conclude perioperative immunonutrition is effective and safe for these endpoints.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials span different formulas, timings and eras of surgical care, and the review predates the largest modern syntheses — its 0.44 risk ratio is the most optimistic of the estimates on this shelf, and the more recent, larger meta-analysis (Matsui 2024) lands closer to 0.71 for infections. Read the range, not the extreme.

cards.headline: Osland 2014 (meta-analysis, 20 studies, 2,005 patients): the benefit depends on timing — perioperative and postoperative administration cut infections, preoperative-only did not, and mortality never moved
cards.summary: Osland 2014 (meta-analysis, 20 studies, 2,005 patients): the benefit depends on timing — perioperative and postoperative administration cut infections, preoperative-only did not, and mortality never moved
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 20 studies (Osland 2014)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (1980–2011) of arginine-dominant pharmaconutrition versus standard nutrition in elective adult surgery, analysed by timing: preoperative (5 comparisons), perioperative (2) and postoperative (14); 2,005 patients in total (1,010 pharmaconutrition, 995 control), most undergoing surgery for gastrointestinal malignancy.
cards.result: No difference in postoperative mortality was seen with pharmaconutrition at any timing. Statistically significant reductions in infectious complications and length of stay were found with perioperative and postoperative administration; perioperative administration also reduced anastomotic dehiscence, and postoperative administration reduced non-infective complications. Preoperative-only pharmaconutrition showed no notable advantage over standard nutrition on any clinical outcome assessed.
cards.watchOut: The timing subgroups rest on very uneven evidence — only 2 perioperative comparisons against 14 postoperative — so 'preoperative doesn't work' is really 'preoperative-only trials were few and small'. The mortality null, by contrast, is consistent across every timing stratum and every synthesis on this shelf.

cards.headline: Matsui 2024 (meta-analysis, 48 RCTs, 4,825 patients): total complications risk ratio 0.78 and infectious complications 0.71, both rated high-certainty
cards.summary: Matsui 2024 (meta-analysis, 48 RCTs, 4,825 patients): total complications risk ratio 0.78 and infectious complications 0.71, both rated high-certainty
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 48 RCTs (Matsui 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (1981–2022) of perioperative immunonutrition (arginine, omega-3 fatty acids or glutamine containing) versus standard nutritional therapy in adults undergoing elective surgery for head and neck or gastrointestinal cancers: 48 studies, 4,825 patients. Primary outcomes: total and infectious postoperative complications of Clavien-Dindo grade II or above within 30 days.
cards.result: Immunonutrition reduced total postoperative complications (risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.93) and infectious complications (risk ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.82) versus standard nutritional therapy, with the certainty of evidence rated high for both outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The broadest and most current synthesis, but it pools head and neck with gastrointestinal surgery and several different nutrient combinations under one label — 'immunonutrition' is a family of formulas, not a single product, and this review cannot say which components carry the effect. Its high-certainty rating applies to the pooled complication outcomes, not to mortality, which is not among its primary endpoints.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent, moderate relative reduction in infectious complications, no mortality effect — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent, moderate relative reduction in infectious complications, no mortality effect — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One double-blind phase 3 trial (206 patients) and three meta-analyses spanning 19 to 48 randomised trials and up to 4,825 patients.
cards.result: Infectious complications: 14% vs 30% in the phase 3 trial; pooled risk ratios 0.44 (Zhang 2012) and 0.71 (Matsui 2024, high certainty) — the true relative reduction is most credibly around a quarter to a third. Total complications risk ratio 0.78 (0.66 to 0.93). Length of stay shorter by about 2–3 days in the older syntheses. Mortality: no difference in any analysis. Timing: benefit with perioperative/postoperative administration, not demonstrated for preoperative-only.
cards.watchOut: The stamp is LIKELY rather than PROBABLE because the intervention is a shifting family of formulas rather than one defined product, the earliest trials are small and single-centre, and the effect size has shrunk as trials accumulated — the signature of early optimism in a literature. The direction, however, has never reversed in any synthesis.

shelves.title: Tube feeding in advanced dementia: no survival benefit in any controlled study ever done, comfort never measured at all — and pressure ulcers were more likely, not less, after tube placement
shelves.question: In advanced dementia, does tube feeding prolong survival or improve comfort versus careful hand feeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Dementia/complications*, mortality · Enteral Nutrition*/mortality · Humans · Malnutrition/prevention & control* · Pressure Ulcer/epidemiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) for survival — the rare case where a null result is consistent across every controlled comparison that exists, while the intervention is used on a third of the relevant population. The Cochrane review (Sampson EL et al., PMID: 19370678) found no randomised trials at all and seven observational controlled studies: no evidence of increased survival with enteral tube feeding, no evidence of benefit for nutritional status or pressure ulcers, and not one study that measured quality of life or comfort — the outcome families are usually told the tube will serve. The largest direct test of the pressure-ulcer rationale (Teno JM et al., PMID: 22782196), a propensity-matched national cohort, found the opposite of the intention: residents who received a PEG tube were more than twice as likely to develop a new stage 2+ pressure ulcer (odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.95 to 2.65), and existing ulcers were less likely to heal (odds ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.89). Survival data point the same way: in a matched Medicare cohort (Hwang D et al., PMID: 24112820), 180-day mortality was 51.9% with a tube versus 49.8% without (P = 0.11), while the tube group cost $2,224 more in hospital care over the following year and spent more days in intensive care. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) — no study has ever shown tube feeding prolongs life or improves comfort in advanced dementia; careful hand feeding remains the default the evidence supports, and the burden of proof sits on the tube. Because no randomised trial exists or is now likely to be done, this verdict rests on observational evidence and is marked Tier C.

cards.headline: Sampson 2009 (Cochrane): zero randomised trials, seven observational studies — no survival benefit, no nutritional or pressure-ulcer benefit, and quality of life measured by nobody
cards.summary: Sampson 2009 (Cochrane): zero randomised trials, seven observational studies — no survival benefit, no nutritional or pressure-ulcer benefit, and quality of life measured by nobody
cards.type: Systematic review of observational studies (Sampson 2009, Cochrane)
cards.people: Systematic review of enteral tube feeding (nasogastric or percutaneous gastrostomy) for older people with advanced dementia and poor intake or eating/swallowing problems. No randomised or controlled trials were found; seven observational controlled studies were included, six assessing mortality and one nutritional outcomes. The review's background notes that in one US survey 34% of 186,835 nursing-home residents with advanced cognitive impairment were tube fed.
cards.result: There was no evidence of increased survival in patients receiving enteral tube feeding. None of the studies examined quality of life, and there was no evidence of benefit in terms of nutritional status or the prevalence of pressure ulcers. Data on adverse effects were lacking. The reviewers conclude that, despite the very large number of patients receiving this intervention, there is insufficient evidence to suggest enteral tube feeding is beneficial in advanced dementia.
cards.watchOut: Observational comparisons in this field are confounded by indication in both directions — tubes are placed in the sickest patients, which biases against tubes, but also in patients whose families and physicians judge them most salvageable, which biases for them. The review's finding is therefore 'no demonstrated benefit', and its most damning gap is not statistical: across seven studies of an intervention justified by comfort and dignity, comfort and quality of life were never measured once.
cards.source: Sampson EL et al. Enteral tube feeding for older people with advanced dementia. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2009. PMID: 19370678. Registry ID: none in the record. systematic review of observational studies (sampson 2009, cochrane) systematic review of enteral tube feeding (nasogastric or percutaneous gastrostomy) for older people with advanced dementia and poor intake or eating/swallowing problems. no randomised or controlled trials were found; seven observational controlled studies were included, six assessing mortality and one nutritional outcomes. the review's background notes that in one us survey 34% of 186,835 nursing-home residents with advanced cognitive impairment were tube fed. there was no evidence of increased survival in patients receiving enteral tube feeding. none of the studies examined quality of life, and there was no evidence of benefit in terms of nutritional status or the prevalence of pressure ulcers. data on adverse effects were lacking. the reviewers conclude that, despite the very large number of patients receiving this intervention, there is insufficient evidence to suggest enteral tube feeding is beneficial in advanced dementia. observational comparisons in this field are confounded by indication in both directions — tubes are placed in the sickest patients, which biases against tubes, but also in patients whose families and physicians judge them most salvageable, which biases for them. the review's finding is therefore 'no demonstrated benefit', and its most damning gap is not statistical: across seven studies of an intervention justified by comfort and dignity, comfort and quality of life were never measured once. sampson el et al. enteral tube feeding for older people with advanced dementia. cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2009. pmid: 19370678. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · dementia/complications*, mortality · enteral nutrition*/mortality · humans · malnutrition/prevention & control* · pressure ulcer/epidemiology · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Teno 2012: propensity-matched national cohort — a PEG tube made a new pressure ulcer more than twice as likely (OR 2.27) and healing of an existing ulcer less likely (OR 0.70)
cards.summary: Teno 2012: propensity-matched national cohort — a PEG tube made a new pressure ulcer more than twice as likely (OR 2.27) and healing of an existing ulcer less likely (OR 0.70)
cards.type: Propensity-matched cohort study (Teno 2012)
cards.people: US nursing-home residents with advanced cognitive impairment and a recent need for eating assistance, drawn from national Minimum Data Set and Medicare data; each resident who had a feeding tube inserted during a hospitalisation was matched to three who did not (1,124 tube recipients in the new-ulcer analysis; 461 residents with an existing ulcer in the healing analysis), with mortality comparable between matched groups.
cards.result: Adjusted for risk factors, residents who received a PEG tube were 2.27 times as likely to develop a new stage 2 or higher pressure ulcer (95% CI 1.95 to 2.65) as matched residents without a tube. Among residents who already had a pressure ulcer, tube placement was associated with a lower likelihood of healing by the first post-hospital assessment (odds ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.89). The authors conclude feeding tubes neither prevent nor help heal pressure ulcers and appear associated with increased ulcer risk in this population.
cards.watchOut: Propensity matching balances what the dataset records; it cannot balance the bedside judgements — immobility, incontinence care, family insistence, a physician's sense of decline — that drive both tube placement and ulcer risk. The plausible mechanisms for real harm exist (tube-fed residents are repositioned less, restrained more, and have more diarrhoea and moisture), but this study establishes association, not mechanism. It does, however, remove 'at least it prevents pressure ulcers' from the list of evidence-based reasons to place a tube.
cards.source: Teno JM et al. Feeding tubes and the prevention or healing of pressure ulcers. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22782196. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hwang 2014: matched Medicare cohort — 180-day mortality 51.9% with a tube vs 49.8% without, and the tube year cost $2,224 more in hospital care with more ICU days
cards.summary: Hwang 2014: matched Medicare cohort — 180-day mortality 51.9% with a tube vs 49.8% without, and the tube year cost $2,224 more in hospital care with more ICU days
cards.type: Propensity-matched cohort study (Hwang 2014)
cards.people: Nursing-home residents with advanced dementia in Medicare claims and Minimum Data Set data (1999–2009): 1,924 residents who had a PEG tube placed during an index hospitalisation, propensity-matched to residents who did not (weighted n = 1,924), with comparable demographics, feeding-tube risk factors, and mortality at baseline matching.
cards.result: Mortality did not differ: 180-day mortality was 51.9% among residents with a feeding tube versus 49.8% among those without (P = 0.11). The tube group cost Medicare $2,224 more in inpatient care over the following year ($10,191 vs $7,967; 95% CI for the difference $1,514 to $2,933) and spent more time in intensive care (1.92 vs 1.29 days). The authors conclude PEG insertion is associated with a small but significant increase in hospital costs and hospital/ICU days, without a survival advantage.
cards.watchOut: Costs are US Medicare inpatient costs from 1999–2009 data and will not transfer exactly to other systems or years; the direction (more hospital contact after tube placement, driven by tube complications and infections) is the transferable part. As with all these cohorts, matching cannot see the family's goals — some tubes are placed for reasons (a trial of nutrition during a reversible illness, a family's settled values) that outcomes data alone do not capture.
cards.source: Hwang D et al. Feeding tubes and health costs postinsertion in nursing home residents with advanced dementia. Journal of Pain and Symptom Management. 2014. PMID: 24112820. cards.headline: Synthesis: survival — no benefit ever shown; comfort — never measured; pressure ulcers — worse with tubes; costs and hospital days — higher. Careful hand feeding is the evidence-supported default
cards.summary: Synthesis: survival — no benefit ever shown; comfort — never measured; pressure ulcers — worse with tubes; costs and hospital days — higher. Careful hand feeding is the evidence-supported default
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Seven observational studies in the Cochrane review plus two large US propensity-matched national cohorts (pressure ulcers; survival and costs) — thousands of tube-fed residents with advanced dementia, and not one randomised trial.
cards.result: Survival: no increase in any controlled study (Cochrane 2009); 180-day mortality 51.9% vs 49.8% in the matched Medicare cohort. Comfort/quality of life: unmeasured in every study. Pressure ulcers: new ulcer odds ratio 2.27 (1.95 to 2.65) with a tube; healing odds ratio 0.70 (0.55 to 0.89). Resource use: +$2,224 hospital costs and more ICU days in the year after placement. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) for survival, with a harm signal on ulcers — the strongest statement observational evidence of this consistency can carry.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about advanced dementia specifically — it does not cover tube feeding after stroke (where recovery changes the calculus; the FOOD question is homed at withheld shelf #8), in motor neurone disease, or during treatment with curative intent. It also cannot answer the individual family's question — what this person would have wanted — which is a values question the evidence informs but does not settle. Tier C is set because every card is observational; the verdict's strength comes from consistency and size, not from design.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sampson EL et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2009 (PMID: 19370678); Teno JM et al. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22782196); Hwang D et al. Journal of Pain and Symptom Management. 2014 (PMID: 24112820).

shelves.title: Measuring the burn to set the feed: calorimetry-guided ICU nutrition hit its targets exactly and moved no outcome in its only direct trial
shelves.question: In critically ill adults, does nutrition guided by indirect calorimetry (early goal-directed energy and protein delivery) improve physical function and mortality compared with standard care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Calorimetry · Dietary Proteins/therapeutic use · Enteral Nutrition/methods · Female · Goals · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Intensive Care Units/statistics & numerical data · Intention to Treat Analysis · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Nutrition Assessment · Nutritional Status* · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Parenteral Nutrition/methods · Quality of Life · Single-Blind Method · Standard of Care · Urea/urine
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the single direct trial is null and the pooled literature disagrees with itself at different time horizons. EAT-ICU (Allingstrup MJ et al., PMID: 28936712) randomised 203 ventilated patients to calorimetry- and urea-guided feeding aiming at 100% of measured requirements versus standard care: energy and protein balances were less negative, but the 6-month physical component score was identical (mean difference 0.0, 95% CI −5.9 to 5.8) and mortality, organ failure, infections, and length of stay did not differ. Two meta-analyses of the small-trial literature (e.g., Duan J et al., PMID: 33639997; 8 trials, 991 patients) found lower short-term mortality with calorimetry guidance (risk ratio 0.77, 0.60–0.98) without differences in ventilation duration or stay — a pooled signal built from trials individually too small to show it, which the largest and most rigorous single trial does not confirm at 6 months. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): measuring energy expenditure is physiologically attractive and may fine-tune delivery, but improved function or survival is unproven where it has been tested hardest.

cards.headline: Allingstrup 2017 (EAT-ICU): calorimetry-guided feeding closed the energy and protein gap — and changed nothing else; 6-month physical function difference 0.0 points
cards.summary: Allingstrup 2017 (EAT-ICU): calorimetry-guided feeding closed the energy and protein gap — and changed nothing else; 6-month physical function difference 0.0 points
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (EAT-ICU, Allingstrup 2017)
cards.people: 203 acutely admitted, mechanically ventilated ICU patients expected to stay over 3 days, in a single-centre randomised outcome-assessor-blinded trial: early goal-directed nutrition with requirements estimated by indirect calorimetry and 24-hour urinary urea, aiming to cover 100% from the first full day using enteral plus parenteral nutrition, versus standard care aiming at 25 kcal/kg/day enterally with parenteral supplementation only if targets were unmet by day 7. 199 patients were analysed.
cards.result: The goal-directed group had significantly less negative energy and protein balances in the ICU (both p<0.001). The primary outcome, the physical component summary score of the SF-36 at 6 months, did not differ (mean difference 0.0, 95% CI −5.9 to 5.8, p=0.99). Neither did mortality, rates of organ failure, serious adverse reactions or infections in the ICU, length of ICU or hospital stay, or days alive without life support at 90 days.
cards.watchOut: Single centre and only 199 analysed patients: the trial can exclude a large functional benefit but not a modest mortality effect, and its intervention bundles calorimetry with early parenteral top-up and a 100% target, so 'calorimetry' alone is not what was tested. The control arm's day-7 parenteral rescue also narrows the contrast.
cards.source: Allingstrup MJ et al. Early goal-directed nutrition versus standard of care in adult intensive care patients: the single-centre, randomised, outcome assessor-blinded EAT-ICU trial. Intensive Care Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28936712. Registry ID: NCT01372176. cards.headline: Duan 2021 (meta-analysis): 8 trials, 991 patients — calorimetry-guided delivery was associated with lower short-term mortality (risk ratio 0.77) but no difference in ventilation days or stay
cards.summary: Duan 2021 (meta-analysis): 8 trials, 991 patients — calorimetry-guided delivery was associated with lower short-term mortality (risk ratio 0.77) but no difference in ventilation days or stay
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 8 RCTs (Duan 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (991 critically ill adults) comparing energy delivery guided by indirect calorimetry with delivery guided by predictive equations; overall trial quality was rated moderate.
cards.result: The calorimetry groups received significantly more energy per day and a higher percentage of measured targets. Short-term mortality was lower with calorimetry guidance (risk ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.60–0.98, I²=3%, p=0.03). There were no significant differences in duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference 0.61 days, −1.08 to 2.29), ICU stay (0.32 days, −2.51 to 3.16), hospital stay (0.30 days, −3.23 to 3.83), or adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A mortality signal assembled from eight small trials (991 patients in total — barely five EAT-ICUs) with moderate quality is fragile: short-term mortality definitions vary, and a second meta-analysis of substantially the same literature found the association only at 28 days, not at 90 days. When the largest constituent trial is null on every outcome, pooled positivity should be read as 'worth a big trial', not as proof.
cards.source: Duan J et al. Energy delivery guided by indirect calorimetry in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Critical Care. 2021. PMID: 33639997. cards.headline: Synthesis: calorimetry measures better than equations, feeds closer to target — and has not yet shown it changes how patients do
cards.summary: Synthesis: calorimetry measures better than equations, feeds closer to target — and has not yet shown it changes how patients do
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One single-centre RCT (EAT-ICU, 199 analysed) plus meta-analyses totalling under 1,100 randomised patients on indirect-calorimetry-guided versus standard or equation-guided ICU nutrition.
cards.result: Delivery: consistently closer to measured energy and protein targets with guidance (EAT-ICU balances p<0.001). Function at 6 months: difference 0.0 (95% CI −5.9 to 5.8). Mortality: null in EAT-ICU at every horizon; pooled short-term mortality risk ratio 0.77 (0.60–0.98) across small trials, not sustained at 90 days in parallel syntheses. Ventilation, stay, infections: no differences. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers the guidance question, not the dose question: how many calories to aim for is shelves #1301/#1302/#3025 territory, and a service could rationally use calorimetry to avoid gross over- or under-feeding without claiming outcome benefit. What is missing is a multicentre trial powered for mortality or function. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is one small single-centre trial plus fragile pooling.
cards.source: Synthesis of Allingstrup MJ et al. Intensive Care Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28936712); Duan J et al. Critical Care. 2021 (PMID: 33639997).

shelves.title: Getting the feed down: erythromycin beats metoclopramide for a day, the combination beats both for a week — and none of it has been shown to change survival
shelves.question: In critically ill adults with enteral feed intolerance, does erythromycin, metoclopramide, or their combination improve feeding success compared with placebo or each other?
shelves.mesh: Antiemetics/therapeutic use · Critical Illness · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Enteral Nutrition/adverse effects · Erythromycin/therapeutic use · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Metoclopramide/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the narrow job of getting feed down in a critically ill patient who is not tolerating it, prokinetics work, combination therapy works best, and nothing here shows they change survival or stay. In the head-to-head trial (Nguyen NQ et al., PMID: 17205032), erythromycin beat metoclopramide at 24 hours (successful feeding 87% vs 62%), but both faded fast; in the companion trial (Nguyen NQ et al., PMID: 17828038), the erythromycin–metoclopramide combination beat erythromycin alone over 7 days, with more calories delivered and less postpyloric feeding, at the cost of more watery diarrhoea (20 of 37 vs 10 of 38). The meta-analysis (Lewis K et al., PMID: 27527069) confirms a moderate-certainty reduction in feeding intolerance (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.55–0.97; 17.3% absolute reduction) and high residual volumes, with no significant effect on vomiting, diarrhoea overall, ICU stay, or mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): use a prokinetic — combination first where monotherapy fails — to rescue enteral feeding, expecting a feeding benefit that wanes over days, not an outcome benefit.

cards.headline: Nguyen 2007 (combination vs erythromycin alone): combination therapy kept feeding successful over 7 days, delivered more calories, and needed less postpyloric feeding — diarrhoea 20/37 vs 10/38
cards.summary: Nguyen 2007 (combination vs erythromycin alone): combination therapy kept feeding successful over 7 days, delivered more calories, and needed less postpyloric feeding — diarrhoea 20/37 vs 10/38
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Nguyen 2007, combination therapy)
cards.people: 75 mechanically ventilated medical ICU patients with feed intolerance (gastric residual volume >250 mL), in a randomised double-blind trial of combination therapy (intravenous erythromycin 200 mg twice daily plus metoclopramide 10 mg four times daily, n=37) versus erythromycin alone (n=38), studied for 7 days; successful feeding meant residual volume <250 mL at a rate ≥40 mL/hr.
cards.result: After 24 hours, gastric residual volume was significantly lower with combination therapy than with erythromycin alone (136 ± 23 mL vs 293 ± 45 mL, p=0.04). Over 7 days the combination group had greater feeding success, received more daily calories, and required less postpyloric feeding. Tachyphylaxis occurred in both groups but was less with combination therapy. There was no difference in length of hospital stay or mortality. Watery diarrhoea was more common with combination therapy (20 of 37 vs 10 of 38, p=0.01) but was not associated with enteric infection, including Clostridium difficile.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 75 patients using a surrogate definition of success (residual volume plus feed rate): it was never powered for pneumonia, stay, or mortality, and gastric residual volume itself is a contested target (the monitoring question is shelf #80). Diarrhoea was common on the combination and, in a modern unit, C. difficile vigilance still applies despite the reassuring finding here.

randomised controlled trial (nguyen 2007, combination therapy) 75 mechanically ventilated medical icu patients with feed intolerance (gastric residual volume >250 ml), in a randomised double-blind trial of combination therapy (intravenous erythromycin 200 mg twice daily plus metoclopramide 10 mg four times daily, n=37) versus erythromycin alone (n=38), studied for 7 days; successful feeding meant residual volume <250 ml at a rate ≥40 ml/hr. after 24 hours, gastric residual volume was significantly lower with combination therapy than with erythromycin alone (136 ± 23 ml vs 293 ± 45 ml, p=0.04). over 7 days the combination group had greater feeding success, received more daily calories, and required less postpyloric feeding. tachyphylaxis occurred in both groups but was less with combination therapy. there was no difference in length of hospital stay or mortality. watery diarrhoea was more common with combination therapy (20 of 37 vs 10 of 38, p=0.01) but was not associated with enteric infection, including clostridium difficile. a single-centre trial of 75 patients using a surrogate definition of success (residual volume plus feed rate): it was never powered for pneumonia, stay, or mortality, and gastric residual volume itself is a contested target (the monitoring question is shelf #80). diarrhoea was common on the combination and, in a modern unit, c. difficile vigilance still applies despite the reassuring finding here. nguyen nq et al. prokinetic therapy for feed intolerance in critical illness: one drug or two? cards.headline: Nguyen 2007 (erythromycin vs metoclopramide): erythromycin won at 24 hours (successful feeding 87% vs 62%) — then both drugs faded, and rescue combination therapy succeeded in 92% on day 1
cards.summary: Nguyen 2007 (erythromycin vs metoclopramide): erythromycin won at 24 hours (successful feeding 87% vs 62%) — then both drugs faded, and rescue combination therapy succeeded in 92% on day 1
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Nguyen 2007, head-to-head)
cards.people: 90 mechanically ventilated medical ICU patients with feed intolerance (gastric residual volume ≥250 mL), randomised double-blind to metoclopramide 10 mg intravenously four times daily (n=45) or erythromycin 200 mg intravenously twice daily (n=45), with open-label combination rescue if intolerance recurred on treatment; studied for 7 days.
cards.result: After 24 hours both drugs reduced mean gastric residual volume (metoclopramide 830 ± 32 mL to 435 ± 30 mL; erythromycin 798 ± 33 mL to 201 ± 19 mL; both p<0.0001), and successful feeding was more frequent with erythromycin (87%) than metoclopramide (62%). The effectiveness of both declined rapidly over time. In patients who failed monotherapy, rescue combination therapy was highly effective (92% on day 1) and maintained effectiveness to day 6 (67%). High pretreatment residual volume predicted poor response.
cards.watchOut: Tachyphylaxis is the story: a day-1 winner is not a week-long strategy, and the trial predates modern concerns about erythromycin's QT effects, drug interactions, and antimicrobial-resistance stewardship when an antibiotic is used as a motility drug. Doses and routes here are intravenous and ICU-specific.

cards.headline: Lewis 2016 (meta-analysis): 13 trials, 1,341 patients — prokinetics reduced feeding intolerance (risk ratio 0.73; 17.3% absolute) with moderate certainty, and did not significantly change mortality, stay, vomiting, or diarrhoea
cards.summary: Lewis 2016 (meta-analysis): 13 trials, 1,341 patients — prokinetics reduced feeding intolerance (risk ratio 0.73; 17.3% absolute) with moderate certainty, and did not significantly change mortality, stay, vomiting, or diarrhoea
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 13 RCTs (Lewis 2016)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (1,341 critically ill adults receiving enteral nutrition) comparing a prokinetic agent with placebo or no intervention, searched to January 2016, with GRADE assessment.
cards.result: Prokinetic agents significantly reduced feeding intolerance (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.55–0.97, p=0.03; moderate certainty), a 17.3% (95% CI 5–26.8%) absolute reduction, reduced high gastric residual volumes (risk ratio 0.69, 0.52–0.91), and increased successful postpyloric tube placement (risk ratio 1.60, 1.17–2.21). There was no significant improvement in vomiting, diarrhoea, ICU length of stay, or mortality, and prokinetics did not significantly increase diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials mix agents, doses, and definitions of intolerance, and most predate current feeding protocols; the feeding-intolerance benefit is moderate certainty while every patient-important outcome (pneumonia, mortality, stay) remains unclear rather than disproven. The review compares prokinetics with placebo — the combination-versus-single question rests on the two Nguyen trials above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: prokinetics rescue feeding, combination beats single agents, effects fade within days — and no trial shows patients live longer or leave sooner
cards.summary: Synthesis: prokinetics rescue feeding, combination beats single agents, effects fade within days — and no trial shows patients live longer or leave sooner
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two single-centre RCTs from one programme (75 and 90 patients) plus a 13-trial meta-analysis (1,341 patients) on prokinetic therapy for enteral feed intolerance in critical illness.
cards.result: Feeding intolerance: pooled risk ratio 0.73 (95% CI 0.55–0.97), 17.3% absolute reduction. Head-to-head at 24 hours: erythromycin 87% vs metoclopramide 62% successful feeding; combination superior to erythromycin alone over 7 days and effective as rescue (92% day 1). Harms: more watery diarrhoea on combination in one trial (20/37 vs 10/38); no pooled diarrhoea increase. Mortality, ICU stay, vomiting: no significant differences anywhere. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Keep the claim narrow: this is a feeding-delivery shelf, not an outcomes shelf, and it sits beside shelf #80 (whether residual volumes should be monitored at all) — if a unit does not chase residual volumes, the trigger for these drugs largely disappears. Erythromycin's use here is as a motilin agonist, not an antibiotic, but stewardship and QT cautions still apply in practice.

shelves.title: Oral supplements after hip fracture: fewer patients with complications in the pooled trials (RR 0.71) — but no clear effect on mortality, on low- or very-low-quality evidence
shelves.question: After hip fracture, do oral nutritional supplements reduce complications and mortality versus routine care?
shelves.mesh: Aftercare · Aged · Cause of Death · Dietary Supplements/adverse effects · Hip Fractures/complications/mortality · Humans · Malnutrition/diet therapy/mortality · Nutritional Support/adverse effects/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for complications, not for survival. The Cochrane review of nutritional interventions after hip fracture (Avenell et al., PMID: 27898998; 41 trials, 3,881 participants) found low-quality evidence that oral multinutrient feeds may reduce the number of participants with complications (123/370 versus 157/367; RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.86; 11 trials) but had little effect on mortality (24/486 versus 31/481; RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.32; 15 trials), and very-low-quality evidence of fewer 'unfavourable outcomes' (death or complications; RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.89). A single-blind randomised trial in a rehabilitation ward (Myint et al., PMID: 22685164; 126 patients) points the same way: less BMI loss, a rehabilitation stay shortened by 3.80 days, and significantly fewer infection episodes on supplements, with no difference in albumin change, functional independence, or mobility scores. Vomiting and diarrhoea were not increased in the pooled data (RR 0.99). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): oral supplements after hip fracture probably prevent some complications; a mortality benefit is unproven and the underlying trials are methodologically weak.

cards.headline: Avenell 2016 (Cochrane): complications RR 0.71 with oral feeds — mortality RR 0.81 and not significant, across 41 trials of 3,881 patients
cards.summary: Avenell 2016 (Cochrane): complications RR 0.71 with oral feeds — mortality RR 0.81 and not significant, across 41 trials of 3,881 patients
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Avenell 2016, Cochrane)
cards.people: 41 randomised and quasi-randomised trials involving 3,881 people aged over 65 recovering from hip fracture, testing nutritional interventions started within the first month after fracture; 18 trials evaluated oral multinutrient feeds providing non-protein energy, protein, vitamins and minerals versus routine care.
cards.result: Oral multinutrient feeds: mortality 24/486 versus 31/481 (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.32; 15 trials; low-quality evidence — little effect). Participants with complications (pressure sore, infection, venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, confusion): 123/370 versus 157/367 (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.86; 11 trials; low-quality evidence). 'Unfavourable outcome' (death or complications): RR 0.67 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.89; 6 studies, 334 participants; very low quality). Vomiting and diarrhoea: RR 0.99 (95% CI 0.47 to 2.05). Nasogastric feeding showed no mortality effect (RR 0.99) and was poorly tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The review authors judged the evidence low or very low quality: fewer than half the trials were at low risk of bias for allocation concealment, incomplete outcome data, or selective reporting. The complication benefit is a count of participants with any of a mixed bag of complications, not a single hard endpoint, and the mortality confidence interval (0.49 to 1.32) excludes neither worthwhile benefit nor harm.
cards.source: Avenell A et al. Nutritional supplementation for hip fracture aftercare in older people. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 27898998. cards.headline: Myint 2013: supplements blunted BMI loss and shortened rehabilitation stay by 3.8 days, with fewer infection episodes — function and mobility unchanged
cards.summary: Myint 2013: supplements blunted BMI loss and shortened rehabilitation stay by 3.8 days, with fewer infection episodes — function and mobility unchanged
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Myint 2013, single-blind)
cards.people: 126 elderly post-surgical proximal femoral fracture patients in an inpatient rehabilitation setting, randomised to a ready-to-use oral liquid supplement (18–24 g protein and 500 kcal per day) plus hospital diet, or hospital diet only; both groups received usual rehabilitation and oral calcium and vitamin D.
cards.result: BMI fell less on supplements: decreases of 0.25 versus 0.72 kg/m² at rehabilitation discharge and 0.03 versus 0.49 kg/m² four weeks after discharge (P = 0.012). Rehabilitation length of stay was shortened by 3.80 days (SE 1.81, P = 0.04) favouring supplements, and the total number of infection episodes was significantly reduced. There was no difference in the rate of change of serum albumin, the Functional Independence Measure, or the Elderly Mobility Scale.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, single-centre, 126 patients; the record reports the infection reduction as significant without giving episode counts, and the functional outcomes patients care about (independence, mobility) did not move — the wins are weight preservation, infections, and bed-days.
cards.source: Myint MW et al. Clinical benefits of oral nutritional supplementation for elderly hip fracture patients: a single blind randomised controlled trial. Age and ageing. 2013. PMID: 22685164. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but soft complication benefit, no survival signal — supplements are cheap and safe here, the evidence is not strong
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but soft complication benefit, no survival signal — supplements are cheap and safe here, the evidence is not strong
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 41 trials (3,881 older hip-fracture patients) plus a concordant 126-patient rehabilitation-ward RCT of a ready-to-use oral supplement (500 kcal, 18–24 g protein daily).
cards.result: Complications: pooled RR 0.71 (0.59 to 0.86) for participants with complications on oral feeds; infections significantly fewer in the single trial. Mortality: RR 0.81 (0.49 to 1.32) — not significant. Function/mobility: no difference where measured. Harms: no excess vomiting or diarrhoea (RR 0.99). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), carried by the Cochrane pool rather than any single trial.
cards.watchOut: Both sources agree the trial base is weak (Cochrane: low/very-low quality; Myint: small and single-blind). This shelf should not be read as proof supplements save lives after hip fracture — no source shows that.
cards.source: Synthesis of Avenell A et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016 (PMID: 27898998); Myint MW et al. Age and ageing. 2013 (PMID: 22685164).

shelves.title: Supplements in malnourished COPD: weight up about 1.7 kg and grip and breathing-muscle strength improved in pooled trials — lung function unmoved, quality-of-life results mixed
shelves.question: In malnourished patients with COPD, do oral nutritional supplements improve weight, grip strength, and quality of life versus dietary advice alone?
shelves.mesh: Body Weight · Enteral Nutrition · Humans · Lung Diseases, Obstructive/complications/therapy · Nutrition Disorders/etiology/therapy · Parenteral Nutrition · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Skinfold Thickness
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for weight and strength in the malnourished, not for lung function. The Cochrane review (Ferreira et al., PMID: 23235577; 17 trials, 632 participants) found that in undernourished patients supplementation produced significant weight gain (MD 1.65 kg, 95% CI 0.14 to 3.16, as final values; MD 1.73 kg, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.17, as change from baseline), better respiratory-muscle strength (maximal inspiratory pressure MD 5.02 cmH₂O and maximal expiratory pressure MD 12.73 cmH₂O in the malnourished), and a clinically significant pooled St George's Respiratory Questionnaire improvement (MD −6.55, 95% CI −11.7 to −1.41) — while FEV₁ did not change (SMD −0.01). A functional-outcomes meta-analysis (Collins et al., PMID: 23432923; 12 RCTs, 448 patients) agrees on strength: handgrip +1.35 kg (P = 0.05), inspiratory and expiratory muscle strength significantly up, with gains concentrated in patients who gained at least 2 kg; quality of life improved in some trials but could not be pooled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in malnourished COPD, supplements buy weight and measurable strength; they do not change the lungs themselves, and the quality-of-life evidence is inconsistent.

cards.headline: Ferreira 2012 (Cochrane): weight +1.65 kg and better breathing-muscle strength in the undernourished — FEV₁ unchanged (SMD −0.01)
cards.summary: Ferreira 2012 (Cochrane): weight +1.65 kg and better breathing-muscle strength in the undernourished — FEV₁ unchanged (SMD −0.01)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Ferreira 2012, Cochrane)
cards.people: 17 randomised trials (632 participants) of at least two weeks of nutritional support (mostly oral supplements) in stable COPD, including nourished and undernourished patients; searches current to April 2012.
cards.result: In undernourished patients (11 RCTs, 325 participants), final weight favoured supplementation (MD 1.65 kg, 95% CI 0.14 to 3.16); change-from-baseline analyses showed MD 1.73 kg (95% CI 1.29 to 2.17) in the malnourished. Fat-free mass index improved (SMD 1.08, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.47 in the undernourished). Six-minute walk change from baseline improved (MD 39.96 m, 95% CI 22.66 to 57.26) though between-group final values did not differ significantly. FEV₁: no difference (SMD −0.01, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.30). Respiratory-muscle strength in malnourished patients: maximal inspiratory pressure MD 5.02 cmH₂O (0.29 to 9.76), maximal expiratory pressure MD 12.73 cmH₂O (4.91 to 20.55). Pooled St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total score in two trials: MD −6.55 (95% CI −11.7 to −1.41); the Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire showed no difference.
cards.watchOut: Much of the evidence is graded low quality, several analyses rest on change-from-baseline (the weaker analysis) where final-value comparisons were null, and the headline quality-of-life result comes from two trials using one questionnaire while a second questionnaire showed nothing.
cards.source: Ferreira IM et al. Nutritional supplementation for stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2012. PMID: 23235577. systematic review and meta-analysis (ferreira 2012, cochrane) 17 randomised trials (632 participants) of at least two weeks of nutritional support (mostly oral supplements) in stable copd, including nourished and undernourished patients; searches current to april 2012. in undernourished patients (11 rcts, 325 participants), final weight favoured supplementation (md 1.65 kg, 95% ci 0.14 to 3.16); change-from-baseline analyses showed md 1.73 kg (95% ci 1.29 to 2.17) in the malnourished. fat-free mass index improved (smd 1.08, 95% ci 0.70 to 1.47 in the undernourished). six-minute walk change from baseline improved (md 39.96 m, 95% ci 22.66 to 57.26) though between-group final values did not differ significantly. fev₁: no difference (smd −0.01, 95% ci −0.31 to 0.30). respiratory-muscle strength in malnourished patients: maximal inspiratory pressure md 5.02 cmh₂o (0.29 to 9.76), maximal expiratory pressure md 12.73 cmh₂o (4.91 to 20.55). pooled st george's respiratory questionnaire total score in two trials: md −6.55 (95% ci −11.7 to −1.41); the chronic respiratory questionnaire showed no difference. much of the evidence is graded low quality, several analyses rest on change-from-baseline (the weaker analysis) where final-value comparisons were null, and the headline quality-of-life result comes from two trials using one questionnaire while a second questionnaire showed nothing. ferreira im et al. nutritional supplementation for stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2012. pmid: 23235577. mesh: body weight · enteral nutrition · humans · lung diseases, obstructive/complications/therapy · nutrition disorders/etiology/therapy · parenteral nutrition · randomized controlled trials as topic · skinfold thickness

cards.headline: Collins 2013: grip strength +1.35 kg and both breathing-muscle pressures significantly up — respiratory function itself unresponsive
cards.summary: Collins 2013: grip strength +1.35 kg and both breathing-muscle pressures significantly up — respiratory function itself unresponsive
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Collins 2013)
cards.people: 12 RCTs (448 participants) in stable COPD testing nutritional support — dietary advice (1 RCT), oral nutritional supplements (10 RCTs), enteral tube feeding (1 RCT) — versus control, analysed for functional outcomes.
cards.result: Nutritional support significantly improved maximal inspiratory mouth pressure (+3.86 cmH₂O, SE 1.89, P = 0.041), maximal expiratory mouth pressure (+11.85 cmH₂O, SE 5.54, P = 0.032), and handgrip strength (+1.35 kg, SE 0.69, P = 0.05), with improvements associated with weight gains of at least 2 kg. Respiratory function (FEV₁, lung capacity, blood gases) was unresponsive to nutritional support. Quality of life improved significantly in some trials, although meta-analysis was not possible; exercise performance and the benefit of exercise rehabilitation programmes were enhanced.
cards.watchOut: The grip result sits exactly at P = 0.05 and the pooled trials are small (448 patients across 12 RCTs, one of them tube feeding rather than oral supplements); the comparison in most trials was usual care rather than the structured dietary advice this question names, so the advice-alone counterfactual is only loosely tested.
cards.source: Collins PF et al. Nutritional support and functional capacity in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Respirology (Carlton, Vic.). 2013. PMID: 23432923. cards.headline: Synthesis: two meta-analyses agree — supplements feed muscle, not lungs; benefit belongs to the malnourished subgroup
cards.summary: Synthesis: two meta-analyses agree — supplements feed muscle, not lungs; benefit belongs to the malnourished subgroup
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two systematic reviews of randomised trials in stable COPD (17 trials, 632 participants; 12 RCTs, 448 participants), overlapping trial bases analysed for nutritional and functional outcomes respectively.
cards.result: Weight: +1.65 to +1.73 kg in undernourished patients. Strength: handgrip +1.35 kg; inspiratory and expiratory pressures significantly improved in both reviews. Lung function: no effect in either review. Quality of life: one pooled questionnaire positive (−6.55 points), another null, a third unpoolable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for malnourished patients; neither review supports supplementing the well-nourished.
cards.watchOut: The two reviews share much of the same small-trial base, so their agreement is not independent replication; effects are surrogate (weight, pressures, grip) rather than admissions or survival, which neither review could establish.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ferreira IM et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2012 (PMID: 23235577); Collins PF et al. Respirology (Carlton, Vic.). 2013 (PMID: 23432923).

shelves.title: Supplements for undernourished older people at home: a 49-person pilot hinted at fewer hospital admissions — the larger follow-up trial found none (29% versus 32% admitted)
shelves.question: In undernourished older people in the community, do oral nutritional supplements reduce complications and hospital admissions versus dietary advice?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Blood Glucose/metabolism · C-Reactive Protein/metabolism · Dietary Supplements · Electrolytes/blood · Female · Hematocrit · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Malnutrition/blood/drug therapy · Prostate-Specific Antigen/blood · Quality of Life · Testosterone/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the only direct community evidence, and with a large caveat: in both trials the supplement was bundled with testosterone, never tested alone against dietary advice. The pilot (Chapman et al., PMID: 19144729) randomised 49 community-dwelling undernourished people over 65 to testosterone, a 475 kcal/day oral supplement, both, or nothing for a year: the combined group had no hospital admissions versus 9 admissions in 13 untreated subjects, and significantly fewer people admitted (0 versus 5, P = 0.03); the supplement-alone arm had 5 admissions in 13 subjects, between the two and not separable at this size. The larger multicentre follow-up (Visvanathan et al., PMID: 27499311) tested the combined package against placebo in 53 undernourished community-dwelling older people for a year and found no difference: 8 of 28 (29%) admitted on treatment versus 8 of 25 (32%) on placebo, with no difference in number or length of hospitalisations (P = 0.842 and P = 0.645) or quality of life. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the community supplement question has never been cleanly tested alone, and the bundled intervention that was tested failed its confirmatory trial.

cards.headline: Chapman 2009 (pilot): combined testosterone + supplement group had zero admissions versus 9 in the untreated group — supplement alone sat in between (5 in 13)
cards.summary: Chapman 2009 (pilot): combined testosterone + supplement group had zero admissions versus 9 in the untreated group — supplement alone sat in between (5 in 13)
cards.type: Randomised pilot trial (Chapman 2009)
cards.people: 49 community-dwelling undernourished people aged over 65 (mean age 77; Mini Nutritional Assessment score <24 and BMI <22 or recent weight loss >7.5% over 3 months), randomised for one year to oral testosterone undecanoate, an oral nutritional supplement (475 kcal/day), both combined, or no treatment.
cards.result: Hospital admissions: none in the combined-treatment group (n = 11), versus 9 admissions (2 elective) in 13 no-treatment subjects, 4 in the testosterone group (n = 12), and 5 in the supplement-only group (n = 13); P = 0.06 for admissions, no-treatment versus combined. The combined group had significantly fewer subjects admitted (0 versus 5, P = 0.03), fewer days in hospital (0 versus 74, P = 0.041), and a longer time to admission (P = 0.017) than no treatment.
cards.watchOut: A 49-person pilot with 11–13 people per arm: the supplement-alone arm cannot be distinguished from either neighbour, the headline contrast is the combined anabolic package against nothing (no placebo, no dietary-advice comparator), and a zero-event arm in 11 people is fragile by construction.
cards.source: Chapman IM et al. Effect of testosterone and a nutritional supplement, alone and in combination, on hospital admissions in undernourished older men and women. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 2009. PMID: 19144729. Registry ID: NCT00117000. cards.headline: Visvanathan 2016 (confirmatory): no difference in admissions — 29% admitted on the package versus 32% on placebo, quality of life unchanged
cards.summary: Visvanathan 2016 (confirmatory): no difference in admissions — 29% admitted on the package versus 32% on placebo, quality of life unchanged
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Visvanathan 2016, multicentre, double-blind)
cards.people: 53 undernourished community-dwelling men and women aged 65 and older (mean age 77, 64% male) — substantially fewer than the 200 planned — randomised for one year to oral testosterone undecanoate plus a high-energy oral nutritional supplement (2108–2416 kJ/day) or placebo medication plus a low-energy 'placebo' supplement (142–191 kJ/day).
cards.result: Sixteen subjects (30%) were admitted to hospital at least once, with 29 admissions in total: 8 subjects (32%) in the placebo arm and 8 (29%) in the intervention group were admitted. There was no difference in the number of hospitalisations (P = 0.842), length of hospitalisation (P = 0.645), or quality of life (mental health P = 0.195, physical health P = 0.451) between the arms.
cards.watchOut: The trial recruited 53 of a planned 200, so it is underpowered to exclude a modest effect — but it is the larger, blinded, placebo-controlled test of the pilot's signal and it found nothing, and like the pilot it tests supplement-plus-testosterone, not supplements versus dietary advice.
cards.source: Visvanathan R et al. The Randomized Control Trial of the Effects of Testosterone and a Nutritional Supplement On Hospital Admissions in Undernourished, Community Dwelling, Older People. The journal of nutrition, health & aging. 2016. PMID: 27499311. cards.headline: Synthesis: pilot promise, confirmatory null — and the supplement-alone question remains untested in the community
cards.summary: Synthesis: pilot promise, confirmatory null — and the supplement-alone question remains untested in the community
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two randomised trials from one research programme in undernourished community-dwelling older people (49 and 53 participants, one year each), both bundling an oral nutritional supplement with testosterone undecanoate.
cards.result: Pilot: 0 admissions on the combined package versus 9 admissions in 13 untreated; supplement alone 5 admissions in 13. Confirmatory: 29% versus 32% admitted, no difference in admissions, hospital days, or quality of life. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: the evidence is two small trials of a bundled intervention, neither of which compares supplements with dietary advice — the comparison this question actually asks about.
cards.watchOut: Absence of a clean test is not proof supplements cannot help selected undernourished people at home; it is proof that the claim 'supplements reduce admissions in the community' currently has no confirmatory support. Hospital-based supplement evidence lives on its own shelves and does not transfer automatically to the community setting.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chapman IM et al. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 2009 (PMID: 19144729); Visvanathan R et al. The journal of nutrition, health & aging. 2016 (PMID: 27499311).

shelves.title: Dietary counselling during head and neck radiotherapy: weight and quality of life held up better than with supplements alone or ad lib eating — counselling was the ingredient that lasted
shelves.question: In head and neck cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy, does intensive dietary counselling with oral supplements preserve weight and quality of life versus ad lib advice?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Counseling · Dietary Proteins/administration & dosage · Dietary Supplements · Energy Intake · Female · Head and Neck Neoplasms/diet therapy/radiotherapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nutritional Physiological Phenomena · Nutritional Status · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with counselling, not supplements alone, as the active ingredient. In the three-arm Ravasco trial (PMID: 15920748; 75 head and neck cancer patients referred for radiotherapy), dietary counselling with regular foods and supplements-plus-usual-diet both raised energy and protein intake during radiotherapy while the ad lib group's intake fell significantly; at 3 months only the counselled group maintained intake, and the reduction in grade 1+2 anorexia, nausea/vomiting, xerostomia and dysgeusia was seen in 90% of counselled patients versus 67% on supplements and 51% ad lib (p < .0001), with quality-of-life function scores tracking nutritional intake. Isenring's trial (PMID: 15226773; 60 outpatients receiving radiotherapy to the gastrointestinal or head and neck area) found the same shape: intensive individualised dietitian counselling with supplements as required produced statistically smaller deteriorations in weight (P < 0.001), nutritional status (P = 0.020) and global quality of life (P = 0.009) than usual practice. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intensive dietary counselling during radiotherapy preserves weight, intake and quality of life; handing over supplements without counselling did not hold its gains at 3 months.

cards.headline: Ravasco 2005: at 3 months only the counselled group kept its intake up — symptom improvement 90% counselled versus 67% supplements versus 51% ad lib
cards.summary: Ravasco 2005: at 3 months only the counselled group kept its intake up — symptom improvement 90% counselled versus 67% supplements versus 51% ad lib
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Ravasco 2005)
cards.people: 75 patients with head and neck cancer referred for radiotherapy, randomised to dietary counselling with regular foods (n = 25), usual diet plus oral supplements (n = 25), or ad lib intake (n = 25); intake, nutritional status (Subjective Global Assessment) and quality of life (EORTC QLQ-C30) measured at baseline, end of radiotherapy, and 3 months.
cards.result: Energy intake after radiotherapy increased in the counselling and supplement groups (p ≤ .05) and protein intake likewise (p ≤ .006), while both decreased significantly in the ad lib group (p < .01). At 3 months the counselling group maintained intakes; the supplement and ad lib groups returned to or below baseline. Over 90% of patients in all groups experienced radiotherapy toxicity during treatment. At 3 months, improvement in grade 1+2 anorexia, nausea/vomiting, xerostomia and dysgeusia occurred in 90% of the counselling group versus 67% of the supplement group versus 51% ad lib (p < .0001). Quality-of-life function scores improved in proportion to nutritional intake and status in the counselling/supplement groups and worsened ad lib; at 3 months only the counselling group maintained or improved overall quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Small (25 per arm), single-centre and necessarily unblinded — counselling trials cannot be blinded, and quality-of-life and symptom outcomes are exactly the ones open-label designs flatter. No survival or treatment-completion endpoint was tested.
cards.source: Ravasco P et al. Impact of nutrition on outcome: a prospective randomized controlled trial in patients with head and neck cancer undergoing radiotherapy. Head & neck. 2005. PMID: 15920748.
