cards.headline: Isenring 2004: intensive dietitian counselling shrank the deterioration in weight (P < 0.001), nutritional status (P = 0.020) and global quality of life (P = 0.009)
cards.summary: Isenring 2004: intensive dietitian counselling shrank the deterioration in weight (P < 0.001), nutritional status (P = 0.020) and global quality of life (P = 0.009)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Isenring 2004)
cards.people: 60 outpatients (51 men, 9 women; mean age 61.9 years) commencing at least 20 fractions of radiotherapy to the gastrointestinal or head and neck area, randomised to intensive individualised nutrition counselling by a dietitian using a standard protocol, with oral supplements if required (n = 29), or usual practice — general advice and a nutrition booklet (n = 31); outcomes at baseline and 4, 8 and 12 weeks.
cards.result: The intervention group had statistically smaller deteriorations in weight (P < 0.001), nutritional status (P = 0.020) and global quality of life (P = 0.009) compared with usual care. Differences in fat-free mass were clinically suggestive but not statistically significant (P = 0.195). The authors conclude weight maintenance, rather than weight gain, is the appropriate aim in this population.
cards.watchOut: The record reports p-values without the absolute weight or quality-of-life differences, mixes gastrointestinal with head and neck radiotherapy patients, and follows patients only 12 weeks; like Ravasco it is small and unblinded.
cards.source: Isenring EA et al. Nutrition intervention is beneficial in oncology outpatients receiving radiotherapy to the gastrointestinal or head and neck area. British journal of cancer. 2004. PMID: 15226773. cards.headline: Synthesis: two small unblinded trials, one consistent message — the dietitian, not the drink, is the intervention
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small unblinded trials, one consistent message — the dietitian, not the drink, is the intervention
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two randomised trials in radiotherapy outpatients (75 head and neck patients; 60 gastrointestinal/head and neck patients) comparing intensive dietary counselling, with supplements as needed, against supplements alone, ad lib intake, or usual advice.
cards.result: Counselling preserved intake, weight, nutritional status and quality of life during radiotherapy in both trials; in the three-arm trial, supplements without counselling matched counselling during treatment but lost the gains by 3 months (symptom improvement 67% versus 90%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for intensive counselling; no trial here supports supplements as a stand-alone prescription.
cards.watchOut: Total randomised evidence is 135 patients, all unblinded, with short follow-up and no hard endpoints (survival, radiotherapy completion, admissions). The stamp grades the consistency and direction of the two trials, not their size.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ravasco P et al. Head & neck. 2005 (PMID: 15920748); Isenring EA et al. British journal of cancer. 2004 (PMID: 15226773).

shelves.title: Feeding to a measured calorie target in the ICU: a pilot's mortality trend (32.3% versus 47.7%) came with longer ventilation — the 417-patient international trial found no difference in infections or death
shelves.question: In critically ill patients, does tight calorie control guided by repeated indirect calorimetry reduce infections versus weight-based feeding targets?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Critical Care/methods · Energy Intake · Energy Metabolism · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Male · Middle Aged · Nutritional Requirements · Nutritional Support/methods · Prospective Studies · Respiration, Artificial · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the pilot and the multicentre trial point different ways. The single-centre TICACOS pilot (Singer et al., PMID: 21340655; 130 ventilated patients) fed the calorimetry group more (2,086 versus 1,480 kcal/day) and saw a trend to lower hospital mortality (32.3% versus 47.7%, p = 0.058) — but ventilation lasted longer (16.1 versus 10.5 days, p = 0.03) and ICU stay likewise (17.2 versus 11.7 days, p = 0.04), and infections were not its demonstrated win. The multicentre TICACOS International trial (Singer et al., PMID: 32534949; 417 patients, stopped early after 6 years of slow recruitment) targeted 80–100% of measured expenditure and found infection rates, pneumonia, ventilation length, ICU and hospital stay all not different between groups, with mortality numerically lower but not significantly different (21 versus 30 deaths). PROPOSED SPLIT: a single-centre pilot suggested benefit at a morbidity price; the larger international test of the same idea found no significant benefit on infections or mortality.

cards.headline: Singer 2011 (TICACOS pilot): hospital mortality 32.3% versus 47.7% (p = 0.058) — but ventilation 16.1 versus 10.5 days and ICU stay 17.2 versus 11.7 days
cards.summary: Singer 2011 (TICACOS pilot): hospital mortality 32.3% versus 47.7% (p = 0.058) — but ventilation 16.1 versus 10.5 days and ICU stay 17.2 versus 11.7 days
cards.type: Randomised pilot trial (Singer 2011, TICACOS)
cards.people: 130 mechanically ventilated patients expected to stay in ICU more than 3 days at a single centre, randomised to enteral nutrition with an energy target set by repeated indirect calorimetry (n = 65) or 25 kcal/kg/day (n = 65), with parenteral supplementation when required; 112 patients appear in the intake comparisons (56 per group).
cards.result: The calorimetry group received more energy (2,086 ± 460 versus 1,480 ± 356 kcal/day, p = 0.01) and protein (76 ± 16 versus 53 ± 16 g/day, p = 0.01). Hospital mortality showed a trend favouring calorimetry in the intention-to-treat group (21/65, 32.3% versus 31/65, 47.7%, p = 0.058), while duration of ventilation (16.1 ± 14.7 versus 10.5 ± 8.3 days, p = 0.03) and ICU stay (17.2 ± 14.6 versus 11.7 ± 8.4 days, p = 0.04) were significantly longer in the calorimetry group.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre pilot whose mortality result is a non-significant trend (p = 0.058) bought with significantly longer ventilation and ICU stay — the opposite of a clean win; the intervention was a bundle (measurement plus actively supervised feeding), so the calorimeter itself may not be the active ingredient.
cards.source: Singer P et al. The tight calorie control study (TICACOS): a prospective, randomized, controlled pilot study of nutritional support in critically ill patients. Intensive care medicine. 2011. PMID: 21340655. cards.headline: Singer 2021 (TICACOS International): infections and mortality not significantly different — 40 versus 31 infections and 30 versus 21 deaths across 417 patients
cards.summary: Singer 2021 (TICACOS International): infections and mortality not significantly different — 40 versus 31 infections and 30 versus 21 deaths across 417 patients
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Singer 2021, TICACOS International, multicentre)
cards.people: 417 newly admitted ventilated adult ICU patients at seven centres with a calorimeter (339 followed the protocol), randomised to nutritional support targeting 80–100% of daily measured resting energy expenditure or an equation-based target (20–25 kcal/kg ideal body weight/day); the trial was stopped after 6 years for slow inclusion, short of its planned 580. Primary endpoint was infection rate.
cards.result: Infection rate (40 in the control group versus 31 in the study group), pneumonia rate, need for surgery, dialysis requirement, length of ventilation, ICU length of stay and hospital length of stay were not different between groups. Mortality (30 deaths in the control group versus 21 in the study group) was not significantly different. Baseline severity was well matched (SOFA 7.1 ± 3.1 versus 7.4 ± 3.3; APACHE II 22.4 ± 7.9 versus 22.2 ± 7.4).
cards.watchOut: The record reports event counts rather than rates with denominators per arm, and the trial stopped early and under-recruited — underpowered for the mortality difference its point counts hint at; it is nonetheless the only multicentre test, and its pre-specified primary endpoint (infections) was null.
cards.source: Singer P et al. TICACOS international: A multi-center, randomized, prospective controlled study comparing tight calorie control versus Liberal calorie administration study. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2021. PMID: 32534949. cards.headline: Synthesis: measure-guided feeding delivers more calories reliably — whether patients do better remains unproven after the larger trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: measure-guided feeding delivers more calories reliably — whether patients do better remains unproven after the larger trial
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Two randomised trials of indirect-calorimetry-guided feeding versus formula-based targets (130 patients, single centre; 417 patients, seven centres).
cards.result: Calories delivered: clearly higher with measurement (2,086 versus 1,480 kcal/day in the pilot). Infections: not significantly different in the multicentre trial, whose primary endpoint they were. Mortality: a non-significant trend in the pilot (32.3% versus 47.7%); numerically fewer deaths but not significant in the larger trial (21 versus 30). Morbidity price in the pilot: significantly longer ventilation and ICU stay. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the mortality question this shelf touches is exactly the kind the developer reviews personally, and the two trials do not agree.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was blinded (feeding targets cannot be), and the pilot's bundle included actively supervised nutrition — attributing its trend to the calorimeter alone overreads the design.
cards.source: Synthesis of Singer P et al. Intensive care medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21340655); Singer P et al. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2021 (PMID: 32534949).

shelves.title: Feeding while prone: pooled data link it to more vomiting (OR 2.38), more pneumonia (OR 2.11) and more feed interruptions (OR 4.75) — yet a protocolised unit fed more, not less safely, and mortality did not differ
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated patients fed while prone, does enteral nutrition increase vomiting or aspiration versus feeding supine?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Critical Illness/therapy · Enteral Nutrition/methods/adverse effects · Prone Position/physiology · Respiration, Artificial/methods/adverse effects · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/therapy/mortality
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — to tolerance, not to survival, on mostly observational evidence. A meta-analysis of enteral nutrition during prone ventilation (Pan et al., PMID: 40176759; 5 studies, 319 patients) found prone feeding associated with more vomiting (OR 2.38, 95% CI 1.61 to 3.50), greater gastric residual volume (OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.47 to 5.03), more ventilator-associated pneumonia (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.12 to 3.96) and far more feeding interruptions (OR 4.75, 95% CI 2.22 to 10.17), with no significant mortality difference (OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.88). The primary studies are less alarming: in a before–after study of a standardised protocol (Reignier et al., PMID: 19709786), patients fed prone with 25-degree head elevation and prophylactic erythromycin received larger volumes (median 1,170 versus 774 mL/day) without increases in residual volume, vomiting, or pneumonia; and in a 19-patient crossover study (van der Voort & Zandstra, PMID: 11511335), gastric residual volumes did not differ between prone and supine periods. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): feeding prone measurably worsens tolerance markers in pooled data, but protocolised delivery appears to offset much of it, and no mortality penalty has been shown.

cards.headline: Pan 2025 (meta-analysis): vomiting OR 2.38, pneumonia OR 2.11, interruptions OR 4.75 with prone feeding — mortality OR 1.11, not significant
cards.summary: Pan 2025 (meta-analysis): vomiting OR 2.38, pneumonia OR 2.11, interruptions OR 4.75 with prone feeding — mortality OR 1.11, not significant
cards.type: Meta-analysis (Pan 2025)
cards.people: 5 studies totalling 319 critically ill ventilated patients comparing enteral nutrition delivered in the prone position versus the supine position; study quality was assessed with the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, the tool used for observational studies. Registered PROSPERO CRD42023441409.
cards.result: Prone versus supine feeding: vomiting OR 2.38 (95% CI 1.61 to 3.50, P < 0.0001); gastric residual volume OR 2.72 (95% CI 1.47 to 5.03, P = 0.001); ventilator-associated pneumonia OR 2.11 (95% CI 1.12 to 3.96, P = 0.02); interruptions in enteral nutrition OR 4.75 (95% CI 2.22 to 10.17, P < 0.0001); energy achievement rate slightly lower but not statistically significant (mean difference −0.88, 95% CI −1.83 to 0.06); mortality OR 1.11 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.88, P = 0.7). Egger's test suggested no significant publication bias for the main outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Only five studies and 319 patients, appraised with an observational-study scale — prone patients are sicker by indication (proning is reserved for worse oxygenation), so confounding by severity runs through every pooled odds ratio here; aspiration itself was not directly measured, with pneumonia standing in as its proxy.
cards.source: Pan J et al. Safety and efficacy of enteral nutrition during prone ventilation: A meta-analysis. The Journal of international medical research. 2025. PMID: 40176759. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42023441409. cards.headline: Reignier 2010: a prone-feeding protocol (25° head-up, faster ramp, prophylactic erythromycin) delivered 1,170 versus 774 mL/day with no rise in vomiting, residuals, or pneumonia
cards.summary: Reignier 2010: a prone-feeding protocol (25° head-up, faster ramp, prophylactic erythromycin) delivered 1,170 versus 774 mL/day with no rise in vomiting, residuals, or pneumonia
cards.type: Before–after study (Reignier 2010)
cards.people: 72 mechanically ventilated patients receiving early enteral nutrition with prone positioning at a single ICU — 34 in the before period (flat when prone, rate increased 500 mL every 24 hours, erythromycin only to treat intolerance) and 38 in the intervention period (25-degree head elevation while prone, rate increased 25 mL/h every 6 hours to 85 mL/h, prophylactic erythromycin from the first turn).
cards.result: Larger feeding volumes were delivered in the intervention group (median volume per day with prone positioning 1,170 mL [IQR 736–1417] versus 774 mL [IQR 513–925], P < 0.001) without increases in residual gastric volume, vomiting, or ventilator-associated pneumonia.
cards.watchOut: A before–after comparison, not a randomised trial: the bundle changed three things at once (position, ramp speed, prophylactic prokinetic), secular improvement cannot be excluded, and the comparison is protocol-versus-old-practice in prone patients — not prone versus supine feeding itself.
cards.source: Reignier J et al. Before-after study of a standardized ICU protocol for early enteral feeding in patients turned in the prone position. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2010. cards.headline: van der Voort 2001 (crossover): gastric residual volumes were the same prone as supine in 19 ventilated patients — high residuals travelled with the patient, not the position
cards.summary: van der Voort 2001 (crossover): gastric residual volumes were the same prone as supine in 19 ventilated patients — high residuals travelled with the patient, not the position
cards.type: Prospective crossover study (van der Voort 2001)
cards.people: 19 consecutive mechanically ventilated ICU patients who were turned prone, each studied for 6 hours supine and 6 hours prone in random order at an unchanged feeding rate, with gastric residual volume measured by nasogastric suction after 3 and 6 hours in each position.
cards.result: Median administered feed volume was 95 mL after 6 hours supine and 110 mL after 6 hours prone (P = 0.85). In 10 patients residual volume was greater prone; in 8 it was greater supine. In 18 of 19 patients, residual volumes were concordant between positions (≥150 mL in both or ≤150 mL in both over 6 hours), leading the authors to conclude enteral feeding can be continued when a patient is turned prone. Significantly more sedatives were used in the prone position.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen patients and six-hour windows: this study can rule out a dramatic immediate effect on residuals and nothing more — it says nothing about vomiting, aspiration, or pneumonia over days of proning.
cards.source: van der Voort PH et al. Enteral feeding in the critically ill: comparison between the supine and prone positions: a prospective crossover study in mechanically ventilated patients. Critical care (London, England). 2001. PMID: 11511335. cards.headline: Synthesis: tolerance is genuinely worse prone in pooled data — delivery protocol, not position alone, decides how much that matters
cards.summary: Synthesis: tolerance is genuinely worse prone in pooled data — delivery protocol, not position alone, decides how much that matters
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: A 5-study meta-analysis (319 patients), a 72-patient before–after protocol study, and a 19-patient physiological crossover study of enteral feeding in prone versus supine ventilated patients.
cards.result: Vomiting, residuals, pneumonia and interruptions: all significantly more frequent with prone feeding in the pooled analysis (ORs 2.11–4.75). Mortality: no difference (OR 1.11, 0.65 to 1.88). Against that, the only protocol study delivered substantially more feed prone (1,170 versus 774 mL/day) with no tolerance penalty, and the crossover study found residuals were a property of the patient, not the position. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: the harm base is observational and confounded by severity; no randomised trial of feeding prone versus supine exists in this record set.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as 'stop feeds when proning': the same evidence base shows protocolised prone feeding succeeding. The honest reading is narrower — expect intolerance, mitigate it (head elevation, prokinetics, ramp discipline), and know the pooled harm signal has never been randomised-tested.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pan J et al. The Journal of international medical research. 2025 (PMID: 40176759); Reignier J et al. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2010 (PMID: 19709786); van der Voort PH et al. Critical care (London, England). 2001 (PMID: 11511335).

shelves.title: Higher-calorie refeeding in anorexia nervosa: medical stability restored sooner (HR 1.67) and 4 days saved — with no excess electrolyte harm; in atypical anorexia the same fixed dose underfeeds
shelves.question: In adolescents with anorexia nervosa, does higher-calorie refeeding shorten hospital stay without increasing refeeding syndrome versus lower-calorie refeeding?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anorexia Nervosa/diet therapy · Child · Energy Intake · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Prospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from one multicentre trial programme. The StRONG trial (Garber et al., PMID: 33074282; 120 adolescents and young adults aged 12–24 hospitalised with anorexia or atypical anorexia nervosa, 111 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis) compared refeeding beginning at 2,000 kcal/day and advancing 200 kcal/day against 1,400 kcal/day advancing 200 kcal every other day: higher-calorie refeeding restored medical stability significantly earlier (hazard ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.53, P = .01), electrolyte abnormalities and other adverse events did not differ by group, and hospital stay was 4.0 days shorter (95% CI −6.1 to −1.9), saving $19,056 in charges per participant. The trial's atypical-anorexia analysis (Garber et al., PMID: 38179719) adds the catch: patients with atypical anorexia (≥85% of median BMI) restored heart rate more slowly (8.7 versus 6.5 days), gained less weight, and had more hypomagnesaemia (29% versus 11%, OR 3.29) because the fixed starting dose delivered fewer kcal/kg (32.4 versus 43.4 kcal/kg) — dose per kilogram, not the diagnosis, predicted outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): starting higher and advancing faster is safe and quicker in hospitalised adolescents — dosed generously enough per kilogram for heavier patients.

cards.headline: Garber 2021 (StRONG): stability restored sooner (HR 1.67), stay 4.0 days shorter, $19,056 saved — electrolyte abnormalities no different
cards.summary: Garber 2021 (StRONG): stability restored sooner (HR 1.67), stay 4.0 days shorter, $19,056 saved — electrolyte abnormalities no different
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (Garber 2021, StRONG)
cards.people: 120 adolescents and young adults aged 12–24 years hospitalised with anorexia nervosa or atypical anorexia nervosa at ≥60% of median BMI at two tertiary inpatient eating-disorder programmes (111 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis; 91% female, mean age 16.4 years), randomised to higher-calorie refeeding (2,000 kcal/day, +200 kcal/day) or lower-calorie refeeding (1,400 kcal/day, +200 kcal every other day). Medical stability was a composite of six indices (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, orthostatics, ≥75% median BMI).
cards.result: Higher-calorie refeeding restored medical stability significantly earlier (hazard ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.53, P = .01). The prespecified safety outcome — incidence of electrolyte abnormalities — and other adverse events did not differ by group. Hospital stay was 4.0 days shorter with higher-calorie refeeding (95% CI −6.1 to −1.9 days), associated with savings of $19,056 (95% CI −$28,819 to −$9,293) in hospital charges per participant.
cards.watchOut: One trial, in two specialist US units with protocolised monitoring and electrolyte replacement — the safety finding is 'no excess events under close surveillance', not 'refeeding syndrome cannot happen'; patients below 60% of median BMI, the group at highest refeeding risk, were not enrolled.
cards.source: Garber AK et al. Short-term Outcomes of the Study of Refeeding to Optimize Inpatient Gains for Patients With Anorexia Nervosa: A Multicenter Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA pediatrics. 2021. PMID: 33074282. Registry ID: NCT02488109. cards.headline: Garber 2024 (StRONG atypical-AN analysis): same fixed dose underfed heavier patients — heart-rate restoration 8.7 versus 6.5 days, hypomagnesaemia 29% versus 11%
cards.summary: Garber 2024 (StRONG atypical-AN analysis): same fixed dose underfed heavier patients — heart-rate restoration 8.7 versus 6.5 days, hypomagnesaemia 29% versus 11%
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (Garber 2024, StRONG)
cards.people: The same 111 StRONG participants, comparing the 43% with atypical anorexia nervosa (above 85% of median BMI) against those with anorexia nervosa, and examining caloric dose in kcal/kg body weight as the predictor of refeeding outcomes.
cards.result: Compared with anorexia nervosa, atypical anorexia nervosa had slower heart-rate restoration (8.7 ± 4.0 versus 6.5 ± 3.9 days, p = .008), less weight gain (3.1 ± 5.9 versus 5.4 ± 2.9 %median BMI, p < .001) and more hypomagnesaemia (29% versus 11%, p = .03, OR 3.29). Atypical patients received a lower dose (32.4 ± 6.9 versus 43.4 ± 9.8 kcal/kg, p < .001); for every 10 kcal/kg increase, heart rate was restored 1.7 days faster, weight gain was 1.6 %median BMI greater, and hypomagnesaemia odds were 70% lower (p = .02).
cards.watchOut: This is a within-trial subgroup analysis, not an independent replication — it qualifies the main result (fixed calorie starts underdose heavier patients) rather than confirming it, and the hypomagnesaemia direction (more with relative underfeeding) is a reminder that 'lower calorie' is not automatically 'safer'.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one strong trial — start higher, advance faster, and dose by kilogram, especially in atypical anorexia
cards.summary: Synthesis: one strong trial — start higher, advance faster, and dose by kilogram, especially in atypical anorexia
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: One multicentre randomised trial (StRONG, 120 enrolled, 111 analysed) of higher- versus lower-calorie refeeding in hospitalised adolescents and young adults with anorexia or atypical anorexia nervosa, plus its pre-planned diagnostic-subgroup analysis.

shelves.title: Oral nutritional supplements in hospitalised older people at nutritional risk: mortality RR 0.46 and serious adverse events RR 0.56 in a Cochrane IPD network meta-analysis — low-certainty, and individualised nutritional care showed no mortality effect (RR 0.98)
shelves.question: In hospitalised older people at nutritional risk, do oral nutritional supplements reduce mortality and complications versus usual hospital care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Malnutrition/diet therapy/mortality/prevention & control · Aged · Hospitalization · Aged, 80 and over · Length of Stay · Quality of Life · Bias
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the certainty label doing heavy work. The 2026 Cochrane network meta-analysis of individual participant data (21 randomised trials, 3,309 hospitalised older participants at risk of or with malnutrition; 12 trials contributing IPD for 1,863 participants) found oral nutritional supplements (ONS) may reduce all-cause mortality versus control (RR 0.46; 95% CI 0.25 to 0.84; absolute difference 57 fewer deaths per 1,000 people, 95% CI 79 fewer to 17 fewer; low-certainty evidence) and may reduce serious adverse events (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.95; 84 fewer per 1,000). By contrast, comprehensive individualised nutritional care may show little to no mortality effect (RR 0.98; 95% CI 0.55 to 1.73) and little to no difference in activities of daily living (standardised mean difference 0.06; 95% CI −0.08 to 0.20); for most other comparisons the evidence was very uncertain. Only 16.1% of outcome assessments were at low risk of bias. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the pooled point estimate is large, but it is low-certainty and sits beside a null for the more intensive individualised-care strategy — a combination that should temper, not erase, the claim.

cards.headline: Kiesswetter 2026 Cochrane IPD network meta-analysis: ONS mortality RR 0.46 (0.25–0.84), serious adverse events RR 0.56 (0.32–0.95); individualised care mortality RR 0.98
cards.summary: Kiesswetter 2026 Cochrane IPD network meta-analysis: ONS mortality RR 0.46 (0.25–0.84), serious adverse events RR 0.56 (0.32–0.95); individualised care mortality RR 0.98
cards.type: Cochrane network meta-analysis of individual participant data (Kiesswetter 2026)
cards.people: 21 randomised trials (72 reports) with 3,309 hospitalised older participants (mean ages 75–85 across trials) at risk of or with established malnutrition, with individual participant data obtained for 12 trials (1,863 participants). Interventions: additional protein (3 studies), energy supplements (2), oral nutritional supplements (8), individualised feeding support (2), and comprehensive individualised nutritional care (8), compared mostly with standard care with or without placebo. Main outcome time point: hospital discharge or 30 days after randomisation.
cards.result: Oral nutritional supplements may reduce all-cause mortality versus control (RR 0.46; 95% CI 0.25 to 0.84; absolute risk difference 57 fewer deaths per 1,000 people, 95% CI 79 fewer to 17 fewer; low-certainty evidence) and may reduce serious adverse events (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.95; 84 fewer per 1,000, 95% CI 131 fewer to 10 fewer; low-certainty). Comprehensive individualised nutritional care may show little to no mortality effect (RR 0.98; 95% CI 0.55 to 1.73; 1 fewer per 1,000) and little to no difference in activities of daily living versus control (SMD 0.06; 95% CI −0.08 to 0.20), or versus energy supplements (SMD −0.15; 95% CI −0.53 to 0.23). For all other treatment comparisons the evidence was very uncertain. Only 16.1% of outcome assessments were at low risk of bias (16.8% at high risk).
cards.watchOut: A relative mortality reduction of 54% (RR 0.46) from low-certainty evidence, in trials where the more intensive individualised-care strategy shows RR 0.98, is internally awkward — small-study effects in the 8 ONS trials could be inflating the estimate, and the network's other comparisons are mostly 'very uncertain'. Treat the direction as suggestive and the size as unproven.
cards.source: Kiesswetter E et al. Oral nutritional interventions in hospitalised older people at nutritional risk: a network meta-analysis of individual participant data. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2026. PMID: 41886673. MeSH: Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Malnutrition/diet therapy/mortality/prevention & control · Aged · Hospitalization · Aged, 80 and over · Length of Stay · Quality of Life · Bias

shelves.title: Slower initial feeding to prevent refeeding syndrome in at-risk adults — unproven: no randomised trial compares initial calorie rates in adults; consensus guidance advises starting low, while adult-ward observational series starting at 1,500–2,000 kcal/day reported no attributable refeeding syndrome
shelves.question: In adults at risk of refeeding syndrome, does slower initial calorie introduction reduce complications versus standard feeding advancement?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Energy Intake · Enteral Nutrition/methods · Female · Humans · Incidence · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Magnesium/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Nutrition Assessment · Parenteral Nutrition/methods · Phosphorus/blood · Potassium/blood · Refeeding Syndrome/diagnosis,epidemiology,prevention & control,therapy · Risk Factors · Societies, Medical · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest answer is that the benefit of starting slow is assumed, not demonstrated, in adults. This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1065 covers caloric restriction AFTER refeeding syndrome has developed in critical illness (the Doig trial); the uncovered slice carded here is prevention — the initial feeding rate in adults at risk who do not yet have the syndrome. No randomised trial comparing initial calorie rates in at-risk adults was found in the records fetched. What exists: the ASPEN consensus recommendations (da Silva 2020), which propose a standard definition (a fall of 10–20%, 20–30%, or over 30% in phosphorus, potassium and/or magnesium, or organ dysfunction, within 5 days of reintroducing calories) and risk-stratified avoidance strategies — consensus built explicitly because the underlying literature varies too much to meta-analyse. The comparative data are observational and mostly from eating-disorder care: a scoping review of higher-calorie refeeding (at least 1,500 kcal/day) on adult hospital wards (Taylor 2026; 11 studies, 4,874 patients exposed) found no deaths or clinically defined refeeding syndrome attributable to higher-calorie starts, with hypophosphataemia in up to about a third, usually mild and managed with supplementation; and the one direct lower-versus-higher calorie comparison carded (Schlapfer 2022) is in patients aged 12–21, not adults — severe refeeding syndrome occurred in 4.4% on lower calories versus 2.6% on higher calories (P = .52), with shorter stays on higher calories. Neither direction of the adult question is established; monitoring and electrolyte replacement, not the starting rate alone, are what the observational series share. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: da Silva 2020 (ASPEN consensus): the start-low approach for at-risk patients rests on expert consensus and a proposed standard definition — the task force was convened because the literature was too variable to settle the question
cards.summary: da Silva 2020 (ASPEN consensus): the start-low approach for at-risk patients rests on expert consensus and a proposed standard definition — the task force was convened because the literature was too variable to settle the question
cards.type: Consensus recommendations (da Silva 2020, ASPEN)
cards.people: Hospitalised adult and paediatric populations with or at risk for refeeding syndrome, addressed by an interprofessional ASPEN task force (Parenteral Nutrition Safety Committee and Clinical Practice Committee) developing consensus recommendations through literature review and structured discussion.
cards.result: The group proposes that refeeding syndrome diagnostic criteria be stratified as a decrease in any one, two, or three of serum phosphorus, potassium and/or magnesium by 10–20% (mild), 20–30% (moderate), or over 30% and/or organ dysfunction from such a decrease and/or thiamine deficiency (severe), occurring within 5 days of reintroduction of calories. The recommendations cover recognising risk and identifying, stratifying, avoiding and managing the syndrome; the record describes the process as consensus developed because of variation in definitions and methods in the reported literature — it reports no comparative trial of initial calorie rates, because the underlying evidence base does not contain one.
cards.watchOut: A consensus document is guidance, not evidence: its calorie-initiation advice for at-risk patients reflects expert practice under uncertainty, and this card must never be cited as proof that slower initiation prevents complications — the document's own framing is that the research base is inconsistent.
cards.source: da Silva JSV et al. ASPEN Consensus Recommendations for Refeeding Syndrome. Nutrition in Clinical Practice. 2020. PMID: 32115791. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Taylor 2026: across 11 adult-ward studies (4,874 patients started at 1,500–2,000 kcal/day), no study reported deaths or clinically defined refeeding syndrome attributable to higher-calorie refeeding
cards.summary: Taylor 2026: across 11 adult-ward studies (4,874 patients started at 1,500–2,000 kcal/day), no study reported deaths or clinically defined refeeding syndrome attributable to higher-calorie refeeding
cards.type: Scoping review of adult-ward higher-calorie refeeding studies (Taylor 2026)
cards.people: Adults with a diagnosed eating disorder (or mixed-age samples treated on adult wards) commencing higher-calorie refeeding (at least 1,500 kcal/day) on admission to adult hospital wards, in 11 studies published 2012–2025, mostly retrospective cohorts with three quasi-experimental before-after designs, totalling 4,874 patients exposed to higher-calorie refeeding.
cards.result: No study reported deaths or clinically defined refeeding syndrome attributable to higher-calorie refeeding. Biochemical hypophosphataemia affected up to around one-third of patients, was usually mild, and was managed with electrolyte supplementation. Of four studies reporting length of stay, two found shorter admissions and faster weight gain with higher-calorie than with lower-calorie protocols. The authors conclude higher-calorie initiation appears feasible without an obvious increase in clinical refeeding syndrome when combined with close monitoring and supplementation, while stressing heterogeneity in definitions and protocols and the absence of randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: Eating-disorder wards are a selected, closely monitored slice of 'adults at risk' — young, otherwise medically stable patients with daily electrolytes and supplementation — so safety there does not transfer automatically to malnourished medical, oncological, or post-surgical adults; and a scoping review maps studies rather than pooling a comparative effect.
cards.source: Taylor J et al. Can higher calorie feeding protocols for eating disorder patients admitted to an adult hospital ward be safely implemented to reduce the length of stay? cards.summary: Schlapfer 2022 (ages 12–21 — NOT an adult cohort): severe refeeding syndrome in 4.4% on lower-calorie (<1,300 kcal/day) versus 2.6% on higher-calorie (≥1,400 kcal/day) starts (P = .52); hypophosphataemia was more frequent on lower calories
cards.type: Retrospective cohort comparison of initial calorie prescriptions (Schlapfer 2022) — population aged 12–21, printed on the face
cards.people: 291 paediatric/adolescent and young-adult patients (ages 12–21 years) with eating disorders (anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, eating disorder not otherwise specified, atypical anorexia nervosa) treated with lower-calorie diets (under 1,300 kcal/day, n = 137) or higher-calorie diets (at least 1,400 kcal/day, n = 154). This is the only direct lower-versus-higher initial-calorie comparison with refeeding outcomes found this session, and its population is younger than this shelf's question — printed here on the face.
cards.result: Six patients (4.4%) in the lower-calorie group and four (2.6%) in the higher-calorie group met criteria for severe refeeding syndrome by the ASPEN consensus definition (P = .52) — the difference made no difference statistically. The higher-calorie group had a significantly shorter length of stay (P = .006). Rates of hypomagnesaemia (P = 1) and hypokalaemia (P = .34) did not differ, and hypophosphataemia was significantly more frequent in the lower-calorie group. The authors conclude higher-calorie diets were associated with decreased length of stay without impacting risk of refeeding syndrome.
cards.watchOut: Ages 12–21 and retrospective: this card is evidence about the direction of the comparison in young eating-disorder patients, not about adults, and it is carded only because no adult equivalent exists — the adult answer on this shelf remains untested, which the stamp states.
cards.source: Schlapfer L et al. Impact of caloric prescriptions and degree of malnutrition on incidence of refeeding syndrome and clinical outcomes in patients with eating disorders: A retrospective review. Nutrition in Clinical Practice. 2022. PMID: 34751947. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: slower initial feeding is consensus practice, not tested benefit — no adult trial compares starting rates, and monitored higher-calorie starts in adult eating-disorder wards showed no attributable refeeding syndrome
cards.summary: Synthesis: slower initial feeding is consensus practice, not tested benefit — no adult trial compares starting rates, and monitored higher-calorie starts in adult eating-disorder wards showed no attributable refeeding syndrome
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: The carded evidence: one consensus guideline (ASPEN 2020), one scoping review of adult-ward higher-calorie refeeding (11 studies, 4,874 patients), and one retrospective lower-versus-higher calorie comparison in 291 patients aged 12–21. No randomised trial in at-risk adults is carded, because none was found in the records fetched.
cards.result: ASPEN 2020 standardises the definition and risk stratification on a consensus basis. Taylor 2026 found no deaths or clinically defined refeeding syndrome attributable to starting at 1,500–2,000 kcal/day on adult wards, with mild hypophosphataemia in up to a third. Schlapfer 2022 (ages 12–21) found severe refeeding syndrome in 4.4% (lower calorie) versus 2.6% (higher calorie), P = .52. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Caloric restriction after refeeding syndrome has already developed is a different question with randomised evidence — it homes on live shelf #1065 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. This shelf covers prevention by initial rate only, and its evidence is weak by construction.
cards.source: Synthesis of da Silva JSV et al. Nutrition in Clinical Practice. 2020 (PMID: 32115791); Taylor J et al. Journal of Eating Disorders. 2026 (PMID: 42995639); Schlapfer L et al. Nutrition in Clinical Practice. 2022 (PMID: 34751947).

shelves.title: Fever costs energy: metabolic rate rises by roughly a tenth to an eighth for each 1 °C of fever — about 250 kcal/day per °C in ICU regression data, with sepsis adding a further rise of its own
shelves.question: In humans, by how much does metabolic rate rise for each 1 °C rise in body temperature during fever?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesia · Calorimetry, Indirect/methods · Dobutamine/administration & dosage · Dopamine/administration & dosage · Energy Metabolism · Female · Fentanyl · Humans · Male · Morphine · Multiple Trauma/metabolism · Neuromuscular Blocking Agents/administration & dosage · Sepsis/metabolism,physiopathology · Severity of Illness Index · Trauma Centers
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Every human calorimetry dataset agrees on direction and approximate size: resting energy expenditure climbs as body temperature climbs. Frankenfield's trauma/sepsis regression put the temperature term at +250 kcal/day for each 1 °C — roughly a tenth to an eighth of a typical resting expenditure, matching the classic textbook account (Guyton & Hall present the Du Bois-era fever calorimetry as about a 13% rise in metabolic rate per 1 °C, presented here as the textbook's account: the original Du Bois reports predate abstract-indexed records and no cardable record with per-degree numbers was fetched this session, so no Du Bois card is claimed). Two cautions run through the modern data: sepsis raises expenditure independently of temperature (Bruder), and in already-hypermetabolic patients the fever increment rides on top of an elevated baseline (Gore's burned children). Shivering, sedation and paralysis move the number as much as temperature does, which is why the per-degree figure is an average slope, not a constant of nature.

cards.headline: Frankenfield 1994: in 56 ventilated trauma and sepsis patients measured 423 times, body temperature entered the energy-expenditure regression at +250 kcal/day per °C
cards.summary: Frankenfield 1994: in 56 ventilated trauma and sepsis patients measured 423 times, body temperature entered the energy-expenditure regression at +250 kcal/day per °C
cards.type: Human calorimetry study (indirect calorimetry with clinical-variable regression), JPEN 1994
cards.people: Twenty-six patients with severe trauma and 30 with sepsis, all mechanically ventilated, measured by open-circuit indirect calorimetry every 12 hours for up to 10 days (423 measurements).
cards.result: Mean resting energy expenditure was 36 ± 7 kcal/kg in trauma versus 45 ± 8 kcal/kg in sepsis (P < .0001). The strongest single correlate of expenditure was minute ventilation (R² = 0.61). In the multiple-regression equation (R² = 0.77), body temperature carried a coefficient of +250 kcal/day per °C, alongside minute ventilation, predicted basal expenditure, dobutamine dose and a +300 kcal/day term for the diagnosis of sepsis itself — i.e. fever and the septic state each add their own increment.
cards.watchOut: A regression coefficient across critically ill patients is not a controlled per-degree experiment: temperature covaries with illness severity and drug doses, and the equation was derived in severe trauma/sepsis only. The +250 kcal/day figure is the temperature term holding the other variables constant.
cards.source: Frankenfield DC et al. Correlation between measured energy expenditure and clinically obtained variables in trauma and sepsis patients. JPEN J Parenter Enteral Nutr. 1994. PMID: 7815669. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Bruder 1998: in 24 sedated head-injured patients with 1,919 hourly measurements, body temperature was the main determinant of energy expenditure — and sepsis raised expenditure independently of fever
cards.summary: Bruder 1998: in 24 sedated head-injured patients with 1,919 hourly measurements, body temperature was the main determinant of energy expenditure — and sepsis raised expenditure independently of fever
cards.type: Human calorimetry study (prospective observational, indirect calorimetry), Crit Care Med 1998
cards.people: Twenty-four patients with severe head injury in a neurosurgical intensive care unit; mean arterial pressure, heart rate, body temperature and hourly energy expenditure by indirect calorimetry recorded 1,919 times, across four sedation regimens (fentanyl/midazolam, plus curarisation, thiopental, or no sedation).
cards.result: The expenditure-to-basal ratio was 1.20 ± 0.15 under thiopental, 1.32 ± 0.24 and 1.32 ± 0.20 under fentanyl-based sedation, and 1.60 ± 0.33 unsedated. In sedated patients, energy expenditure correlated significantly with body temperature (P < .0001, r² = .27), and correcting expenditure for temperature abolished the apparent difference between sedation regimens — the low expenditure under thiopental was attributable to its hypothermia. Sepsis significantly increased energy expenditure independently of fever. Heart rate correlated weakly (r² = .13); mean arterial pressure did not.
cards.watchOut: The record reports a correlation, not a per-degree slope, so no °C coefficient is claimed from this card; unsedated patients include shivering and agitation, which inflate expenditure beyond the pure temperature effect.
cards.source: Bruder N et al. Influence of body temperature, with or without sedation, on energy expenditure in severe head-injured patients. Crit Care Med. 1998. PMID: 9504588. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Gore 2003: in 84 burned children, severe fever (≥40 °C) carried a resting expenditure 1.68 times predicted basal versus 1.38 afebrile — about a fifth higher again — with greater muscle protein loss
cards.summary: Gore 2003: in 84 burned children, severe fever (≥40 °C) carried a resting expenditure 1.68 times predicted basal versus 1.38 afebrile — about a fifth higher again — with greater muscle protein loss
cards.type: Human calorimetry study (retrospective analysis of experimental measurements), Arch Surg 2003
cards.people: Eighty-four children aged 2–18 years with burns covering ≥40% of body surface, stratified by rectal temperature at the time of simultaneous indirect calorimetry and leg phenylalanine balance: afebrile <39.0 °C (n = 28), mild fever 39.0–39.4 °C (n = 26), moderate 39.5–39.9 °C (n = 18), severe ≥40.0 °C (n = 12). Groups were similar in age, weight and burn size.
cards.result: Severe fever was associated with significantly higher resting energy expenditure than the afebrile state (expenditure-to-predicted-basal ratio 1.68 ± 0.30 versus 1.38 ± 0.39, P < .05) — a 0.30 absolute difference in the ratio, about 22% higher in relative terms, across a temperature separation of roughly 1–2 °C — and with greater net leg phenylalanine loss (−10.8 ± 7.2 versus −6.0 ± 6.2 mg/min per 100 mL leg volume, P < .05). Plasma glucose and leukocytosis did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional temperature strata in already-hypermetabolic burned children, not a within-child temperature ramp; the per-degree slope implied (~10–20% per °C) is an inference across strata and is labelled as such. Children, not adults.
cards.source: Gore DC et al. Influence of fever on the hypermetabolic response in burn-injured children. Arch Surg. 2003. PMID: 12578413. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Body Temperature · Burns/metabolism · Calorimetry, Indirect · Child · Energy Metabolism · Female · Fever/metabolism · Humans · Male · Muscle Proteins/metabolism · Phenylalanine/metabolism · Retrospective Studies

cards.headline: Synthesis: about a tenth to an eighth more energy per degree of fever — the textbook's ~13% per °C sits inside what ICU calorimetry measures, with sepsis and shivering as separate, additive costs
cards.summary: Synthesis: about a tenth to an eighth more energy per degree of fever — the textbook's ~13% per °C sits inside what ICU calorimetry measures, with sepsis and shivering as separate, additive costs
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human calorimetry studies above (Frankenfield 1994; Bruder 1998; Gore 2003), with the classic figure presented as the Guyton & Hall textbook account of the Du Bois-era fever calorimetry.
cards.result: The carded human data converge on the textbook account: Guyton & Hall present metabolic rate as rising about 13% for each 1 °C of fever (the Du Bois calorimetry tradition), and the modern measurements are consistent with that slope — a +250 kcal/day-per-°C regression term on a resting expenditure of roughly 2,000 kcal/day in Frankenfield's critically ill adults, temperature as the dominant determinant once sedation is accounted for in Bruder's hourly data, and roughly a fifth higher expenditure across the afebrile-to-severe-fever span in Gore's burned children. Two modifiers are part of the physiology, not noise: sepsis adds expenditure independently of temperature, and shivering or its pharmacological suppression swings expenditure by as much as a degree of fever. For feeding calculations the honest statement is a slope of roughly 10–13% per °C above normal, applied to the individual's own baseline.
cards.watchOut: No carded study is a controlled experiment that ramps one person's temperature degree by degree; the per-degree figure is assembled from a regression coefficient, a temperature-correlation analysis and cross-strata comparison, and the classic Du Bois reports themselves were not carded because no abstract-indexed record with per-degree numbers was fetched this session — the 13% figure is carried as the textbook's account, per the physiology rules.
cards.source: Synthesis of Frankenfield DC et al., JPEN 1994 (PMID: 7815669); Bruder N et al., Crit Care Med 1998 (PMID: 9504588); Gore DC et al., Arch Surg 2003 (PMID: 12578413). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: About 20 g of high-quality protein per meal maximises muscle protein synthesis in young adults (~0.24 g/kg) — older adults need about 0.40 g/kg to reach the same plateau, and spreading 20 g doses every 3 hours beats bolus or pulse feeding
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what protein dose per meal maximises muscle protein synthesis, and is the dose–response blunted in older adults?
shelves.mesh: Carbon Isotopes · Cross-Over Studies · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Egg Proteins, Dietary/administration & dosage · Humans · Leucine/metabolism · Male · Muscle Proteins/biosynthesis · Muscle, Skeletal/metabolism · Oxidation-Reduction · Phosphorylation · Serum Albumin/biosynthesis · Weight Lifting/physiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, for the post-exercise per-meal dose question in men. The dose–response is concordant across three tracer programmes: muscle protein synthesis rises with ingested protein to a plateau at 20 g of egg protein (Moore 2009, 6 young men) and 20 g of whey (Witard 2014, 48 men — +49% above the 0 g condition at 20 g, +56% at 40 g, i.e. no meaningful further gain), and a 20 g dose every 3 hours outperforms the same 80 g given as 8 × 10 g or 2 × 40 g over 12 hours of recovery (Areta 2013, 24 men). The age question is answered by Moore's 2015 retrospective dose–response analysis: older men (~71 years) need 0.40 ± 0.19 g/kg per meal to reach the plateau versus 0.24 ± 0.06 g/kg in younger men (~22 years) — a blunted, right-shifted response, not an absent one; basal synthesis rates did not differ. Two limits run through all four cards: every carded dose–response cohort is male, and the 'maximal' dose depends on the muscle mass exercised (whole-body exercise shifted the plateau toward 40 g in one study). Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep (leucine-driven mTORC1 signalling), named as textbook framing. The protein shelves live #935 and pack #5126 ask supplementation outcomes in frail and sarcopenic-older populations — different questions, verified from their files.

cards.headline: Moore 2009: muscle protein synthesis was maximally stimulated at 20 g of egg protein after resistance exercise in 6 young men — more protein was oxidised, not used
cards.summary: Moore 2009: muscle protein synthesis was maximally stimulated at 20 g of egg protein after resistance exercise in 6 young men — more protein was oxidised, not used
cards.type: Human tracer study (randomised crossover, [1-¹³C]leucine infusion), Am J Clin Nutr 2009
cards.people: Six healthy young men on five separate occasions, performing intense leg resistance exercise and then consuming, in random order, 0, 5, 10, 20 or 40 g of whole egg protein, with synthesis measured over 4 hours by primed constant [1-¹³C]leucine infusion. N = 6 — a small classic tracer study, printed plainly under the physiology small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: Muscle protein synthesis displayed a dose response and was maximally stimulated at 20 g; albumin synthesis also plateaued at 20 g. Leucine oxidation was significantly increased after 20 and 40 g ingestion, and phosphorylation of candidate signalling proteins (S6 kinase, S6, eIF2B-epsilon) was not enhanced by any dose — the authors read the stimulation as driven by amino-acid availability, with protein above the plateau simply oxidised.
cards.watchOut: N = 6 young men, leg-only exercise, 4-hour post-exercise window; the 20 g ceiling is specific to this muscle mass and window.
cards.source: Moore DR et al. Ingested protein dose response of muscle and albumin protein synthesis after resistance exercise in young men. Am J Clin Nutr. 2009. PMID: 19056590. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Witard 2014: in 48 resistance-trained young men, 20 g of whey raised myofibrillar synthesis 49% above the no-protein condition and 40 g added nothing further — 40 g raised oxidation and urea production
cards.summary: Witard 2014: in 48 resistance-trained young men, 20 g of whey raised myofibrillar synthesis 49% above the no-protein condition and 40 g added nothing further — 40 g raised oxidation and urea production
cards.type: Human tracer study (randomised dose–response trial, [¹³C₆]phenylalanine infusion), Am J Clin Nutr 2014
cards.people: Forty-eight resistance-trained young men (~80 kg) who ate a standardised high-protein breakfast, performed unilateral leg exercise, and then ingested 0, 10, 20 or 40 g of whey protein isolate, with myofibrillar synthesis and whole-body phenylalanine oxidation and urea production measured over 4 hours by tracer infusion.
cards.result: Myofibrillar synthesis (mean ± SD) rose above the 0 g condition (0.041 ± 0.015%/h) by 49% with 20 g whey and 56% with 40 g (both P < 0.05) — a relative rise of about half, with the 20 g and 40 g conditions not meaningfully different from each other — while 10 g did not stimulate synthesis. Phenylalanine oxidation and urea production increased with 40 g whey: the 20 g dose is sufficient for maximal stimulation in ~80 kg resistance-trained young men, and protein beyond that is oxidised and turned to urea.
cards.watchOut: Young resistance-trained men only; the 49%/56% figures are relative to the 0 g condition and are labelled relative, with the absolute synthesis rate (0.041%/h) beside them. The 20 g ceiling does not transfer to whole-body exercise (see Synthesis).
cards.source: Witard OC et al. Myofibrillar muscle protein synthesis rates subsequent to a meal in response to increasing doses of whey protein at rest and after resistance exercise. Am J Clin Nutr. 2014. PMID: 24257722. Registry ID: ISRCTN92528122 (as on the record). cards.headline: Areta 2013: over 12 hours of recovery, 4 × 20 g of whey every 3 hours stimulated 31–48% more myofibrillar synthesis than 8 × 10 g or 2 × 40 g (24 trained men)
cards.summary: Areta 2013: over 12 hours of recovery, 4 × 20 g of whey every 3 hours stimulated 31–48% more myofibrillar synthesis than 8 × 10 g or 2 × 40 g (24 trained men)
cards.type: Human tracer study (randomised distribution trial, [¹³C₆]phenylalanine infusion), J Physiol 2013
cards.people: Twenty-four healthy trained men in three groups of 8, resistance exercise followed by 80 g of whey protein over 12 hours of recovery as either 8 × 10 g every 1.5 hours (pulse), 4 × 20 g every 3 hours (intermediate) or 2 × 40 g every 6 hours (bolus), with muscle biopsies at rest and 1, 4, 6, 7 and 12 hours.
cards.result: All feeding patterns raised synthesis above rest across 1–12 hours (88–148%, P < 0.02), but the intermediate pattern (20 g every 3 hours) elicited greater synthesis than pulse and bolus (31–48% higher, P < 0.02, relative figures). Signalling showed the opposite hierarchy (bolus > intermediate > pulse) — phosphorylation alone did not predict the synthetic outcome. Twenty grams every 3 hours was superior for stimulating synthesis throughout the day.
cards.watchOut: N = 8 per group, young trained men, 12-hour window only; the 31–48% advantage is relative to the other feeding patterns and is labelled relative. The dose and the distribution are confounded by design (total protein identical, timing different) — the card answers distribution, not total intake.
cards.source: Areta JL et al. Timing and distribution of protein ingestion during prolonged recovery from resistance exercise alters myofibrillar protein synthesis. J Physiol. 2013. PMID: 23459753. cards.headline: Moore 2015: older men (~71 years) needed 0.40 g/kg per meal to reach the synthesis plateau versus 0.24 g/kg in younger men (~22 years) — basal rates were the same, the response was blunted
cards.summary: Moore 2015: older men (~71 years) needed 0.40 g/kg per meal to reach the synthesis plateau versus 0.24 g/kg in younger men (~22 years) — basal rates were the same, the response was blunted
cards.type: Human tracer study (retrospective pooled dose–response analysis), J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2015
cards.people: Retrospective pooled analysis of tracer studies measuring myofibrillar synthesis in healthy older (~71 years) and younger (~22 years) men after ingesting 0–40 g of high-quality protein as a single bolus, with dose normalised to body mass and, where available, lean body mass. The record does not print a total participant number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Basal synthesis rates did not differ (older 0.027 ± 0.04%/h versus young 0.028 ± 0.03%/h, P = 0.53). Breakpoint analysis showed the slope of the first line segment was lower in older men (P < 0.05) and synthesis plateaued after 0.40 ± 0.19 g/kg body mass in older men versus 0.24 ± 0.06 g/kg in younger men (P = 0.055), and 0.60 ± 0.29 versus 0.25 ± 0.13 g/kg lean body mass (P < 0.01) — a right-shifted, blunted dose–response: older men are less sensitive to low intakes and require a greater relative per-meal intake to maximally stimulate synthesis.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective pooling of the group's own studies, men only; the per-body-mass breakpoint difference is borderline (P = 0.055) while the per-lean-mass difference is robust (P < 0.01) — both are printed. N not documented in the record, printed on the face.
cards.source: Moore DR et al. Protein ingestion to stimulate myofibrillar protein synthesis requires greater relative protein intakes in healthy older versus younger men. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2015. PMID: 25056502. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ~20 g (0.24 g/kg) per meal is the young-adult ceiling; older adults are right-shifted to ~0.40 g/kg; and the same daily protein works better as 20 g doses every 3 hours
cards.summary: Synthesis: ~20 g (0.24 g/kg) per meal is the young-adult ceiling; older adults are right-shifted to ~0.40 g/kg; and the same daily protein works better as 20 g doses every 3 hours
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human tracer studies above (Moore 2009; Witard 2014; Areta 2013; Moore 2015), framed by Boron & Boulpaep's account of leucine-driven mTORC1 signalling.
cards.result: The per-meal answer is a plateau, not a staircase: synthesis rises to a ceiling at ~20 g of high-quality protein in young men after leg exercise (Moore; Witard), the ceiling is in absolute grams only when muscle mass and body mass are matched — a whole-body exercise study in the same programme found 40 g superior to 20 g (Macnaughton 2016, cited in prose as a qualification, not carded) — and the distribution matters as much as the dose, with 20 g every 3 hours beating both pulse and bolus patterns (Areta). Ageing blunts the response rather than erasing it: basal synthesis is unchanged, but older men need roughly two-thirds more protein per meal (0.40 versus 0.24 g/kg) to reach their plateau (Moore 2015). The textbook framing (Boron & Boulpaep) is a leucine threshold for mTORC1 activation that rises with age — consistent with the right-shifted curve, and presented as textbook framing.
cards.watchOut: All carded cohorts are men; women's per-meal ceilings and older women's dose–responses are not established by these cards, and acute 4–12-hour tracer synthesis is a surrogate for, not proof of, long-term muscle-mass change. One card is N = 6 and one record prints no N; both are labelled on their faces.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moore DR et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2009 (PMID: 19056590); Witard OC et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2014 (PMID: 24257722); Areta JL et al., J Physiol 2013 (PMID: 23459753); Moore DR et al., J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2015 (PMID: 25056502). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Diet-induced thermogenesis by macronutrient (physiology): protein burns off roughly a fifth to a third of its energy as heat, carbohydrate roughly a twentieth to a tenth, and fat almost none — the ranking protein > carbohydrate > fat is consistent across calorimetry studies
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much extra energy is burned as diet-induced thermogenesis after protein, carbohydrate and fat meals?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Amino Acids/pharmacology · Blood Glucose/analysis · Body Temperature/drug effects · Calorimetry, Indirect · Catecholamines/urine · Diabetes Mellitus/blood,physiopathology,urine · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood,physiopathology · Energy Metabolism · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Insulin/blood · *Insulin Resistance · Obesity/physiopathology · Reference Values
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): digesting, absorbing and storing a meal costs energy — diet-induced thermogenesis (DIT) — and the cost differs sharply by macronutrient. The exact percentages most often quoted (protein 20–30% of its energy, carbohydrate 5–10%, fat 0–3%) are the textbook/synthesis account, stated here as such; the carded records confirm the ranking and anchor the protein end directly. Westerterp's 2004 synthesis puts a mixed diet's DIT at 5–15% of daily energy expenditure with the oxidation hierarchy alcohol > protein > carbohydrate > fat reflected in thermogenesis. Tappy's programme measured infused amino acids at 21.1% of infused energy in lean subjects by indirect calorimetry. Johnston 2002 found postprandial thermogenesis about twofold higher (a relative comparison) on a high-protein than a high-carbohydrate low-fat diet day in 10 young women. Aita 2022 measured all three single-macronutrient-rich meals head-to-head over 2 hours: DIT was 6.44% of ingested energy after the protein meal, 3.49% after carbohydrate and 2.32% after fat — a truncated 2-hour window, so these are lower bounds on the full postprandial totals, with the ranking intact. The ICU-feeding calorimetry shelves ask different questions (energy targets in critical illness) and are not duplicated. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (ranking and approximate magnitudes concordant; exact percentages vary with dose, window and method).

cards.headline: Westerterp 2004: a mixed diet's diet-induced thermogenesis is 5–15% of daily energy expenditure, with the thermogenesis hierarchy running protein above carbohydrate above fat
cards.summary: Westerterp 2004: a mixed diet's diet-induced thermogenesis is 5–15% of daily energy expenditure, with the thermogenesis hierarchy running protein above carbohydrate above fat
cards.type: Synthesis / review of human diet-induced thermogenesis studies (Westerterp synthesis)
cards.people: A synthesis of the human diet-induced thermogenesis literature (measuring conditions, meal energy content and macronutrient composition reviewed); a review, carded as the field's synthesis — no single cohort, N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Most studies measure DIT as the increase in energy expenditure above basal metabolic rate. The hierarchy of macronutrient oxidation in the postprandial state is reflected in DIT, in the sequence alcohol, protein, carbohydrate, fat. A mixed diet consumed at energy balance produces diet-induced energy expenditure of 5 to 15% of daily energy expenditure, with higher values at relatively high protein (and alcohol) consumption and lower values at high fat consumption. The author concludes the main determinants of DIT are the energy content and the protein and alcohol fractions of the diet, and that protein-induced thermogenesis contributes to satiety.
cards.watchOut: A narrative synthesis, not a primary experiment, and its record carries no MeSH list (fallback text used in the source line). Its abstract gives the mixed-diet range and the ranking; the familiar per-nutrient percentages (protein 20–30%, carbohydrate 5–10%, fat 0–3%) come from the wider synthesis/textbook account, not from this abstract.
cards.source: Westerterp KR et al. Diet induced thermogenesis. Nutr Metab (Lond). 2004. PMID: 15507147. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Tappy 1993: the thermic effect of infused amino acids was 21.1% of infused energy in lean healthy subjects — protein's heat cost measured directly
cards.summary: Tappy 1993: the thermic effect of infused amino acids was 21.1% of infused energy in lean healthy subjects — protein's heat cost measured directly
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (amino-acid infusion with indirect calorimetry, Tappy programme)
cards.people: 6 lean healthy subjects, 6 obese nondiabetic subjects and 6 subjects with type 2 diabetes, each infused with glucose (13.9 µmol/kg fat-free mass/min) with or without amino acids (4.2 mg/kg fat-free mass/min), with indirect calorimetry; the healthy-human leg is the 6 lean subjects, N = 6 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: The thermic effect of the infused amino acids, as a percentage of infused energy measured by indirect calorimetry, was 21.1 ± 3.2% in lean subjects, 23.8 ± 1.8% in obese subjects and 20.0 ± 2.9% in subjects with diabetes (no significant difference). The authors conclude the thermic effect of protein is not altered in insulin-resistant patients. For this shelf's healthy-human question, the lean value — about a fifth of protein energy dissipated as heat — is the anchor measurement.
cards.watchOut: Intravenous amino acids, not an eaten protein meal — infusion bypasses gut handling, so the figure anchors protein's metabolic heat cost rather than the exact DIT of dietary protein; small groups (6 per group).
cards.source: Tappy L et al. Thermic effect of infused amino acids in healthy humans and in subjects with insulin resistance. Am J Clin Nutr. 1993. PMID: 8503362. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Johnston 2002: postprandial thermogenesis averaged about twofold higher on a high-protein than a high-carbohydrate low-fat diet day in 10 healthy young women
cards.summary: Johnston 2002: postprandial thermogenesis averaged about twofold higher on a high-protein than a high-carbohydrate low-fat diet day in 10 healthy young women
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (randomised crossover diet-day comparison, indirect calorimetry)
cards.people: 10 healthy, normal-weight, non-smoking women aged 19–22 years in a randomised crossover comparison of one high-protein, low-fat diet day versus one high-carbohydrate, low-fat diet day, with resting energy expenditure measured fasting and 2.5 hours after each meal; N = 10 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: Postprandial thermogenesis at 2.5 hours after meals averaged about twofold higher on the high-protein diet than on the high-carbohydrate diet (a relative comparison), with significant differences after breakfast and dinner (p < 0.05). Body temperature was slightly higher on the high-protein day (p = 0.08 after dinner). Nitrogen balance was greater on the high-protein day (7.6 ± 0.9 versus −0.4 ± 0.5 g N/day; p < 0.05) and next-morning urea nitrogen higher (13.9 ± 0.9 versus 11.2 ± 1.0 mg/dL; p < 0.05). The authors conclude an added energy cost is associated with high-protein, low-fat diets.
cards.watchOut: Whole diet days differing in protein and carbohydrate together, measured at a single 2.5-hour post-meal time point — it gives the protein-versus-carbohydrate contrast (about twofold, relative) rather than absolute per-nutrient percentages.
cards.source: Johnston CS et al. Postprandial thermogenesis is increased 100% on a high-protein, low-fat diet versus a high-carbohydrate, low-fat diet in healthy, young women. J Am Coll Nutr. 2002. PMID: 11838888. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Aita 2022: head-to-head single meals — 2-hour diet-induced thermogenesis was 6.44% of ingested energy for protein, 3.49% for carbohydrate and 2.32% for fat
cards.summary: Aita 2022: head-to-head single meals — 2-hour diet-induced thermogenesis was 6.44% of ingested energy for protein, 3.49% for carbohydrate and 2.32% for fat
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (isocaloric macronutrient meals, respiratory gas analysis)
cards.people: Healthy male participants who underwent FDG-PET brown-fat assessment and 2 hours of respiratory gas analysis after isocaloric carbohydrate-rich, protein-rich or fat-rich meals; N not documented in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Calculated DIT at 2 hours was 6.44 ± 2.01% of ingested energy after the protein-rich meal, 3.49 ± 2.00% after the carbohydrate-rich meal and 2.32 ± 0.90% after the fat-rich meal. DIT after the carbohydrate meal correlated positively with brown adipose tissue activity (p = 0.011) and was about twice as high in the high-BAT group as the low-BAT group (4.35 ± 1.74% versus 2.12 ± 1.76%; p < 0.035), while DIT after fat or protein meals did not correlate with BAT activity. The authors conclude brown fat contributes significantly to DIT after carbohydrate but hardly after protein or fat meals.
cards.watchOut: A 2-hour measurement window captures only part of the postprandial period (protein thermogenesis runs longer), so these percentages are lower bounds, not full-meal totals; participant number is not stated in the record's abstract (N not documented), and the record carries no MeSH list (fallback text used).

cards.headline: Synthesis: protein > carbohydrate > fat in every carded comparison, with protein's heat cost anchored at about a fifth of its energy — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: protein > carbohydrate > fat in every carded comparison, with protein's heat cost anchored at about a fifth of its energy — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Carded human data: the Westerterp 2004 synthesis, 6 lean subjects in the Tappy infusion study, 10 young women in the Johnston crossover, and healthy men in the Aita meal study (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Four concordant legs: the synthesis ranking and 5–15% mixed-diet range; a direct calorimetric protein value of 21.1% of energy; an about-twofold protein-versus-carbohydrate contrast over a diet day; and a head-to-head meal ranking of 6.44% (protein) > 3.49% (carbohydrate) > 2.32% (fat) over 2 hours. Together they support the textbook account (Ganong) that protein burns off roughly a fifth to a third of its energy as diet-induced thermogenesis, carbohydrate roughly a twentieth to a tenth, and fat almost none — with the exact figure depending on dose and measurement window. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Laboratory calorimetry over hours: DIT percentages are not a weight-loss prescription, and meal size, protein dose, insulin resistance and measurement window all move the numbers.
cards.source: Synthesis of Westerterp KR. Nutrition & metabolism. 2004 (PMID: 15507147); Tappy L et al. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 1993 (PMID: 8503362); Johnston CS et al. Journal of the American College of Nutrition. 2002 (PMID: 11838888); Aita S et al. Frontiers in nutrition. 2022 (PMID: 36386942). Textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (energy-balance chapter) — framing, not evidence cards.

shelves.title: Energy expenditure and NEAT (physiology): doubly labelled water puts free-living total expenditure at roughly 7–12 MJ/day depending on body size and activity, and when volunteers were overfed by 1,000 kcal/day, two-thirds of the rise in expenditure came from NEAT — whose activation predicted who resisted fat gain
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is total daily energy expenditure measured by doubly labelled water, and how much does non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) change with overfeeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · *Energy Metabolism · Deuterium Oxide · *Energy Intake · Basal Metabolism · *Movement · Weight Gain · Calorimetry, Indirect
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): total daily energy expenditure is the sum of basal metabolic rate, the thermic effect of food, and activity thermogenesis — the last split into exercise and non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT: posture, fidgeting, and the activities of daily life). Doubly labelled water is the reference method for measuring the total in free-living people: the carded validation study found expenditure by doubly labelled water averaged within 3 ± 6% of intake-balance during parenteral nutrition (Schoeller 1986, the Schoeller programme's validation work). Free-living totals from the carded population studies run from 7.1 MJ/day (about 1,700 kcal/day) in chronically energy-deficient urban men to 11.2 and 12.2 MJ/day (about 2,680 and 2,920 kcal/day) in urban-control and rural men, with physical activity levels (TEE/BMR) of 1.54 to 1.90 (Borgonha 2000), and 9.35 ± 2.00 MJ/day (about 2,235 kcal/day) in a 21-day study of healthy men (Kurpad 1997). The NEAT experiment (Levine 1999): 16 non-obese volunteers overfed by 1,000 kcal/day for 8 weeks increased total expenditure mainly through NEAT — two-thirds of the increase in total daily energy expenditure was due to increased NEAT — and changes in NEAT accounted for the 10-fold differences in fat storage and directly predicted resistance to fat gain (r = 0.77, p < 0.001); the companion report showed leptin rose with fat mass but did not mediate the NEAT activation. The fetched Levine abstract does not print the absolute kcal/day range of NEAT change, so none is claimed here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Schoeller 1986: doubly labelled water agreed with intake-balance to within 3 ± 6% — the validation on which all free-living totals rest
cards.summary: Schoeller 1986: doubly labelled water agreed with intake-balance to within 3 ± 6% — the validation on which all free-living totals rest
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (doubly labelled water validation against intake-balance)
cards.people: 5 patients receiving total parenteral nutrition for at least 10 days before the metabolic period, given oral doses of about 0.1 g ²H₂O and 0.25 g H₂¹⁸O per kg total body water, with saliva and urine sampling over 14 days and energy stores re-estimated from weight change. N = 5 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small validation study).
cards.result: Energy expenditure from doubly labelled water averaged 3 ± 6% greater than intake-balance expenditure. The authors concluded the doubly labelled water method is a noninvasive, nonrestrictive method for measuring energy expenditure in patients receiving parenteral nutrition. Because intake in these patients was fully known and body stores were tracked, this is a true accuracy test of the isotope method rather than a comparison of two estimates — the carded population totals on this shelf inherit this roughly ±6% accuracy scale.
cards.watchOut: Five patients on parenteral nutrition — a population chosen because intake was exactly known, not because it resembles free-living volunteers; the method's assumptions (isotope fractionation, background isotope variation from food and water) were later refined, so 3 ± 6% is the founding accuracy figure, not the last word.
cards.source: Schoeller DA, Kushner RF, Jones PJ. Validation of doubly labeled water for measuring energy expenditure during parenteral nutrition. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 1986. PMID: 3014856. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Levine 1999 (Science): overfeeding by 1,000 kcal/day for 8 weeks — two-thirds of the expenditure rise was NEAT, and NEAT activation predicted the 10-fold range of fat gain
cards.summary: Levine 1999 (Science): overfeeding by 1,000 kcal/day for 8 weeks — two-thirds of the expenditure rise was NEAT, and NEAT activation predicted the 10-fold range of fat gain
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (controlled 8-week overfeeding experiment)
cards.people: 16 non-obese volunteers fed 1,000 kcal per day in excess of weight-maintenance requirements for 8 weeks, with changes in energy storage and in each expenditure component measured (the Levine/Jensen Mayo programme).
cards.result: Two-thirds of the increase in total daily energy expenditure with overfeeding was due to increased nonexercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) — the energy of fidgeting, maintenance of posture and other physical activities of daily life. Changes in NEAT accounted for the 10-fold differences in fat storage that occurred and directly predicted resistance to fat gain with overfeeding (correlation coefficient 0.77, p < 0.001). The authors' conclusion: as humans overeat, activation of NEAT dissipates excess energy to preserve leanness, and failure to activate NEAT may result in ready fat gain. The fetched abstract does not print the absolute kcal/day values of the NEAT change, so this card claims the fraction (two-thirds) and the prediction strength only.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen volunteers in a metabolic-ward overfeeding protocol: NEAT was derived as the residual expenditure component after basal, thermic and exercise components were measured, so its size inherits every other component's measurement error — and 8 weeks of forced overfeeding is not the same exposure as years of free-living positive balance.
cards.source: Levine JA, Eberhardt NL, Jensen MD. Role of nonexercise activity thermogenesis in resistance to fat gain in humans. Science. 1999. PMID: 9880251. Registry ID: none in the record.
