cards.headline: Levine 1999 (JCEM companion): leptin rose with overfeeding but tracked fat mass, not NEAT — leptin does not mediate the NEAT response
cards.summary: Levine 1999 (JCEM companion): leptin rose with overfeeding but tracked fat mass, not NEAT — leptin does not mediate the NEAT response
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (mechanism analysis within the controlled overfeeding experiment)
cards.people: The same 16 non-obese humans studied before and after the 8-week overfeeding protocol, with plasma leptin, adipose-tissue leptin mRNA and the components of energy expenditure measured.
cards.result: Adipocyte leptin expression was up-regulated with overfeeding and leptin concentrations increased; leptin correlated with body fat before and after overfeeding. Changes in leptin with overfeeding were strongly related to changes in body fat, but not to changes in NEAT, while changes in NEAT correlated inversely with fat gain. The authors concluded it is unlikely that leptin mediates activation of NEAT with overfeeding in non-obese humans; rather, leptin directly reflects body fat mass and fat mass gain.
cards.watchOut: A negative mediation result in 16 subjects cannot exclude a modest leptin contribution, and the study is a re-analysis of the same experiment as the Science card — it sharpens the mechanism claim but is not independent evidence for the NEAT effect itself.
cards.source: Levine JA, Eberhardt NL, Jensen MD. Leptin responses to overfeeding: relationship with body fat and nonexercise activity thermogenesis. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 1999. PMID: 10443673. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Borgonha 2000: free-living totals by doubly labelled water were 11.2, 7.1 and 12.2 MJ/day across urban, energy-deficient and rural men (PAL 1.79, 1.54, 1.90)
cards.summary: Borgonha 2000: free-living totals by doubly labelled water were 11.2, 7.1 and 12.2 MJ/day across urban, energy-deficient and rural men (PAL 1.79, 1.54, 1.90)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (free-living doubly labelled water population measurement)
cards.people: 18 healthy south Indian men in three groups of 6: urban controls, urban-slum chronically energy-deficient men (mean BMI 17.0 kg/m²), and rural men (mean BMI 18.1 kg/m²); total energy expenditure and basal metabolic rate measured free-living by doubly labelled water, with whole-body calorimetry comparison in the urban groups.
cards.result: Total energy expenditure by doubly labelled water was 11.2 MJ/day (about 2,680 kcal/day) in urban controls, 7.1 MJ/day (about 1,700 kcal/day) in the chronically energy-deficient group, and 12.2 MJ/day (about 2,920 kcal/day) in rural men; the deficient group's expenditure was significantly lower. Calorimetry gave 10.3 ± 1.6 and 7.3 ± 0.2 MJ/day in the two urban groups — no significant difference between methods, with a mean difference of −0.5 ± 1.1 MJ/day (about 6% of the doubly-labelled-water value). Physical activity level (TEE/BMR) was 1.79, 1.54 and 1.90 respectively: chronically energy-deficient men conserved energy chiefly by reducing activity.
cards.watchOut: Six men per group, all male, at the low end of the body-size range — the absolute MJ/day values describe small, lean men and should not be read as totals for larger Western populations; the kcal/day figures in parentheses are unit conversions of the printed MJ values.
cards.source: Borgonha S, Shetty PS, Kurpad AV. Total energy expenditure & physical activity level in chronically energy deficient Indian males measured by the doubly labelled water technique. Indian Journal of Medical Research. 2000. PMID: 10935321. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Basal Metabolism · Body Water/metabolism · Calorimetry · *Energy Metabolism · Humans · Male

cards.headline: Kurpad 1997: 21 days of doubly labelled water in healthy men gave total expenditure of 9.35 ± 2.00 MJ/day, with 21% variation between individuals
cards.summary: Kurpad 1997: 21 days of doubly labelled water in healthy men gave total expenditure of 9.35 ± 2.00 MJ/day, with 21% variation between individuals
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (free-living doubly labelled water measurement with method comparison)
cards.people: 6 adult, healthy, weight-stable male volunteers (body weights 42.3–70.4 kg) studied over 21 days with multipoint slope-intercept isotope analysis of daily urine samples, basal metabolic rate by indirect calorimetry, and a 7-day activity recall for comparison.
cards.result: Total energy expenditure by the isotopic technique was 9.35 ± 2.00 MJ/day (about 2,235 kcal/day), with an inter-individual variation of 21.4%. Expenditure predicted from measured BMR (5.59 ± 0.99 MJ/day) plus recalled activity (PAL 1.54 ± 0.12) was 8.66 ± 2.20 MJ/day — not significantly different, though the isotopic value ran about 0.7 MJ/day (7.9%) higher. The PAL calculated from measured TEE/BMR varied more between individuals (12.2%) than the recalled PAL (7.9%): questionnaires compress the true spread of free-living expenditure that doubly labelled water reveals.
cards.watchOut: Six men over one 21-day period in one city and season; the study is carded for its directly measured total and its demonstration of between-person spread, not as a normative value for other populations.

cards.headline: Synthesis: doubly labelled water is accurate to a few percent, free-living totals span roughly 7–12 MJ/day with size and activity, and NEAT is the adjustable component that decides who stores overfeeding as fat
cards.summary: Synthesis: doubly labelled water is accurate to a few percent, free-living totals span roughly 7–12 MJ/day with size and activity, and NEAT is the adjustable component that decides who stores overfeeding as fat
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis across Schoeller 1986 (validation, n = 5), Levine 1999 ×2 (overfeeding, n = 16), Borgonha 2000 (n = 18) and Kurpad 1997 (n = 6) — the primary human doubly-labelled-water and NEAT literature carded this session.
cards.result: The method card validates the population cards: doubly labelled water sits within about 3 ± 6% of a known energy balance. Measured totals then scale as physiology predicts — lowest where chronic deficiency has suppressed activity (7.1 MJ/day, PAL 1.54), highest in active rural life (12.2 MJ/day, PAL 1.90). The overfeeding experiment identifies which component moves when intake jumps: NEAT supplied two-thirds of the expenditure increase and its inter-individual variation (r = 0.77 against fat gain) is the mechanism behind the 10-fold range of fat storage on identical overfeeding.
cards.watchOut: The population totals come from small groups of lean Indian men and the NEAT result from 16 ward-studied volunteers; the absolute kcal/day range of NEAT change with overfeeding is not printed in the fetched Levine abstract and is deliberately not claimed on this shelf.

shelves.title: Human brown adipose tissue: present in adults, recruited by cold in nearly everyone, switchable by a β3-agonist — with a measurable but not yet isolated energy cost
shelves.question: In adult humans, how much functional brown adipose tissue is there, how is it activated (cold, β3-agonism), and how much energy can it expend?
shelves.mesh: Adipose Tissue, Brown · Cold Temperature · Energy Metabolism · Positron-Emission Tomography · Thermogenesis · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Three 2009 PET-CT studies established that adult humans carry functional brown adipose tissue (BAT): cold activated it in 23 of 24 healthy men (van Marken Lichtenbelt), biopsy-confirmed UCP1-positive depots from neck to thorax appeared in 7.5% of women and 3.1% of men across 1,972 clinical scans (Cypess — the lower clinical-scan prevalence reflects scanning without deliberate cold stimulation), and cold raised glucose uptake 15-fold in paracervical fat in Virtanen's volunteers. On energy: Ouellet's tracer-PET study in 6 men showed cold-activated BAT oxidative metabolism rises with total energy expenditure and inversely with shivering — BAT is a genuine nonshivering-thermogenesis effector, though the record does not print a single kcal figure for BAT alone. Pharmacological activation works too: a single 200 mg dose of the β3-agonist mirabegron raised BAT activity in all 12 men studied and raised resting metabolic rate by 203 ± 40 kcal/day (+13%) (Cypess 2015). Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall framing (UCP1 uncoupling, sympathetic activation) is named as textbook framing. Small PET groups (5–24) are labelled on the face; absolute BAT mass/energy figures beyond the fetched records are presented as the textbook's account, not as carded data.

cards.headline: van Marken Lichtenbelt 2009: mild cold (16 °C) activated brown fat in 23 of 24 healthy men — activity was lower in overweight/obese men
cards.summary: van Marken Lichtenbelt 2009: mild cold (16 °C) activated brown fat in 23 of 24 healthy men — activity was lower in overweight/obese men
cards.type: Human physiological study (cold-exposure FDG PET-CT), N Engl J Med 2009
cards.people: Twenty-four healthy men (10 lean, BMI <25; 14 overweight or obese, BMI ≥25) studied under thermoneutral conditions (22 °C) and during mild cold exposure (16 °C), with ¹⁸F-FDG PET-CT for BAT activity, DXA body composition and indirect calorimetry.
cards.result: Brown-adipose-tissue activity was observed in 23 of the 24 subjects (96%) during cold exposure but not under thermoneutral conditions, and activity was significantly lower in the overweight or obese subjects than in the lean subjects. Adult men therefore retain cold-recruitable BAT as a near-universal trait, with activity — not mere presence — varying with adiposity.
cards.watchOut: Men only, and 'activity' is FDG uptake under a specific cold protocol — prevalence under other protocols differs (see the Cypess clinical-scan card). The abstract excerpt reports the lean-vs-obese contrast qualitatively; no invented effect size is printed.
cards.source: van Marken Lichtenbelt WD, Vanhommerig JW, Smulders NM, Drossaerts JM, et al. Cold-activated brown adipose tissue in healthy men. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2009. PMID: 19357405. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cypess 2009: across 1,972 patients' clinical PET-CT scans, substantial UCP1-confirmed brown fat depots appeared in 7.5% of women and 3.1% of men
cards.summary: Cypess 2009: across 1,972 patients' clinical PET-CT scans, substantial UCP1-confirmed brown fat depots appeared in 7.5% of women and 3.1% of men
cards.type: Human imaging cohort (retrospective PET-CT series with biopsy confirmation), N Engl J Med 2009
cards.people: Three thousand six hundred and forty consecutive ¹⁸F-FDG PET-CT scans in 1,972 patients performed for various diagnostic reasons, screened for substantial depots (adipose-density tissue >4 mm with maximal FDG uptake ≥2.0 g/mL) from anterior neck to thorax; UCP1 immunostaining performed on neck/supraclavicular biopsies from surgical patients.
cards.result: Positive scans were seen in 76 of 1,013 women (7.5%) and 30 of 959 men (3.1%) — a female:male ratio greater than 2:1 (P < 0.001) — and women had a greater mass of brown adipose tissue. Biopsy tissue from the depot region contained UCP1-immunopositive multilocular adipocytes, confirming the imaging depots are brown fat. Because these scans were not cold-stimulation studies, the percentages are a floor for depot prevalence under ambient clinical conditions, not a measure of maximal recruitable BAT.
cards.watchOut: Clinical scans in patients (not healthy volunteers) without standardised cold exposure — prevalence here and in the cold-challenge studies answer different questions and are not contradictory.
cards.source: Cypess AM, Lehman S, Williams G, Tal I, et al. Identification and importance of brown adipose tissue in adult humans. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2009. PMID: 19357406. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Virtanen 2009: cold increased glucose uptake 15-fold in supraclavicular fat, and biopsies proved UCP1-positive brown adipocytes in healthy adults (N = 5)
cards.summary: Virtanen 2009: cold increased glucose uptake 15-fold in supraclavicular fat, and biopsies proved UCP1-positive brown adipocytes in healthy adults (N = 5)
cards.type: Human physiological study (cold-exposure PET with tissue biopsy), N Engl J Med 2009
cards.people: Five healthy subjects underwent PET during cold exposure; biopsy specimens of the paracervical/supraclavicular adipose tissue were obtained from the first three consecutive subjects for UCP1 mRNA and protein, morphology and biochemical analysis. Very small study — N = 5 (biopsies in 3) printed on the face.
cards.result: Cold-induced glucose uptake was increased by a factor of 15 in paracervical and supraclavicular adipose tissue. Biopsies documented UCP1 mRNA and protein, numerous multilocular intracellular lipid droplets on morphology, and concordant biochemistry — together documenting substantial amounts of metabolically active brown adipose tissue in healthy adult humans. This is the tissue-level proof behind the imaging signals in the larger 2009 studies.
cards.watchOut: N = 5 (biopsy subset 3), printed on the face — carded as the classic tissue-proof study. Glucose uptake is a marker of activation, not a direct measure of heat produced.
cards.source: Virtanen KA, Lidell ME, Orava J, Heglind M, et al. Functional brown adipose tissue in healthy adults. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2009. PMID: 19357407. cards.headline: Ouellet 2012: tracer PET in 6 men — cold-activated BAT oxidative metabolism rose with total energy expenditure and fell as shivering rose (N = 6)
cards.summary: Ouellet 2012: tracer PET in 6 men — cold-activated BAT oxidative metabolism rose with total energy expenditure and fell as shivering rose (N = 6)
cards.type: Human physiological study (multi-tracer PET during cold exposure), J Clin Invest 2012
cards.people: Six healthy men under controlled cold exposure, studied with PET using ¹¹C-acetate (oxidative metabolism), ¹⁸F-FDG (glucose uptake) and ¹⁸F-fluoro-thiaheptadecanoic acid (fatty-acid turnover) in brown fat, skeletal muscle and subcutaneous fat. Small study — N = 6 printed on the face.
cards.result: All subjects showed substantial fatty-acid and glucose uptake on cold exposure. Cold activated oxidative metabolism in BAT but not in adjoining skeletal muscle or subcutaneous adipose tissue; the activation was associated with an increase in total energy expenditure, BAT activity was inversely related to shivering, and BAT radiodensity rose (indicating triglyceride use). The study demonstrates that BAT acts as a nonshivering-thermogenesis effector in humans — while not printing a standalone kcal/day figure attributable to BAT alone, which this shelf therefore does not invent.
cards.watchOut: N = 6, printed on the face. The MeSH 'Animals' tag reflects the journal record's indexing; the carded experiment is the human cold-exposure study described in the abstract.
cards.source: Ouellet V, Labbé SM, Blondin DP, Phoenix S, et al. Brown adipose tissue oxidative metabolism contributes to energy expenditure during acute cold exposure in humans. The Journal of Clinical Investigation. 2012. PMID: 22269323. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cypess 2015: one 200 mg dose of the β3-agonist mirabegron activated BAT in all 12 men and raised resting metabolic rate by 203 ± 40 kcal/day (+13%)
cards.summary: Cypess 2015: one 200 mg dose of the β3-agonist mirabegron activated BAT in all 12 men and raised resting metabolic rate by 203 ± 40 kcal/day (+13%)
cards.type: Human physiological study (single-dose β3-agonist challenge with PET-CT), Cell Metab 2015
cards.people: Twelve healthy male subjects given a single oral 200 mg dose of mirabegron (a β3-adrenergic agonist approved for overactive bladder) versus placebo, with BAT metabolic activity measured by ¹⁸F-FDG PET-CT. Small study — N = 12 printed on the face.
cards.result: Mirabegron led to higher BAT metabolic activity in all twelve subjects (P = 0.001) and increased resting metabolic rate by 203 ± 40 kcal/day (+13%; P = 0.001); BAT metabolic activity significantly predicted the change in resting metabolic rate (P = 0.006). A β3-agonist can therefore stimulate human BAT thermogenesis pharmacologically, without cold — at a dose (200 mg) four times the usual bladder dose, a qualification the record's dose makes explicit.
cards.watchOut: N = 12, single high dose, men only; the +203 kcal/day is whole-body resting metabolic rate change, not BAT-only combustion. The tested product is named as the record names it (mirabegron, Myrbetriq, Astellas) for clarification, per the naming rule.
cards.source: Cypess AM, Weiner LS, Roberts-Toler C, Franquet Elía E, et al. Activation of human brown adipose tissue by a β3-adrenergic receptor agonist. Cell Metabolism. 2015. PMID: 25565203. cards.headline: Synthesis: adults carry real, UCP1-positive brown fat that cold recruits in nearly everyone and a β3-agonist can switch on — its whole-body energy signal is measurable, its standalone calorie burn is not yet pinned down
cards.summary: Synthesis: adults carry real, UCP1-positive brown fat that cold recruits in nearly everyone and a β3-agonist can switch on — its whole-body energy signal is measurable, its standalone calorie burn is not yet pinned down
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the five carded human studies above (van Marken Lichtenbelt 2009; Cypess 2009; Virtanen 2009; Ouellet 2012; Cypess 2015), framed by the Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall account of UCP1-mediated nonshivering thermogenesis as textbook framing.
cards.result: Amount: depots run from anterior neck to thorax; without cold stimulation they are detectable in 7.5% of women and 3.1% of men on clinical scans, but with mild cold (16 °C) activity appears in 96% of healthy men — presence is common, activity is state-dependent, and activity falls with adiposity. Identity is proven at tissue level (UCP1-positive multilocular adipocytes; 15-fold cold-induced glucose uptake). Activation: cold is the physiological switch; a single 200 mg mirabegron dose is the pharmacological proof, raising resting metabolic rate 203 ± 40 kcal/day (+13%) with BAT activity predicting the rise. Energy: BAT oxidative metabolism tracks total cold-induced expenditure and substitutes for shivering (Ouellet), but no carded record isolates a BAT-only kcal/day figure — larger textbook estimates of BAT's maximal contribution are presented as the textbook's account (Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep framing), not as measured human data.
cards.watchOut: FDG uptake indexes activation, not heat; extrapolating scan signals to daily calorie burn is the common overreach this shelf avoids. No animal BAT data are carded.

shelves.title: Albumin synthesis regulation in humans: ~7% of the pool replaced daily — doubled by protein loss, raised by feeding, suppressed by inflammation
shelves.question: In humans, how is the albumin synthesis rate regulated — what do tracer studies show about the effects of oncotic pressure, inflammation, nutrition and nephrotic-range protein loss on hepatic albumin synthesis?
shelves.mesh: Serum Albumin · Leucine · Nephrotic Syndrome · Renal Dialysis · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for synthesis-rate regulation as measured by human tracer studies (this shelf is deliberately NOT about low albumin as a prognostic marker). The measurement exists and is reproducible: Ballmer 1990's flooding-dose [¹³C]leucine method gave a fractional synthesis rate of 7.2 ± 1.3%/day and absolute synthesis of 157 ± 39 mg/kg/day in healthy postabsorptive men. Regulation, from the carded human studies: (1) protein loss — in nephrotic adults, absolute albumin synthesis more than doubled (160 ± 19 vs 71 ± 4 mg/kg/day) in proportion with fibrinogen synthesis, without raised CRP or serum amyloid A (de Sain-van der Velden/Kaysen 1998, N = 7 + 8) — a coordinated hepatic response to loss, not an acute-phase artefact; (2) nutrition — raising dietary protein in nephrotic patients raised synthesis from 12.61 ± 1.20 to 17.60 ± 1.25 g/1.73 m²/day (Kaysen 1987, n = 13), though serum albumin and lipids barely moved because losses rose too; (3) inflammation — in 79 HEMO haemodialysis patients followed with repeat kinetic measurements, a fall in albumin synthesis accompanied a stable >0.3 g/dL decline in serum albumin and tracked rising α1-acid glycoprotein (Kaysen 2004). Oncotic pressure: the classic hypothesis that falling plasma oncotic pressure directly signals hepatic albumin synthesis is presented as the textbook's account (Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall framing) — the fetched human records demonstrate the loss/nutrition/inflammation limbs directly and do not isolate an oncotic-pressure signal, and the shelf says so rather than dressing the hypothesis as measured fact. Small tracer groups are labelled on the face.

cards.headline: Ballmer 1990: the human albumin synthesis measurement — flooding-dose [¹³C]leucine gave FSR 7.2 ± 1.3%/day and absolute synthesis 157 ± 39 mg/kg/day in healthy men
cards.summary: Ballmer 1990: the human albumin synthesis measurement — flooding-dose [¹³C]leucine gave FSR 7.2 ± 1.3%/day and absolute synthesis 157 ± 39 mg/kg/day in healthy men
cards.type: Human tracer methods study (stable-isotope albumin synthesis), Am J Physiol 1990
cards.people: Healthy postabsorptive males given a rapid intravenous flooding dose of [¹³C]leucine (57 mg/kg, 19.4 atoms%), with plasma sampling to 90 minutes and liver-biopsy enrichment measured in surgical patients; albumin fractional synthesis rate (FSR) calculated from leucine enrichment incorporated into albumin by gas isotope-ratio mass spectrometry. The record does not print the volunteer number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Plasma free-leucine enrichment peaked at 10 minutes; liver enrichment ran at 101.5–80.5% of the plasma value between 10 and 90 minutes. The FSR of albumin was 7.2 ± 1.3%/day and the absolute synthesis rate 157 ± 39 mg/kg/day — rates comparable to those obtained by other (radioisotope) methods, achieved with a stable-isotope technique usable in most clinical conditions, even while albumin losses are occurring or when repeated assessment is required. This is the yardstick every regulation study on this shelf is measured with.
cards.watchOut: A methods record: its values are healthy postabsorptive reference rates. N not documented in the record, printed on the face.
cards.source: Ballmer PE, McNurlan MA, Milne E, Heys SD, et al. Measurement of albumin synthesis in humans: a new approach employing stable isotopes. The American Journal of Physiology. 1990. PMID: 2260648. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). MeSH: Adult · Carbon Isotopes · Humans · Isotope Labeling · Kinetics · Leucine · Liver · Male · Reference Values · Serum Albumin

cards.headline: de Sain-van der Velden & Kaysen 1998: in nephrotic adults, albumin synthesis more than doubled (160 vs 71 mg/kg/day) in proportion with fibrinogen — a coordinated response to urinary loss, without inflammation markers raised (N = 7 + 8)
cards.summary: de Sain-van der Velden & Kaysen 1998: in nephrotic adults, albumin synthesis more than doubled (160 vs 71 mg/kg/day) in proportion with fibrinogen — a coordinated response to urinary loss, without inflammation markers raised (N = 7 + 8)
cards.type: Human tracer study (stable-isotope protein synthesis in nephrotic syndrome), Kidney Int 1998
cards.people: Seven nephrotic adults (plasma albumin 22.3 ± 0.7 g/L, i.e. about 2.2 g/dL; proteinuria 12 g/day) and 8 healthy controls, studied with a primed/continuous 6-hour infusion of L-[1-¹³C]valine to measure fibrinogen and albumin synthesis rates. Small tracer study — groups of 7 and 8 printed on the face.
cards.result: Absolute synthesis rate (ASR) of albumin was 160 ± 19 mg/kg/day in nephrotic patients vs 71 ± 4 in controls (P < 0.0001), and ASR of fibrinogen was 31 ± 3 vs 21 ± 1 mg/kg/day (P < 0.05); the two synthesis rates were strongly correlated (P = 0.0046). Plasma α2-macroglobulin was also elevated and correlated with albumin synthesis rate, whereas serum amyloid A and C-reactive protein were NOT elevated. The liver's answer to urinary protein loss is thus a specific, coordinated up-regulation of a group of plasma proteins including albumin — synthesis rises to meet loss (though not enough to normalise the level), and the rise is not driven by a measurable acute-phase response in these patients.
cards.watchOut: N = 7 + 8, printed on the face. Cross-sectional patient-vs-control contrast; the trigger signal for the coordinated response (oncotic pressure vs another loss sensor) is not isolated by this design — see the balance.
cards.source: de Sain-van der Velden MGM, Kaysen GA, de Meer K, Stellaard F, et al. Proportionate increase of fibrinogen and albumin synthesis in nephrotic patients: measurements with stable isotopes. Kidney International. 1998. PMID: 9453016. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kaysen 1987: raising dietary protein in nephrotic patients raised albumin synthesis from 12.6 to 17.6 g/1.73 m²/day — but serum albumin and lipids barely changed because losses rose too (n = 13)
cards.summary: Kaysen 1987: raising dietary protein in nephrotic patients raised albumin synthesis from 12.6 to 17.6 g/1.73 m²/day — but serum albumin and lipids barely changed because losses rose too (n = 13)
cards.type: Human tracer/metabolic study (albumin synthesis under dietary protein manipulation), Kidney Int 1987
cards.people: Thirteen nephrotic patients in whom albumin synthesis rate, urinary albumin loss and serum albumin, protein, cholesterol and triglycerides were measured; in 8 of them, changes in synthesis and urinary excretion were induced by altering dietary protein intake, with multiple regression analysis of the responses.
cards.result: On a low-protein diet, albumin synthesis was 12.61 ± 1.20 g/1.73 m²/day — within normal limits — despite markedly elevated serum triglycerides (265 ± 65 mg/dL) and cholesterol (325 ± 44 mg/dL). When dietary protein was increased, synthesis rose to 17.60 ± 1.25 g/1.73 m²/day, while triglycerides (306 ± 75 mg/dL) and cholesterol (376 ± 55 mg/dL) changed little. Nutrition therefore does drive albumin synthesis in humans, measurably and within days — but in nephrotic syndrome the extra albumin is largely lost in urine, which is why feeding alone does not restore the serum level.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen patients (8 in the diet-manipulation limb). Synthesis units (g/1.73 m²/day) are the record's own and differ from the mg/kg/day scaling of the other cards — not interchangeable without conversion.
cards.source: Kaysen GA, Gambertoglio J, Felts J, Hutchison FN. Albumin synthesis, albuminuria and hyperlipemia in nephrotic patients. Kidney International. 1987. PMID: 3613408. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Kaysen 2004 (HEMO): when haemodialysis patients' serum albumin fell by >0.3 g/dL, albumin synthesis fell with it — and the fall tracked rising α1-acid glycoprotein (inflammation), in 79 patients with repeat kinetic studies
cards.summary: Kaysen 2004 (HEMO): when haemodialysis patients' serum albumin fell by >0.3 g/dL, albumin synthesis fell with it — and the fall tracked rising α1-acid glycoprotein (inflammation), in 79 patients with repeat kinetic studies
cards.type: Human kinetic cohort study (repeat albumin synthesis measurement, HEMO), Kidney Int 2004
cards.people: Seventy-nine patients in the NIH-sponsored HEMO Study with baseline albumin synthesis measured kinetically ([¹²⁵I] human serum albumin disappearance), serum albumin, transferrin, CRP, α1-acid glycoprotein (α1AG), ceruloplasmin and IL-6, plus monthly equilibrated normalised protein catabolic rate (enPCR) over 2 years; synthesis re-measured when albumin fell >0.3 g/dL on two sequential measurements or at 2 years. Fifty-nine patients (21 decliners, 38 stable) had synthesis measured twice.
cards.result: A decline in albumin concentration and synthesis was associated with an increase in α1AG when data from all patients were analysed — the study's design question answered in the affirmative: falling serum albumin in stable dialysis patients is accompanied by reduced synthesis, and the reduction is associated with increased acute-phase protein levels (inflammation), rather than being explained by protein intake (enPCR) alone. This is the inflammation limb of synthesis regulation, measured kinetically in humans: inflammation suppresses albumin synthesis even when the serum level moves only modestly.
cards.watchOut: Observational within a trial cohort: inflammation and synthesis move together; the design associates, it does not randomise inflammation. The fetched abstract is truncated at the α1AG finding, so no CRP/IL-6 effect sizes are printed here.
cards.source: Kaysen GA, Dubin JA, Müller HG, Rosales L, et al. Inflammation and reduced albumin synthesis associated with stable decline in serum albumin in hemodialysis patients. Kidney International. 2004. PMID: 15086482. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: albumin synthesis is a regulated hepatic output — roughly 7%/day at baseline, doubled by protein loss, raised by feeding, suppressed by inflammation
cards.summary: Synthesis: albumin synthesis is a regulated hepatic output — roughly 7%/day at baseline, doubled by protein loss, raised by feeding, suppressed by inflammation
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human tracer studies above (Ballmer 1990; de Sain-van der Velden & Kaysen 1998; Kaysen 1987; Kaysen 2004), framed by the Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall account of plasma-protein synthesis and oncotic pressure as textbook framing.
cards.result: Baseline: a healthy liver replaces about 7.2% of the albumin pool daily (≈157 mg/kg/day) by the stable-isotope measurement. Loss: urinary protein loss more than doubles absolute synthesis (160 vs 71 mg/kg/day), coordinately with fibrinogen and without an acute-phase signature — a specific response to loss. Nutrition: dietary protein raises synthesis within days (12.6 → 17.6 g/1.73 m²/day), though in nephrotic patients the increment leaks out in urine. Inflammation: in dialysis patients, synthesis falls as α1-acid glycoprotein rises and serum albumin drifts down — suppression, the mirror image of the loss response. The oncotic-pressure hypothesis — that the liver senses falling plasma colloid oncotic pressure and answers with synthesis — is the textbook's framing for the loss response (Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall); the fetched human records establish the response itself but do not isolate oncotic pressure as the measured signal, and this shelf presents it exactly that way. Nothing here is about albumin as a prognostic blood test — that is a different shelf family by design.
cards.watchOut: Tracer cohorts are small (7–13) except HEMO (79); synthesis units differ between records and are kept in each record's own scaling. No animal albumin-regulation data are carded.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 2260648, 9453016, 3613408, 15086482), with Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall textbook framing. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Whole-body protein turnover: feeding balances protein chiefly by suppressing breakdown
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are whole-body protein synthesis, breakdown and net balance rates in the fasted and fed states, measured by leucine/nitrogen tracer kinetics — and how do feeding and age change the balance chiefly through synthesis or breakdown?
shelves.mesh: Protein Biosynthesis · Proteins/metabolism · Leucine/metabolism · Fasting · Aging/metabolism · Nitrogen/metabolism · Kinetics · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of protein metabolism — a body protein pool in continuous turnover, with insulin and amino-acid supply shifting the balance between synthesis and proteolysis — the tracer literature is concordant on the central mechanism. In a classic leucine-infusion study (N = 6, printed plainly), feeding achieved positive leucine balance by cutting degradation from 89.5 to 31.7 µmol/kg/h with no apparent change in synthesis in the short-infusion protocol. In 12 elderly women, meal feeding likewise increased flux and oxidation and decreased breakdown, with no effect of feeding on synthesis. The largest dataset (91 young and 66 older adults, phenylalanine/tyrosine tracers) found basal turnover higher, not lower, with age — older adults had greater synthesis and breakdown and a less negative net balance — and women had higher turnover than men at every age. The settled teaching: in the acute fed/fasted transition the lever is breakdown suppression; protocol duration and tracer recycling can manufacture apparent synthesis effects, which is why the classic paper's own methodological warning belongs on the face. Cross-point: the per-meal muscle protein synthesis dose–response is a different, muscle-level quantity, shelved separately.

cards.headline: Melville 1989 (N = 6, printed plainly): feeding cut leucine degradation from 89.5 to 31.7 µmol/kg/h with no apparent change in synthesis
cards.summary: Melville 1989 (N = 6, printed plainly): feeding cut leucine degradation from 89.5 to 31.7 µmol/kg/h with no apparent change in synthesis
cards.type: Tracer kinetic study (L-[1-13C]leucine infusion), fed versus fasted
cards.people: Six healthy adult volunteers (N = 6 — a classic small tracer study, labelled plainly per the reference-floor rule) studied with L-[1-13C]leucine infusion under 8-hour (4 h post-absorptive then 4 h mixed feeding) and 24-hour (12 h feeding, 12 h fasting) protocols.
cards.result: In the 8-hour protocol, moving from the post-absorptive state to mixed feeding produced positive leucine balance by decreasing degradation from 89.5 ± 5.0 to 31.7 ± 7.3 µmol leucine/kg/h (P < 0.001), with no apparent change in synthesis. In the 24-hour protocol, estimated synthesis during feeding appeared 35% higher than during fasting (P < 0.01) — but when infusion was limited to the last 4 hours of each period, synthesis estimates did not differ (71.3 ± 6.5 fed vs 66.2 ± 5.6 µmol/kg/h fasted) while degradation was 43% lower during feeding (P < 0.002). Residual tracer was still detectable in breath and plasma 12 hours after a 12-hour infusion ended, supporting the authors' conclusion that label recycling inflates synthesis estimates in prolonged infusions.
cards.watchOut: N = 6. The study's enduring value is as much methodological as numerical: apparent feeding effects on synthesis depend on infusion design, and later work must be read with the recycling warning in mind.
cards.source: Melville S et al. The role of degradation in the acute control of protein balance in adult man: failure of feeding to stimulate protein synthesis as assessed by L-[1-13C]leucine infusion. Metabolism. 1989. PMID: 2493121. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pannemans 1998: in 12 elderly women, feeding raised flux and oxidation and lowered breakdown — again with no effect on synthesis
cards.summary: Pannemans 1998: in 12 elderly women, feeding raised flux and oxidation and lowered breakdown — again with no effect on synthesis
cards.type: Tracer and nitrogen-balance study across three controlled diets
cards.people: 12 elderly women consuming three 2-week diets differing in protein quantity and source (animal/vegetable splits of energy from protein), with nitrogen balance and 4-hour fasted / 4-hour fed protein-turnover measurements at the end of each period.
cards.result: Mean nitrogen balance did not differ significantly from zero on the two higher-protein diets and was not affected by protein source. Meal feeding resulted in increased protein flux and protein oxidation and decreased protein breakdown compared with post-absorptive values; there was no effect of feeding on protein synthesis. Protein source mattered for the breakdown lever: on the high-vegetable-protein diet, breakdown in the absorptive state was not inhibited to the same extent as on the high-animal-protein diet, resulting in less net protein synthesis (net balance) during the vegetable-protein diet.
cards.watchOut: Twelve women, one sex and one age band, with 2-week diet periods: the feeding mechanism generalises cautiously, and the source comparison is between the specific diets tested, not all animal versus all vegetable proteins.
cards.source: Pannemans DLE et al. Effect of protein source and quantity on protein metabolism in elderly women. Am J Clin Nutr. 1998. PMID: 9846851. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hirsch 2020: in 157 adults, basal turnover was higher in older than young adults — synthesis +28.5 and breakdown +15.4 mg/kg lean mass/h — and higher in women than men
cards.summary: Hirsch 2020: in 157 adults, basal turnover was higher in older than young adults — synthesis +28.5 and breakdown +15.4 mg/kg lean mass/h — and higher in women than men
cards.type: Cross-sectional basal tracer-kinetic comparison by age and sex
cards.people: 91 younger (18–38 years; 52% female) and 66 older (51–81 years; 53% female) healthy adults; basal whole-body protein kinetics measured with L-[ring-2H5]phenylalanine and L-[ring-2H2]tyrosine tracers, plus muscle fractional synthetic rate.
cards.result: There were no group-by-sex interactions. Older individuals had greater whole-body protein synthesis (mean difference old − young 28.54 ± 8.15 mg/kg lean body mass/h; P = 0.001) and breakdown (15.44 ± 7.33 mg/kg lean body mass/h; P = 0.038), but a less negative net balance (older −18.11 ± 21.60 vs young −31.22 ± 7.42 mg/kg lean body mass/h; P < 0.001). Basal muscle fractional synthetic rate did not differ significantly by age (difference 0.007 ± 0.003%/h; P = 0.052). Across the age range, females had greater whole-body turnover than males (synthesis difference 19.10 ± 7.00 and breakdown difference 19.22 ± 6.31 mg/kg lean body mass/h; P < 0.01). The authors interpret the pattern as an age-related shift toward more efficient amino-acid reutilisation.
cards.watchOut: Basal (fasted) measurements only, cross-sectional: the age contrast mixes cohort and ageing effects, and whole-body rates — dominated by visceral turnover — must not be read as muscle protein kinetics, which this same study found age-stable at the fractional level.
cards.source: Hirsch KR et al. Comparison of basal whole-body protein kinetics and muscle protein synthesis between young and older adults. Physiol Rep. 2020. PMID: 33278070. cards.headline: Synthesis: the fed-state lever is breakdown suppression; ageing raises basal turnover rather than slowing it
cards.summary: Synthesis: the fed-state lever is breakdown suppression; ageing raises basal turnover rather than slowing it
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Three primary human tracer datasets (N = 6 classic leucine study; 12 elderly women across controlled diets; 157 adults in a basal age/sex comparison). Framing follows Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of protein turnover and its hormonal control, as textbook context, not as an evidence card. Cross-point: the per-meal dose–response of muscle protein synthesis is a fractional, muscle-level quantity shelved separately — it does not answer this whole-body question.
cards.result: Two independent feeding studies, a decade and two tracer designs apart, found the same acute mechanism: feeding moves whole-body balance positive chiefly by suppressing protein breakdown (in the classic study, degradation roughly halved-to-thirded, 89.5 to 31.7 µmol/kg/h), with oxidation rising and no consistent acute stimulation of whole-body synthesis once tracer recycling is controlled. Basal turnover does not fall with age: older adults turned protein over faster and ran a less negative basal net balance than the young, and women turned over more than men — patterns that reframe sarcopenia as a problem of anabolic response and muscle-specific kinetics rather than of a slowing whole-body engine.
cards.watchOut: Tracer, infusion duration, feeding composition and normalisation (per kg body weight vs per kg lean mass) all move the numbers; cross-study rate comparisons are protocol-bound, and the smallest study (N = 6) is labelled as such on its card. No anchor in this pack was refused: every carded record had a verifiable abstract this session.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Resting metabolic rate: prediction equations fit groups but miss individuals by ±300–450 kcal/day — Mifflin–St Jeor and Oxford lead on individual accuracy, indirect calorimetry is the reference
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is resting metabolic rate measured by indirect calorimetry by age, sex and body composition — and how accurate are the standard prediction equations (Mifflin–St Jeor, Harris–Benedict, Schofield) against measured values in non-obese and obese adults?
shelves.mesh: Basal Metabolism · Calorimetry, Indirect · Energy Metabolism · Body Mass Index · Predictive Value of Tests
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the verdict on equation accuracy, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on metabolic rate and energy balance as textbook framing, not as an evidence card. The settled finding is about the equations, and it is consistent across a systematic review and two primary validation studies using different calorimetry rigs: no standard equation is accurate at the individual level. The systematic review found Mifflin–St Jeor the most reliable of the four common equations, predicting resting metabolic rate within 10% of the indirect-calorimetry measurement in more nonobese and obese individuals than Harris–Benedict, Owen or WHO/FAO/UNU, with the narrowest error range — while noting older adults and US ethnic minorities were underrepresented in both development and validation (Frankenfield 2005). Against a gas-exchange-corrected reference measurement, all 13 equations correlated well yet overpredicted on average by 89–312 kcal/day; the Mifflin, Oxford and Müller equations were within 200 kcal/day for over 60% of individuals, and only the Oxford equations performed better in both sexes separately (Galgani 2018, N = 69). In a smaller cross-validation the ranking flipped at group level — Harris–Benedict and WHO had the lowest mean bias (−14 and −25 kcal/day) — yet every equation's individual limits of agreement were moderate to large (about ±314 to ±445 kcal/day), and equations underestimated progressively as fat-free mass rose (Flack 2016, N = 30). That disagreement on which equation 'wins' at group level, alongside unanimity that individual error stays large, is exactly what the cards show: group means can look right while the person in front of you is off by several hundred kilocalories. Cross-points, not duplicated: the doubly-labelled-water shelf asks total daily expenditure, and the diet-induced thermogenesis shelf asks the post-meal rise — this shelf asks the resting rate and its estimation.

cards.headline: Frankenfield 2005 (systematic review): Mifflin–St Jeor is the most reliable of the four common equations — within 10% of measured RMR in more nonobese and obese individuals, with the narrowest error range
cards.summary: Frankenfield 2005 (systematic review): Mifflin–St Jeor is the most reliable of the four common equations — within 10% of measured RMR in more nonobese and obese individuals, with the narrowest error range
cards.type: Systematic review (RMR prediction equations vs indirect calorimetry), J Am Diet Assoc 2005
cards.people: Systematic review of published validation studies comparing predictive equations against indirect calorimetry in nonobese and obese people and in various ethnic and age groups, restricted to reports of individual-level data and graded with American Dietetic Association evidence-analysis tools; the four equations in common clinical use were Harris–Benedict, Mifflin–St Jeor, Owen and WHO/FAO/UNU.
cards.result: The Mifflin–St Jeor equation was the most reliable, predicting resting metabolic rate within 10% of measured in more nonobese and obese individuals than any other equation, and it had the narrowest error range. No validation work concentrating on individual errors was found for the WHO/FAO/UNU equation. Older adults and US-residing ethnic minorities were underrepresented in both equation development and validation. The panel's conclusion: noteworthy errors persist when any equation is applied to individuals, and valid indirect-calorimetry measurement eliminates estimation error when an estimate fails a patient in a clinically relevant way.
cards.watchOut: A review of validation studies, carded as the synthesis it is; its 'most reliable' verdict is about the proportion of individuals within 10%, not about group-mean bias — the primary cards below use bias and limits of agreement, a different and complementary yardstick.

cards.headline: Galgani 2018: against gas-exchange-corrected calorimetry in 69 healthy adults, all 13 equations overpredicted RMR on average (89–312 kcal/day); Oxford equations performed best in both sexes
cards.summary: Galgani 2018: against gas-exchange-corrected calorimetry in 69 healthy adults, all 13 equations overpredicted RMR on average (89–312 kcal/day); Oxford equations performed best in both sexes
cards.type: Human primary validation study (RMR equations vs corrected indirect calorimetry), Clin Sci 2018
cards.people: Sixty-nine healthy volunteers (29 men, 40 women; age 32 ± 8 years; body mass index 25.5 ± 3.8 kg/m2) whose resting metabolic rate was measured by indirect calorimetry and then corrected by simulating gas exchange with pure gases and high-precision mass-flow regulators; 13 published equations were compared with that corrected reference by Bland–Altman analysis.
cards.result: All equations correlated well with the reference (r > 0.67, P < 0.0001) but on average overpredicted it by 89–312 kcal/day (P < 0.05). Twelve equations showed a constant bias across the RMR range, not significantly different from zero for nine of them. Three equations — Mifflin, Oxford and Müller — had an absolute predicted-minus-reference difference of 200 kcal/day or less in over 60% of individuals; of those, only the Oxford equations performed better in both men and women separately. The authors conclude the Oxford equations are a valid alternative in healthy adults and that gas-exchange correction is good practice for reliable RMR assessment.
cards.watchOut: The reference itself was corrected for calorimeter error — part of the apparent equation bias in the wider literature is instrument error, which is this study's methodological point. Young, mildly overweight sample (mean BMI 25.5); older and leaner populations are thinner ground.
cards.source: Galgani JE, Castro-Sepulveda M, Pérez-Luco C, Fernández-Verdejo R. Validity of predictive equations for resting metabolic rate in healthy humans. Clinical science (London, England : 1979). 2018. PMID: 29967004. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Flack 2016: in 30 adults, Harris–Benedict and WHO had the lowest group bias (−14 and −25 kcal/day) — yet every equation's individual limits of agreement ran to ±314–445 kcal/day, worsening as fat-free mass rose
cards.summary: Flack 2016: in 30 adults, Harris–Benedict and WHO had the lowest group bias (−14 and −25 kcal/day) — yet every equation's individual limits of agreement ran to ±314–445 kcal/day, worsening as fat-free mass rose
cards.type: Human primary cross-validation study (RMR equations vs indirect calorimetry), J Acad Nutr Diet 2016
cards.people: Thirty men and women aged 18–65 years from Grand Forks, North Dakota (body mass index 19–39, nonobese and obese, primarily white), studied in spring/summer 2014; predicted resting metabolic rate from the Harris–Benedict, WHO, Mifflin–St Jeor, Nelson and Wang equations and three Sabounchi meta-equations was compared with indirect calorimetry by Bland–Altman bias and limits of agreement.
cards.result: Bias (mean ± 2 SD) was lowest for Harris–Benedict (−14 ± 378 kcal/24 h) and WHO (−25 ± 394 kcal/24 h), the two equations whose predictions did not differ significantly from measured values; all other equations' mean predictions differed significantly. But the 2-SD limits of agreement were moderate or large for every equation (314–445 kcal/24 h) — group-level accuracy coexisted with poor individual accuracy. Prediction bias was inversely associated with the magnitude of RMR and with fat-free mass: as fat-free mass increased, the equations further underestimated RMR.
cards.watchOut: N = 30 and primarily white — the fat-free-mass finding is a within-sample association, not a correction formula. Its group-level winner (Harris–Benedict) differs from the other cards' winners; the shelf reports the disagreement rather than crowning one equation.
cards.source: Flack KD, Siders WA, Johnson L, Roemmich JN. Cross-Validation of Resting Metabolic Rate Prediction Equations. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. 2016. PMID: 27138231. cards.headline: Synthesis: equations estimate group RMR adequately but miss individuals by hundreds of kcal/day — Mifflin–St Jeor/Oxford lead on individual accuracy, fat-free mass drives underestimation, and indirect calorimetry remains the reference
cards.summary: Synthesis: equations estimate group RMR adequately but miss individuals by hundreds of kcal/day — Mifflin–St Jeor/Oxford lead on individual accuracy, fat-free mass drives underestimation, and indirect calorimetry remains the reference
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above (Frankenfield 2005; Galgani 2018; Flack 2016), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Ganong account of metabolic rate as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: What is settled: (1) measured resting metabolic rate by indirect calorimetry is the reference standard, and calorimeter correction itself shifts the comparison; (2) every standard equation shows small group-mean bias in some sample yet individual limits of agreement of roughly ±300–450 kcal/day — the person-level error is the physiology-relevant fact; (3) on individual-level criteria (proportion within 10%, or within 200 kcal/day), Mifflin–St Jeor and the Oxford equations lead, while group-bias rankings vary by sample and should not be over-read; (4) error is systematic, not random noise — it grows with fat-free mass and with the magnitude of RMR itself, and validation is thin in older adults and ethnic minorities. Absolute resting-rate values by age and sex are properties of the measured cohorts in the primary studies rather than a single normative table, and this shelf does not fabricate one. No refusals on this shelf: all three slated anchors verified from abstract-present records. No animal data are carded.
cards.watchOut: Equation rankings depend on the accuracy criterion (within-10% proportion vs mean bias vs limits of agreement) and on the sample's age, adiposity and fat-free mass — each card names its criterion so the rankings are never pooled into a single league table.

shelves.title: Bioelectrical impedance phase angle at 50 kHz: reference values by age, sex and ethnicity
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the bioelectrical impedance phase angle at 50 kHz by age, sex and ethnicity — its population reference values and percentile curves — and how tightly does it track body cell mass and nutritional state?
shelves.mesh: Electric Impedance · Reference Values · Body Composition/physiology · Age Factors · Sex Factors · Ethnicity/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing is thin for impedance specifically: Boron & Boulpaep's body-composition chapters frame the water compartments, and this shelf rests on the primary measurement literature, as the slate row directs). Two very large 2026 reference studies and one determinants study draw a consistent SHAPE but population-specific VALUES. In 13,256 Chinese adults measured at 50 kHz, phase angle peaked at 30–39 years in Han and Korean men and 40–49 years in Yao men and in all women, fell steeply after 50 in men, and was always higher in men; the 5th–95th percentile ranges were 5.33–7.16° (Han men), 4.62–6.34° (Han women), 5.53–7.65° (Korean men), 5.04–6.79° (Korean women), 5.15–6.94° (Yao men) and 4.49–6.12° (Yao women). In 5,049 healthy Colombians the same arc appeared — rising through adolescence and early adulthood, peaking at 40–49, declining thereafter, men above women at every age. The determinants study (1,442 people with dilution-measured body composition) explains why no universal number can exist yet: phase angle tracks fat-free mass (positive) and the extracellular-to-intracellular water ratio (negative), and even with age, height, race and composition in the model only 42–54% of its variance is explained. Impedance-derived indices are not dilution measurements and must not be presented as such. Until devices and populations are harmonised, a phase angle is interpretable only against its own population's age- and sex-specific percentiles.

cards.headline: Lu 2026 China National Health Survey (13,256 healthy adults, BIA at 50 kHz): phase angle 5th–95th percentiles 5.33–7.16° in Han men and 4.62–6.34° in Han women, with ethnic-group and age-peak differences
cards.summary: Lu 2026 China National Health Survey (13,256 healthy adults, BIA at 50 kHz): phase angle 5th–95th percentiles 5.33–7.16° in Han men and 4.62–6.34° in Han women, with ethnic-group and age-peak differences
cards.type: Population reference-value study at 50 kHz (Lu 2026)
cards.people: 13,256 healthy participants (4,793 men, 8,463 women) aged 20–80 years from the China National Health Survey — 9,616 Han, 2,136 Korean and 1,504 Yao individuals; phase angle measured by bioelectrical impedance analysis at 50 kHz, with age-, sex- and ethnicity-specific percentiles (5th to 95th) built by generalised additive models.
cards.result: Phase angle peaked at 30–39 years in Han and Korean men and at 40–49 years in Yao men; in women the peak was 40–49 years in all ethnic groups, with a steep decline after 50 years in men and a gradual decline in women. Men had higher values than women across all ethnicities and ages. The reference ranges (5th–95th percentiles) were 5.33–7.16° for Han men, 4.62–6.34° for Han women, 5.53–7.65° for Korean men, 5.04–6.79° for Korean women, 5.15–6.94° for Yao men and 4.49–6.12° for Yao women.
cards.watchOut: The ranges are percentile bands pooled across ages 20–80, so a value near the band edge may be mid-range for one decade and extreme for another — the age-specific centile tables in the full text are the usable form; and the record does not name the BIA device, so cross-device application is an assumption, not a finding.

cards.headline: Carrera-Gil 2026 (5,049 healthy Colombians, ages 10–94): phase angle rises to a peak at 40–49 years and declines thereafter, men higher than women at every age — the first Latin American reference curves
cards.summary: Carrera-Gil 2026 (5,049 healthy Colombians, ages 10–94): phase angle rises to a peak at 40–49 years and declines thereafter, men higher than women at every age — the first Latin American reference curves
cards.type: Population reference-value study (Carrera-Gil 2026)
cards.people: 5,049 healthy individuals (3,113 females) aged 10–94 years in a cross-sectional Colombian study; phase angle calculated from resistance and reactance by bioelectrical impedance analysis, with smoothed centile curves and tables (3rd to 97th percentiles) by the Lambda-Mu-Sigma method, by sex and age.
cards.result: Phase angle followed a non-linear pattern with age, increasing during adolescence and early adulthood, peaking around midlife (40–49 years) and declining thereafter. Males consistently exhibited higher phase angle values than females across all age groups. The record's abstract reports the shape and the centile method but does not print the degree values of the centiles, so no Colombian degree values are quoted here.
cards.watchOut: Its contribution is confirmatory shape in a second continent and the adolescent limb (ages 10+) that the adult studies lack; without printed centile values in the record, it cannot supply numbers for a clinic — those live in its full-text tables, and importing the Chinese ranges into a Colombian patient would repeat exactly the population error this shelf warns against.

cards.headline: Gonzalez 2016 (1,442 people with dilution-measured composition): phase angle tracks fat-free mass and the extracellular:intracellular water ratio — and even fully adjusted models explain only 54% (men) and 42% (women) of its variance
cards.summary: Gonzalez 2016 (1,442 people with dilution-measured composition): phase angle tracks fat-free mass and the extracellular:intracellular water ratio — and even fully adjusted models explain only 54% (men) and 42% (women) of its variance
cards.type: Determinants study with reference-method body composition (Gonzalez 2016)
cards.people: 1,442 participants (women 58.5%; Caucasian 40.2%) from body-composition studies, with total-body water by tritium dilution, intracellular water by total-body potassium, fat-free and fat mass by DXA, underwater weighing and total-body water, and phase angle by a single-frequency bioelectrical impedance system.
cards.result: Women had significantly larger extracellular-to-intracellular water (ECW:ICW) ratios and fat mass than men. The highest positive correlation was between phase angle and fat-free mass by underwater weighing (both sexes); the highest negative correlation was with the ECW:ICW ratio (both sexes). Age, race, height, ECW:ICW and fat-free mass were significant determinants in multivariate regression, with age the most significant predictor in both sexes — yet the explained variance remained low (adjusted R² = 0.539 in men, 0.421 in women). The record's abstract reports determinants and correlations, not phase-angle degree values, so none are quoted from it here.
cards.watchOut: This is the biological-meaning card, and its message is cautionary: phase angle is a composite electrical index of body cell mass and water distribution, not a direct measure of either — about half its variance is unexplained even with reference methods in hand, so single-value interpretations ('low phase angle = malnutrition') outrun the evidence.
cards.source: Gonzalez MC et al. Phase angle and its determinants in healthy subjects: influence of body composition. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 2016. PMID: 26843156. cards.headline: Synthesis: phase angle at 50 kHz rises to a midlife peak (30s–40s), is higher in men, and falls with age — but its values are population- and device-specific, so it is read against local percentiles, not a universal range
cards.summary: Synthesis: phase angle at 50 kHz rises to a midlife peak (30s–40s), is higher in men, and falls with age — but its values are population- and device-specific, so it is read against local percentiles, not a universal range
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: the Chinese multi-ethnic reference study (13,256 adults, 50 kHz), the Colombian reference study (5,049 people, ages 10–94) and the determinants study (1,442 people with dilution and potassium reference methods).
cards.result: The life-course shape is concordant on two continents: increase to a peak in the 30s–40s, decline thereafter (steeply after 50 in men), men above women throughout, and modest ethnic-group offsets within one country (Korean ranges highest, Yao lowest in the Chinese data). The determinants record grounds the shape in composition — fat-free mass up, extracellular water share down — while showing that composition explains only about half the variance. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the pattern is consistent, but reference values remain population- and device-bound and the quantity's biological meaning is incompletely resolved, so no universal normal range is claimed.
cards.watchOut: Device, electrode placement, fasting state and recent exercise all move impedance values and are not standardised across the carded studies; a phase angle carried between devices or populations without local reference values should be treated as uninterpretable, not as approximately normal.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lu Z et al. Annals of medicine. 2026 (PMID: 41887716); Carrera-Gil F et al. European journal of clinical nutrition. 2026 (PMID: 42000911); Gonzalez MC et al. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 2016 (PMID: 26843156), all carded above. Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (body-fluid compartments / body composition) — thin for impedance specifically; the shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature. Cross-point: dilution-measured water compartments are a different measurement and a different shelf's question (Slate 8 row S8-4-29) — impedance indices are not dilution measurements.

shelves.title: 25(OH)D distribution, VDSP-standardised: 13.0% of 55,844 Europeans below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL), 40.4% below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL); standardisation itself moved Canada's below-50 fraction from 29.0% to 36.8%
shelves.question: In general populations, what does the serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D distribution look like — median, spread and the fractions below the deficiency / inadequacy thresholds — by age, sex, ancestry, latitude and season, once values are standardised to the reference measurement procedure (VDSP)?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Distribution · Aged · Breast Feeding · Child · Child, Preschool · Ethnicity · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Middle Aged · Pregnancy · Prevalence · Racial Groups · Sex Distribution · United States · Vitamin D · Vitamin D Deficiency · Reference Values · Nutrition Surveys · Seasons
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, calcium / vitamin D chapters (framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature, and says so). This is a DISTRIBUTION shelf, not a supplementation or threshold-recommendation shelf. Four VDSP-era population reports agree on the central lesson: standardisation to the reference measurement procedure moves the whole distribution and reclassifies deficiency — in Canada the fraction below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) rose from 29.0% to 36.8% after standardisation, and in Europe 13.0% of 55,844 people sat below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) on standardised values (40.4% below 50 nmol/L, 20 ng/mL), with a clear winter excess and far higher deficiency in dark-skinned subgroups. Unstandardised historical values are not comparable with VDSP-standardised ones, and that non-comparability is core content. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Canada standardised (Sarafin 2015): re-expressing two Canadian Health Measures Survey cycles (~5,600 people each) to the reference procedure raised the fraction below 40 nmol/L (16 ng/mL) from 16.4% to 19.4% and below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) from 29.0% to 36.8%
cards.summary: Canada standardised (Sarafin 2015): re-expressing two Canadian Health Measures Survey cycles (~5,600 people each) to the reference procedure raised the fraction below 40 nmol/L (16 ng/mL) from 16.4% to 19.4% and below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) from 29.0% to 36.8%
cards.type: Primary population physiology dataset (VDSP standardisation of a national survey, Canada)
cards.people: The Canadian Health Measures Survey, cycles 1 and 2 — each cycle a new cross-sectional national sample of approximately 5,600 individuals; original immunoassay 25(OH)D values standardised in two steps to the NIST / Ghent University reference measurement procedures.
cards.result: After standardisation (cycles 1 and 2 combined), the percentage of Canadians with 25(OH)D below 40 nmol/L (16 ng/mL) increased from 16.4% (original) to 19.4% (standardised), and the percentage below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) increased from 29.0% to 36.8%. Standardised distributions were similar across age and sex groups, with slightly higher values in cycle 2 in the young and old — reversing the original data, which had suggested cycle 2 was lower for all age groups. The authors conclude the shifts show why standardisation matters for judging population deficiency and for comparing national surveys.
cards.watchOut: The standardisation is a two-step statistical conversion of immunoassay values, not a re-measurement of every sample: the size of the shift is itself assay-dependent, which is the point of the card.
cards.source: Sarafin K et al. Standardizing 25-hydroxyvitamin D values from the Canadian Health Measures Survey. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 2015. PMID: 26423385. cards.headline: Europe standardised (Cashman 2016): across 55,844 Europeans on VDSP-standardised values, 13.0% were below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) — 17.7% in extended winter versus 8.3% in summer — and 40.4% were below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL)
cards.summary: Europe standardised (Cashman 2016): across 55,844 Europeans on VDSP-standardised values, 13.0% were below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) — 17.7% in extended winter versus 8.3% in summer — and 40.4% were below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL)
cards.type: Primary population physiology dataset (VDSP-standardised pooled European surveys)
cards.people: 55,844 individuals from representative childhood/teenage and adult/older-adult population studies across Europe: VDSP protocols applied to 14 population studies (reanalysis of subsets in 11, complete analysis in 3), combined with 4 previously standardised studies; biobanked sera re-measured by certified liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry.
cards.result: The pooled standardised estimate, irrespective of age group, ethnic mix and latitude, was that 13.0% of the 55,844 individuals had serum 25(OH)D below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) on average over the year, with 17.7% in those sampled during extended winter (October–March) and 8.3% in summer (April–November, as printed). By the alternate deficiency definition of below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL), prevalence was 40.4%. Dark-skinned ethnic subgroups had a much higher (3- to 71-fold) prevalence of values below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) than white populations.
cards.watchOut: A pooled estimate across heterogeneous national samples, ages and latitudes: the 13.0% headline is an average over that mix, and the season and skin-pigmentation gradients printed on this card are as much the content as the pooled figure.
cards.source: Cashman KD et al. Vitamin D deficiency in Europe: pandemic?. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 2016. PMID: 26864360. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Germany standardised (Rabenberg 2018): standardising three national surveys (1998–2011) raised mean 25(OH)D and lowered deficiency prevalence — yet about 15% of adults still sat below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL)
cards.summary: Germany standardised (Rabenberg 2018): standardising three national surveys (1998–2011) raised mean 25(OH)D and lowered deficiency prevalence — yet about 15% of adults still sat below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL)
cards.type: Primary population physiology dataset (VDSP standardisation of national surveys, Germany, with temporal analysis)
cards.people: Three representative German national health surveys conducted between 1998 and 2011, including persons aged 1–79 years; original serum 25(OH)D measurements retrospectively standardised as part of the ODIN project, with deficiency, insufficiency and sufficiency defined as below 30, 30 to below 50, and at least 50 nmol/L (below 12, 12 to below 20, and at least 20 ng/mL).
cards.result: Compared with the original levels, standardised levels showed higher means overall and in age- and sex-specific analyses; after standardisation the prevalence of deficiency was lower in all surveys and the prevalence of sufficiency higher. Nevertheless, even after standardisation about 15% of adults and 12.5% of children had serum 25(OH)D below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL). The authors conclude standardisation has a substantial impact on estimates of vitamin D status in Germany and should become common practice.
cards.watchOut: Direction of the standardisation shift differs by country and assay (here means rose; in Canada the low tail grew): never assume standardisation moves every survey the same way.
cards.source: Rabenberg M et al. Implications of standardization of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D data for the evaluation of vitamin D status in Germany, including a temporal analysis. BMC public health. 2018. PMID: 29980236. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (calcium / vitamin D; brief framing — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature). The US brief (Looker 2011) supplies the NHANES 2001–2006 frame in Institute of Medicine categories without printing distribution numbers. The standardised numbers come from Canada (Sarafin 2015: below 50 nmol/L, 20 ng/mL, in 36.8% after standardisation versus 29.0% before), Europe (Cashman 2016: 55,844 people; 13.0% below 30 nmol/L, 12 ng/mL; 17.7% winter versus 8.3% summer; 40.4% below 50 nmol/L, 20 ng/mL; 3- to 71-fold higher deficiency in dark-skinned subgroups) and Germany (Rabenberg 2018: standardisation raised means, yet about 15% of adults remained below 30 nmol/L, 12 ng/mL). PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the base is large, representative and standardised to the reference measurement procedure; what is not established is any single unstandardised number, because assay and standardisation move the distribution itself.
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers a distribution question only: it recommends no supplementation dose and no treatment threshold — those live on the vitamin D treatment shelves.

shelves.title: DXA body-composition references in four populations: NHANES, LEAD (10,894 adults), Mexican (9,518) and Singapore (537) — lean mass read against fat mass, per device
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are DXA whole-body body-composition reference values — fat-mass index, lean-mass index, appendicular lean-mass index, percentage fat and android/gynoid distribution — by age, sex and ancestry, and how much does the reference population move the values used to define low lean mass and sarcopenia?
shelves.mesh: Absorptiometry, Photon/methods · Body Composition · Reference Values · Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Intra-Abdominal Fat/diagnostic imaging · Singapore · Austria · United States
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, energy balance / body-composition sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary densitometry-reference literature, and says so. Four adult population datasets, carded PER DEVICE as the measurement demands (scanner generation and software move soft-tissue values): NHANES 1999-2004 fan-beam whole-body data (ages 8-85, partitioned by sex and ethnicity) providing percentage fat, fat-mass index, lean-mass index and appendicular lean-mass index references; the Austrian LEAD cohort (10,894 adults aged 18-81, GE-Lunar Prodigy) with visceral adipose tissue mass; 9,518 healthy Mexican adults with total and appendicular lean-mass references; and 537 Singaporean adults (Hologic Discovery Wi) with Lambda-Mu-Sigma percentiles, in whom lean-mass indices fell with age in men (r -0.45 to -0.54) but barely in women. Ancestry-specific centiles are the content. This shelf cards DXA soft-tissue data only — DXA bone density / T-score references are a different shelf, and bioelectrical-impedance phase angle is a different method. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: NHANES DXA references (Kelly 2009): whole-body fan-beam data 1999-2004, ages 8-85 — percentage fat, fat-mass index, lean-mass index and appendicular lean-mass index partitioned by sex and ethnicity
cards.summary: NHANES DXA references (Kelly 2009): whole-body fan-beam data 1999-2004, ages 8-85 — percentage fat, fat-mass index, lean-mass index and appendicular lean-mass index partitioned by sex and ethnicity
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (DXA whole-body body-composition reference values, NHANES)
cards.people: The NHANES population-based sample from 15 counties across the United States (1999-2004), scanned with modern fan-beam DXA systems; the dataset was partitioned by gender and ethnicity, adult reference values were normalised to age, and measures analysed were percentage fat, fat mass/height2, lean mass/height2, appendicular lean mass/height2, percentage fat trunk/percentage fat legs ratio, trunk/limb fat mass ratio, bone mineral content and bone mineral density, for subjects aged 8 to 85 years.
cards.result: The study's product is the reference-value set itself, together with an obesity classification scheme that used body-mass-index thresholds and prevalences in young adults to generate matching fat-mass-index classification thresholds. The fetched record does not print the numeric centile tables, and this card claims none; the values are intended for evaluating adult and childhood abnormalities of fat, lean and bone and for clinical-trial entry criteria.
cards.watchOut: Fan-beam NHANES data spanning children and adults: only the adult, age-normalised limb belongs to this shelf's question, and the values are bound to the NHANES acquisition and analysis pipeline.
cards.source: Kelly TL et al. Dual energy X-Ray absorptiometry body composition reference values from NHANES. PloS one. 2009. PMID: 19753111. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: LEAD cohort (Ofenheimer 2020): 10,894 Austrian adults aged 18-81 (GE-Lunar Prodigy) — lean-mass index rose with fat-mass index and BMI category at every age; visceral adipose mass was higher in men and rose with age in both sexes
cards.summary: LEAD cohort (Ofenheimer 2020): 10,894 Austrian adults aged 18-81 (GE-Lunar Prodigy) — lean-mass index rose with fat-mass index and BMI category at every age; visceral adipose mass was higher in men and rose with age in both sexes
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (DXA body-composition and VAT reference values, LEAD cohort, GE-Lunar)
cards.people: 10,894 participants aged 18-81 years recruited 2011-2019 by the Austrian LEAD population-based cohort, scanned on a GE-Lunar Prodigy DXA; reference curves for fat-mass index, lean-mass index, appendicular lean-mass index, android/gynoid and trunk/limb fat-mass ratios and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) mass were constructed by age and sex using the LMS method.
cards.result: All lean-mass and fat-mass parameters indicating central fat accumulation were higher in men, whereas other fat-mass indices were higher in women. Lean-mass index differed between each fat-mass-index subgroup and BMI category in all ages, and increased with fat-mass index percentiles and BMI classes — so a low-lean-mass judgement depends on the fat mass it is read against. VAT mass was higher in men than women and increased across all age groups in both sexes. The fetched record does not print the numeric centile tables, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: GE-Lunar Prodigy values: Lunar and Hologic systems (card below) do not yield interchangeable soft-tissue numbers; VAT by DXA is an estimated compartment, not a directly imaged one.
cards.source: Ofenheimer A et al. Reference values of body composition parameters and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) by DXA in adults aged 18-81 years-results from the LEAD cohort. cards.headline: Mexican reference values (Clark 2016): 9,518 healthy subjects — strong sex gaps in lean mass after age 12; male lean mass rose to age 20 while female values plateaued after about age 15
cards.summary: Mexican reference values (Clark 2016): 9,518 healthy subjects — strong sex gaps in lean mass after age 12; male lean mass rose to age 20 while female values plateaued after about age 15
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (DXA lean-mass and fat-mass reference values, Mexican population)
cards.people: 9,518 healthy subjects aged 7-89 years from the baseline of the Health Workers Cohort Study in Mexico, with DXA-measured total lean body mass, appendicular lean body mass and fat mass, expressed also as indices (mass in kg divided by height in metres squared); the final analysis included 2,829 males and 6,694 females as printed in the record.
cards.result: Strong sex gaps in total and appendicular lean mass and their indices appeared after age 12 years (P<0.01). Lean mass values continued to increase in males up to age 20, while females plateaued at approximately age 15; significant sex differences were also seen for fat mass and fat-mass index. The fetched record does not print the numeric age-band tables, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: The cohort spans ages 7-89: the childhood limb is outside this shelf's adult question, and the printed subgroup counts (2,829 + 6,694) sum slightly above the printed total of 9,518 — both are reproduced here exactly as the record prints them.

cards.headline: Yishun study, Singapore (Soh 2022): 537 adults aged 21-90 (Hologic Discovery Wi) — lean-mass index fell with age in men (r -0.45) but not women (r -0.06); android/gynoid fat ratio rose with age in both sexes
cards.summary: Yishun study, Singapore (Soh 2022): 537 adults aged 21-90 (Hologic Discovery Wi) — lean-mass index fell with age in men (r -0.45) but not women (r -0.06); android/gynoid fat ratio rose with age in both sexes
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (DXA body-composition percentile references, Singaporean adults, Hologic)
cards.people: 537 community-dwelling adults (57.5% women) aged 21 to 90 years recruited from the Yishun residential town in Singapore, scanned by whole-body DXA (Hologic Discovery Wi); age- and sex-specific percentile references for fat-mass index, lean-mass index, appendicular lean-mass index, android/gynoid percentage fat ratio and trunk/limb percentage fat ratio were generated by the Lambda-Mu-Sigma method.
cards.result: All parameters correlated significantly with age in both sexes except lean-mass index in women. In men, lean-mass index (r=-0.45) and appendicular lean-mass index (r=-0.54) were negatively associated with age, while in women the same correlations were none (r=-0.06) to weak (r=-0.14). The android/gynoid and trunk/limb fat ratios rose with age in men (r 0.37 and 0.43) and women (r 0.52 and 0.48; all P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The smallest dataset on this shelf (537 adults) and a single-town, multi-ethnic Singaporean sample: its centiles are population references for that setting, and its Hologic values are not interchangeable with the Lunar values above.
cards.source: Soh BP et al. Body composition reference values in Singaporean adults using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-The Yishun study. PloS one. 2022. PMID: 36269751.
