cards.headline: Synthesis: DXA body-composition references are established in four populations — and the reference population moves the answer: lean mass must be read against fat mass and BMI, and age patterns differ by sex and ancestry
cards.summary: Synthesis: DXA body-composition references are established in four populations — and the reference population moves the answer: lean mass must be read against fat mass and BMI, and age patterns differ by sex and ancestry
cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (energy balance / body composition; framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary densitometry-reference literature). NHANES 1999-2004 (Kelly 2009) supplies US fan-beam references partitioned by sex and ethnicity with a fat-mass-index obesity classification; LEAD (10,894 Austrian adults, 2020) shows lean-mass index rising with fat-mass index and BMI at every age and VAT mass higher in men and rising with age; the Mexican cohort (9,518 subjects, 2016) shows lean-mass sex gaps opening after age 12; and the Yishun study (537 Singaporean adults, 2022) shows lean-mass indices falling with age in men but not women. Values used to define low lean mass and sarcopenia therefore depend on device, sex, age and ancestry together — this shelf cards soft-tissue DXA only, cross-pointing bone-density references and impedance methods rather than re-carding them.

shelves.question: In general populations, what is the distribution of plasma total homocysteine — median, spread and upper percentiles by age, sex, folate status and MTHFR genotype — and how far did population folic-acid fortification shift the whole distribution?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Ganong, one-carbon and B-vitamin metabolism sections (framing brief — rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature, and says so). All values are in µmol/L (the unit used in both US and metric practice for this analyte; it is not reported in mmol/L). Four population datasets agree on the shape: homocysteine is higher in men than women, rises with age, and is driven strongly by folate status, smoking and coffee. Post-fortification US adults (NHANES 1999–2002, n=9,196) had age-adjusted means of 8.39 µmol/L (non-Hispanic white), 8.92 (non-Hispanic black) and 8.12 (Mexican American/Hispanic). Pre-fortification Norway (Hordaland, n=11,941) gives the widest 95% ranges — 5.1–16.5 µmol/L in women and 6.2–18.7 in men aged 40–42 — narrowing to 4.8–12.8 and 6.2–14.7 in the favourable-lifestyle subgroup. Pre- and post-fortification distributions are nutritionally different populations and are never merged here. This is a distribution shelf, not a treatment shelf: homocysteine-lowering B-vitamin trials live on their own shelves (cross-point live #203), not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Post-fortification US reference values (NHANES 1999–2002, n=9,196): age-adjusted plasma total homocysteine 8.39 µmol/L in non-Hispanic white, 8.92 in non-Hispanic black and 8.12 in Mexican American/Hispanic adults (Ganji 2006)
cards.summary: Post-fortification US reference values (NHANES 1999–2002, n=9,196): age-adjusted plasma total homocysteine 8.39 µmol/L in non-Hispanic white, 8.92 in non-Hispanic black and 8.12 in Mexican American/Hispanic adults (Ganji 2006)
cards.type: Primary physiology / population distribution study (NHANES, post-fortification)
cards.people: 9,196 US adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys 1999–2001 and 2001–2002 — the nationally representative surveys conducted after cereal fortification with folic acid was implemented; distributions by age, sex and race-ethnicity.
cards.result: Plasma total homocysteine was higher in men than in women and in older than younger persons; in ages 19–30, 31–50 and 51–70 (but not >70) men had significantly higher means than women (P < 0.0001). A race-ethnicity difference existed only over age 70, where non-Hispanic black subjects had significantly higher concentrations than non-Hispanic white or Mexican American/Hispanic subjects (P < 0.05). Age-adjusted concentrations did not differ significantly between the three groups overall (8.39, 8.92 and 8.12 µmol/L respectively). The rate of increase with age was greater in non-Hispanic black persons aged ≥50 than in other groups.
cards.watchOut: Post-fortification data only: these means describe a folate-replete-by-policy population and must not be applied to unfortified populations — the Hordaland card below is the pre-fortification contrast.
cards.source: Ganji V et al. Population reference values for plasma total homocysteine concentrations in US adults after the fortification of cereals with folic acid. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 2006. PMID: 17093148. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hordaland Homocysteine Study (n=11,941): 95% reference range at age 40–42 was 5.1–16.5 µmol/L in women and 6.2–18.7 in men — narrowing to 4.8–12.8 and 6.2–14.7 with high folate, non-smoking and low coffee (Nygård 1998)
cards.summary: Hordaland Homocysteine Study (n=11,941): 95% reference range at age 40–42 was 5.1–16.5 µmol/L in women and 6.2–18.7 in men — narrowing to 4.8–12.8 and 6.2–14.7 with high folate, non-smoking and low coffee (Nygård 1998)
cards.type: Primary physiology / population distribution study (Hordaland, pre-fortification Norway)
cards.people: 11,941 apparently healthy Norwegian participants — 9,165 aged 40–42 years, 2,351 aged 65–67 years and 425 of intermediate ages — with lifestyle indexes (folate intake, smoking, coffee consumption) recorded.
cards.result: In multivariate analysis, sex, age, folate intake, smoking status and coffee consumption were the strongest determinants of total homocysteine, and the combined effect of the three modifiable factors exceeded each alone. A profile of low folate intake, smoking and coffee consumption was associated with a high median and pronounced skewness toward high values; the contrasting profile (high folate, non-smoking, <1 cup/day coffee) had an almost normal distribution with a median 3.0–4.8 µmol/L lower. Among all 40–42-year-olds the 95% reference ranges were 5.1–16.5 µmol/L (women) and 6.2–18.7 (men); in the high-folate, non-smoking, <5 cups/day subgroup they were 4.8–12.8 and 6.2–14.7 µmol/L.
cards.watchOut: A 1998 unfortified population with two narrow age bands doing most of the work: the ranges describe lifestyle-stratified Norwegians, not a universal clinical interval.
cards.source: Nygård O et al. Major lifestyle determinants of plasma total homocysteine distribution: the Hordaland Homocysteine Study. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 1998. PMID: 9459374. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Healthy Turkish sample (N=159, printed small): mean homocysteine 8.91 ± 1.41 µmol/L — men 9.51 ± 1.40 vs women 7.38 ± 1.36 (P < 0.001), rising with age (r = 0.49); upper-20% cut-off 12.26 µmol/L (Taskin 2006)
cards.summary: Healthy Turkish sample (N=159, printed small): mean homocysteine 8.91 ± 1.41 µmol/L — men 9.51 ± 1.40 vs women 7.38 ± 1.36 (P < 0.001), rising with age (r = 0.49); upper-20% cut-off 12.26 µmol/L (Taskin 2006)
cards.type: Primary physiology / population distribution study (healthy Turkish sample, N=159 — small)
cards.people: 159 healthy native Turkish individuals (a small sample — N printed on the face, per the reference-floor labelling rule); plasma homocysteine by HPLC; age groups 20–40, 41–60 and ≥61 years.
cards.result: Mean homocysteine was 8.91 ± 1.41 µmol/L and the median 8.35 µmol/L (men 8.80, women 7.0). Levels were higher in men than women in every age group (overall men 9.51 ± 1.40 vs women 7.38 ± 1.36 µmol/L; P < 0.001) and increased significantly with age (r = 0.49). The cut-off marking the upper 20% of the distribution was 12.26 µmol/L. Postmenopausal women over 60 had significantly higher concentrations than premenopausal women aged 20–40. No significant correlations were found with BMI, glucose, lipids, CRP, creatinine, smoking or alcohol, except blood pressure and uric acid.
cards.watchOut: N=159 is a small reference sample: its percentiles are imprecise and it is carded as a regional supporting dataset, never as the load-bearing interval — the load rests on NHANES and Hordaland.
cards.source: Taskin G et al. Plasma total homocysteine levels in a healthy Turkish population sample. Acta cardiologica. 2006. PMID: 16485731. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Canary Islands representative sample (n=557, ages 18–65): median homocysteine 11.9 µmol/L — men 13.1 vs women 10.9 (P < 0.001); hyperhomocysteinaemia (≥15 µmol/L) in 21.4% overall, 32.2% of men and 13.4% of women (Henríquez 2007)
cards.summary: Canary Islands representative sample (n=557, ages 18–65): median homocysteine 11.9 µmol/L — men 13.1 vs women 10.9 (P < 0.001); hyperhomocysteinaemia (≥15 µmol/L) in 21.4% overall, 32.2% of men and 13.4% of women (Henríquez 2007)
cards.type: Primary physiology / population distribution study (Canary Islands Nutrition Survey)
cards.people: 557 participants aged 18–65 from the population-based Canary Islands Nutrition Survey (ENCA), with two 24-hour dietary recalls, plasma homocysteine and serum vitamin B12 by immunoassay, and folate by an automated ionic-capturing method.
cards.result: Median plasma homocysteine was 11.9 µmol/L, higher in men (13.1) than women (10.9; P < 0.001) and positively associated with age in both sexes (P < 0.001). Hyperhomocysteinaemia (≥15 µmol/L) prevalence was 21.4% overall, 32.2% in men and 13.4% in women. Homocysteine correlated negatively with serum folate (r = −0.32, P < 0.001), erythrocyte folate (r = −0.26, P < 0.001) and serum vitamin B12 (r = −0.28, P < 0.001); men in the lowest quartiles of serum B12 and folate had significantly higher homocysteine than the other quartiles.
cards.watchOut: An unfortified European population with a high ≥15 µmol/L prevalence — the contrast with post-fortification NHANES means is the fortification lesson, not evidence of a sicker population in any other sense.
cards.source: Henríquez P et al. Nutritional determinants of plasma total homocysteine distribution in the Canary Islands. European journal of clinical nutrition. 2007. PMID: 16885934. cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong (one-carbon metabolism) — framing brief; the shelf rests on the population surveys. NHANES post-fortification (n=9,196) centres the US distribution at age-adjusted means of 8.12–8.92 µmol/L by race-ethnicity; Hordaland (n=11,941) shows how wide the unfortified distribution runs and how much folate intake, smoking and coffee move its median (3.0–4.8 µmol/L) and its upper tail; the Turkish (N=159, small) and Canary Islands (n=557) samples confirm the sex and age gradients in unfortified settings. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the distribution's shape and determinants; no single interval is asserted, because fortification status alone moves the whole distribution.
cards.watchOut: Never merge pre- and post-fortification data into one interval, and never use this distribution shelf to argue for or against homocysteine-lowering treatment — that question lives on the B-vitamin treatment shelves.

shelves.title: Nutrition-risk screening in hospitalised adults (NRS-2002 / MUST / MST / MNA-SF): pooled against SGA — MUST sensitivity 0.84 / specificity 0.85, NRS-2002 0.76 / 0.86 — and NRS-2002's own derivation is trial-level (128 trials sorted by treatment benefit), not patient-level accuracy
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults, how valid are the bedside nutrition-risk screening tools — NRS-2002 (Nutritional Risk Screening 2002: impaired nutrition, disease severity, age ≥70), MUST, MST and MNA-SF — against Subjective Global Assessment and ESPEN reference standards: what pooled sensitivity and specificity does each deliver, and what did NRS-2002's derivation (a retrospective analysis of 128 controlled trials) and its prospective hospital validation actually show?
shelves.mesh: Enteral Nutrition · Humans · Likelihood Functions · Logistic Models · Malnutrition/diagnosis/therapy · Mass Screening/standards · Meta-Analysis as Topic · Nutrition Assessment · Nutritional Support · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Parenteral Nutrition · ROC Curve · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Factors · Sensitivity and Specificity · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: A screening-validity shelf, not a treatment shelf: no card implies screening-triggered nutritional support improves outcomes in screen-positive patients. NRS-2002's derivation (the ESPEN working group's own report, programme-labelled) is trial-level — across 128 controlled trials, support helped in 43 of 75 at-risk-classified trials vs 14 of 53 not-at-risk (P = 0.0006; likelihood ratio 1.7) — and that distinction prints on the face wherever the derivation is quoted. Patient-level validity, pooled in the 2024 synthesis (60 studies, 21 meta-analysed) against Subjective Global Assessment, is moderate: MUST sensitivity 0.84 / specificity 0.85, MST 0.81 / 0.79, NRS-2002 0.76 / 0.86 — MUST, not NRS-2002, had the strongest pooled profile, and this shelf is not an NRS-2002 vindication. Reference standards differ (SGA, ESPEN criteria, clinician assessment) and pooled figures are never merged across them; the single-centre Turkish validation (N = 271, geriatrician reference) found 88% / 92%, well above the pooled NRS-2002 sensitivity, and that gradient prints.

cards.headline: NRS-2002 derivation (Kondrup 2003 — the ESPEN working group's own report, programme-labelled): the score's validation is trial-level, not patient-level diagnostic accuracy — among 128 controlled trials of nutritional support vs spontaneous intake, 43 of 75 trials in patients the system classified at-risk showed a positive effect of support, vs 14 of 53 in not-at-risk patients (P = 0.0006), a likelihood ratio of 1.7 (95% CI 1.2–2.3, as reversed in the record: 2.3–1.2)
cards.summary: NRS-2002 derivation (Kondrup 2003 — the ESPEN working group's own report, programme-labelled): the score's validation is trial-level, not patient-level diagnostic accuracy — among 128 controlled trials of nutritional support vs spontaneous intake, 43 of 75 trials in patients the system classified at-risk showed a positive effect of support, vs 14 of 53 in not-at-risk patients (P = 0.0006), a likelihood ratio of 1.7 (95% CI 1.2–2.3, as reversed in the record: 2.3–1.2)
cards.type: Derivation report — retrospective analysis of 128 controlled trials (programme-labelled: ESPEN working group's own report; trial-level validation)
cards.people: No patients were enrolled for this report: NRS-2002's components (impaired nutritional status, severity of disease, age ≥70) were built from controlled-trial datasets, converted to absent/mild/moderate/severe grades, and then tested against all 128 known published randomised trials of nutritional support vs spontaneous intake — 75 trials in at-risk-classified patients and 53 in not-at-risk patients; likelihood ratios were 1.4 for 71 parenteral-nutrition trials and 2.9 for 56 enteral/oral trials. The ESPEN working group's own report.
cards.result: Among the 75 trials in patients classified as nutritionally at-risk, 43 showed a positive effect of nutritional support on clinical outcome; among the 53 not-at-risk trials, 14 showed a positive effect (P = 0.0006). This corresponded to a likelihood ratio (true positive / false positive) of 1.7 (95% CI printed in the record as 2.3–1.2) overall, 1.4 (1.9–1.0) for parenteral nutrition and 2.9 (5.9–1.4) for enteral or oral nutrition. The authors conclude the system can distinguish trials with a positive effect from trials with no effect, and can therefore probably also identify patients likely to benefit from nutritional support.
cards.watchOut: The distinction prints on the face: this validation asks whether the score sorts TRIALS by treatment benefit, not whether it correctly classifies an individual patient's nutritional state. It cannot be quoted as patient-level sensitivity or specificity, and it does not by itself show that screening-triggered support improves outcomes in screen-positive patients.

cards.headline: Nutrition-screening validity synthesis (Cortés-Aguilar 2024 — 60 studies in the review, 21 meta-analysed, 51 tools and 9 reference standards): against Subjective Global Assessment, MUST sensitivity 0.84 (95% CI 0.73–0.91) / specificity 0.85 (0.75–0.91), MST 0.81 / 0.79, NRS-2002 sensitivity 0.76 (0.58–0.87) / specificity 0.86 (0.76–0.93); against ESPEN criteria MUST reached sensitivity 0.97 with wide intervals (0.53–0.99)
cards.summary: Nutrition-screening validity synthesis (Cortés-Aguilar 2024 — 60 studies in the review, 21 meta-analysed, 51 tools and 9 reference standards): against Subjective Global Assessment, MUST sensitivity 0.84 (95% CI 0.73–0.91) / specificity 0.85 (0.75–0.91), MST 0.81 / 0.79, NRS-2002 sensitivity 0.76 (0.58–0.87) / specificity 0.86 (0.76–0.93); against ESPEN criteria MUST reached sensitivity 0.97 with wide intervals (0.53–0.99)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of nutrition-screening validity in hospitalised adults
cards.people: Validation studies of malnutrition-risk screening tools in hospitalised adults, searched to November 2023 (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL); 60 studies met inclusion criteria and 21 were meta-analysed, covering 51 screening tools and 9 reference standards; risk of bias assessed with QUADAS-2 and the review registered in INPLASY (INPLASY202090028), as its abstract states. A synthesis — pooled figures are never merged across reference standards.
cards.result: Against SGA: MUST sensitivity 0.84 (95% CI 0.73–0.91) and specificity 0.85 (0.75–0.91); MST sensitivity 0.81 (0.67–0.90) and specificity 0.79; MNA-SF was meta-analysed against ESPEN criteria (sensitivity 0.99, 0.41–0.99; specificity 0.60, 0.45–0.73); NRS-2002 against SGA had sensitivity 0.76 (0.58–0.87) and specificity 0.86 (0.76–0.93). Against ESPEN criteria, MUST sensitivity was 0.97 (0.53–0.99) with specificity 0.80 (0.50–0.94). The authors conclude MUST demonstrated high accuracy, while noting the quality of included studies varied greatly. (One specificity interval in the record for MST reads 0.72–0.74 as published and is not reprinted here beyond the point estimates.)
cards.watchOut: Reference standards differ across the evidence (SGA, ESPEN criteria, clinician assessment) and pooled figures are never merged across standards. MUST, not NRS-2002, had the strongest pooled profile in this synthesis — this shelf must not be framed as an NRS-2002 vindication, and several intervals (notably MUST vs ESPEN and MNA-SF vs ESPEN) are very wide.

cards.headline: Turkish NRS-2002 prospective validation (Bolayir 2019, 271 consecutive hospitalised adults against experienced geriatricians' detailed assessment): sensitivity 88%, specificity 92%, positive predictive value 87%, negative predictive value 92% and test–retest kappa 0.956
cards.summary: Turkish NRS-2002 prospective validation (Bolayir 2019, 271 consecutive hospitalised adults against experienced geriatricians' detailed assessment): sensitivity 88%, specificity 92%, positive predictive value 87%, negative predictive value 92% and test–retest kappa 0.956
cards.type: Prospective single-centre validation against clinician (geriatrician) assessment
cards.people: 271 consecutive hospitalised patients aged >18 years admitted to surgical and medical wards of a university hospital in Turkey, in a single-centre non-interventional validity study; the reference standard was detailed nutrition assessment by two experienced geriatricians (whose concordance was excellent, so the first geriatrician's decisions were taken as the gold standard).
cards.result: Against the geriatricians' assessment, the Turkish NRS-2002 had sensitivity 88% and specificity 92%, with positive predictive value 87% and negative predictive value 92%. Test–retest agreement was excellent (kappa coefficient 0.956). The authors conclude NRS-2002 is a valid tool to assess malnutrition risk in Turkish hospitalised patients.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre validation (N = 271) against a clinician reference standard — not against SGA — and its sensitivity (88%) sits well above the pooled NRS-2002 sensitivity against SGA (0.76) on the synthesis card: the gradient prints, and the two figures are never merged, because the reference standards differ.

cards.headline: Synthesis: bedside nutrition-risk screening is a trial-sorting derivation (NRS-2002, validated at trial level against 128 controlled trials) plus patient-level validity that is moderate and reference-standard-dependent — pooled against SGA, MUST 0.84 / 0.85, MST 0.81 / 0.79 and NRS-2002 0.76 / 0.86, with a single-centre NRS-2002 validation at 88% / 92% against clinician assessment

cards.type: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the NRS-2002 derivation (128 controlled trials, no enrolled patients), the 2024 validity synthesis (60 studies, 21 meta-analysed) and the Turkish prospective validation (N = 271).
cards.result: What the base supports: these tools identify a risk group with moderate accuracy, and NRS-2002's founding claim is the narrower, trial-level one — that its classification sorts trials by whether nutritional support helped. No card on this shelf implies that screening-triggered nutritional support improves outcomes in screen-positive individual patients; that claim is not what any of these reports tested at patient level.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Serum zinc and selenium population distributions (PHYS): zinc timing-bound (−15.3 µg/dL by evening in NHANES), selenium geography-bound (means 80.7–100.6 µg/L) with no universal reference value feasible — whole-blood dataset kept matrix-separate
shelves.question: What are the population distributions of serum zinc and serum selenium in adults — what means and below-cutoff proportions does the US national survey report (including the effect of time of day of the blood draw), what did the Northern Ireland population surveys find for zinc and copper, and why does the critical review of 36 selenium studies conclude that no universal reference value is feasible? (PHYSIOLOGY: matrix discipline binds — the Czech dataset is whole blood, flagged wherever it appears; µmol/L values carry µg/dL equivalents.)

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Matrix discipline binds this shelf: the Czech dataset is whole blood and its values are never printed beside serum values without the matrix attached. Zinc — 3 datasets: NHANES 2011–2014 (4,347 participants aged ≥6 — a mixed child/adult survey whose adult-relevant strata print as such; means 84.9 µg/dL in males and 80.6 µg/dL in females, with afternoon and evening draws lower by 9.7 and 15.3 µg/dL in the adjusted model and 8.6% of males / 8.2% of females aged ≥10 below the suggested cutoffs); two Northern Ireland surveys (≈4,375 adults; 1983–84 zinc 12.1 µmol/L in men, ≈79 µg/dL, and 11.6 µmol/L in women, ≈76 µg/dL, with copper 17.2 / 19.0 µmol/L, ≈109 / ≈121 µg/dL — US-unit equivalents per the standing rule); and 1,216 Czech blood donors whose zinc (median 5,800 µg/L) and selenium (76 µg/L) are whole-blood values. Selenium — 4 datasets + 1 synthesis, counted separately on the face: Barcelona (150 adults; mean 80.7 ± 10 µg/L), Italian regions (4,201 adults; regional means 87–93 µg/L), Tehran (adult mean 100.6 ± 13 µg/L; adult N not separately documented in the abstract, labelled as such), and the whole-blood Czech observation (counted in neither serum set); the TRACY critical review of 36 suitable papers concludes geographical variability makes a single universal reference value infeasible — labelled a synthesis, not a dataset. Diurnal/fasting effects on zinc are large and print beside every mean; soil/dietary geography drives selenium (means 80.7–100.6 µg/L across the serum datasets, i.e. 8.07–10.06 µg/dL) and no universal interval is printed. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for population- and matrix-dependence; EMERGING for any single cutoff.

cards.headline: Zinc dataset 1 of 3 (Hennigar 2018, The Journal of Nutrition — NHANES 2011–2014, 4,347 participants aged ≥6 years): mean serum zinc was 84.9 ± 0.8 µg/dL in males and 80.6 ± 0.6 µg/dL in females; afternoon and evening draws were lower than morning draws by 9.7 and 15.3 µg/dL respectively in the adjusted model, and 8.6% of males and 8.2% of females aged ≥10 years fell below the suggested cutoffs
cards.summary: Zinc dataset 1 of 3 (Hennigar 2018, The Journal of Nutrition — NHANES 2011–2014, 4,347 participants aged ≥6 years): mean serum zinc was 84.9 ± 0.8 µg/dL in males and 80.6 ± 0.6 µg/dL in females; afternoon and evening draws were lower than morning draws by 9.7 and 15.3 µg/dL respectively in the adjusted model, and 8.6% of males and 8.2% of females aged ≥10 years fell below the suggested cutoffs
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — serum zinc, US national survey (zinc dataset 1 of 3)
cards.people: 4,347 males and females aged ≥6 years in NHANES 2011–2014 (a mixed child/adult national survey — its adult-relevant strata print as such: the below-cutoff proportions are for ages ≥10, and 3.8% of children under 10 were below cutoff, as published). Serum zinc by the survey's standard methods; dietary and supplemental zinc assessed. The record's abstract states the analysis was registered as ISRCTN96013840, printed in its source line.
cards.result: Mean ± SE serum zinc was 84.9 ± 0.8 µg/dL in males and 80.6 ± 0.6 µg/dL in females (P < 0.0001). In adjusted regression, afternoon and evening blood draws were negatively associated with serum zinc (β = −9.7 and −15.3; P < 0.0001), while serum albumin (β = 16.1; P < 0.0001) and haemoglobin (β = 1.0; P = 0.0048) were positively associated. Hypoalbuminaemia (OR 11.2, 99% CI 3.4 to 37.3 — a relative odds measure), anaemia in females (OR 3.4, 1.7 to 6.9) and pregnancy (OR 9.6, 2.9 to 31.9) increased the odds of being below the cutoff. Zinc from diet or supplements did not affect serum zinc (P > 0.01). Approximately 8.6% of males and 8.2% of females aged ≥10 years were below the serum zinc cutoff.
cards.watchOut: Time of day is a first-order effect here (up to −15.3 µg/dL by evening): no serum zinc mean from any dataset on this shelf may be compared without draw timing. The dataset spans ages ≥6 — it is not an adults-only sample, and its child stratum is not carded as adult data.
cards.source: Hennigar SR et al. Serum Zinc Concentrations in the US Population Are Related to Sex, Age, and Time of Blood Draw but Not Dietary or Supplemental Zinc. The Journal of nutrition. 2018. cards.headline: Zinc dataset 2 of 3 (McMaster 1992, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition — two Northern Ireland population surveys, ≈4,375 adults aged 25–64): in 1983–84 mean serum zinc was 12.1 ± 1.7 µmol/L in men (≈79 µg/dL) and 11.6 ± 1.4 µmol/L in women (≈76 µg/dL); mean serum copper was 17.2 ± 3.1 µmol/L in men (≈109 µg/dL) and 19.0 ± 3.9 µmol/L in women (≈121 µg/dL) — US-unit equivalents added per the standing rule
cards.summary: Zinc dataset 2 of 3 (McMaster 1992, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition — two Northern Ireland population surveys, ≈4,375 adults aged 25–64): in 1983–84 mean serum zinc was 12.1 ± 1.7 µmol/L in men (≈79 µg/dL) and 11.6 ± 1.4 µmol/L in women (≈76 µg/dL); mean serum copper was 17.2 ± 3.1 µmol/L in men (≈109 µg/dL) and 19.0 ± 3.9 µmol/L in women (≈121 µg/dL) — US-unit equivalents added per the standing rule
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — serum zinc and copper, Northern Ireland surveys (zinc dataset 2 of 3; copper limb carded as published alongside)
cards.people: Non-fasting adults aged 25–64 in two independent Northern Ireland population surveys: 1983–84 (1,144 men; 1,055 women neither pregnant nor taking oestrogens/progestogens) and 1986–87 (1,142 men; 1,034 women). Serum zinc and copper in µmol/L as published, with µg/dL equivalents (zinc ×6.54, copper ×6.35) added per the standing US-units rule.
cards.result: In 1983–84, copper in 1,144 males was 17.2 ± 3.1 µmol/L (≈109 µg/dL) and zinc 12.1 ± 1.7 µmol/L (≈79 µg/dL); copper in 1,055 females was 19.0 ± 3.9 µmol/L (≈121 µg/dL) and zinc 11.6 ± 1.4 µmol/L (≈76 µg/dL). In 1986–87, copper in 1,142 males was 17.9 ± 3.3 µmol/L (≈114 µg/dL) and zinc 13.2 ± 2.1 µmol/L (≈86 µg/dL); copper in 1,034 females was 20.1 ± 3.9 µmol/L (≈128 µg/dL) and zinc 12.7 ± 2.0 µmol/L (≈83 µg/dL). Zinc but not copper decreased from early morning to late afternoon; both were unaffected by reported postprandial time. Copper rose with age in both sexes; zinc showed only a slight upward trend.
cards.watchOut: Two surveys four years apart differ by ~1 µmol/L in zinc within the same population — survey-to-survey drift of that size is part of this shelf's content, and the diurnal fall (morning to late afternoon) prints beside every mean, as in the NHANES dataset.

cards.summary: Zinc/selenium dataset — WHOLE BLOOD, matrix-labelled (Benes 2000, Central European Journal of Public Health — 1,216 healthy adult blood donors, Czech Republic): median zinc 5,800 µg/L and selenium 76 µg/L in WHOLE BLOOD — never printed beside serum values without the matrix attached
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — trace elements in WHOLE BLOOD (matrix-labelled; zinc dataset 3 of 3 and a selenium whole-blood observation, counted in neither serum set)
cards.people: 1,216 adult blood donors (896 men, 320 women; average age 33) in the Czech Republic, 1996–1998, with trace elements in whole blood by atomic absorption spectrometry (a separate child sample of 758 in the same paper is not counted in this adult dataset). Matrix discipline binds this card: whole blood, not serum.
cards.result: Adult medians in whole blood were: cadmium 0.7 µg/L, copper 800 µg/L, mercury 0.78 µg/L, lead 41 µg/L, selenium 76 µg/L (7.6 µg/dL) and zinc 5,800 µg/L (580 µg/dL). Statistically significant differences between men and women were found for copper, mercury, lead and zinc. The authors note the concentrations correspond to published values for populations not occupationally exposed.
cards.watchOut: WHOLE BLOOD: whole-blood zinc (~5,800 µg/L, largely erythrocyte zinc) is roughly sevenfold serum zinc and the two matrices must never be merged or compared as if one scale. This dataset is counted as zinc dataset 3 of 3 with its matrix flag, and is NOT counted among the serum selenium datasets.

cards.summary: Selenium dataset 1 of 4 (Torra 1997, Biological Trace Element Research — 150 healthy adults, Barcelona): mean serum selenium 80.7 ± 10 µg/L (8.07 µg/dL), range 60–106 µg/L, by graphite-furnace atomic spectrometry
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — serum selenium, Barcelona (selenium dataset 1 of 4)
cards.people: 150 healthy subjects aged 18–70 from the general population of Barcelona, Spain, randomly sampled; serum selenium by graphite furnace atomic spectrometry following the stabilised-temperature-platform-furnace concept, as published.
cards.result: Serum selenium ranged between 60 and 106 µg/L with a mean of 80.7 ± 10 µg/L (8.07 ± 1.0 µg/dL). No subject was below the 45 µg/L threshold the authors cite in connection with coronary and cancer risk literature, and the authors consider the values within safe limits — their interpretive framing, printed as such.
cards.watchOut: A single-city sample of 150: soil/dietary geography drives selenium, so this mean is a Barcelona value, not a Spanish or European one.

cards.summary: Selenium dataset 2 of 4 (Morisi 1989, Annali dell'Istituto Superiore di Sanità — 4,201 adults across Italian regions): regional mean serum selenium 87–93 µg/L (8.7–9.3 µg/dL), approximately 5 µg/L higher than the means in ten European countries, with a decreasing trend above age 60
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — serum selenium, Italian regions (selenium dataset 2 of 4)
cards.people: 4,201 adult subjects (with 1,217 children in the same programme, not counted here) drawn from populations previously enrolled in Italian epidemiological prevention programmes, with standardised methods, as published.
cards.result: Mean observed values for the various adult populations examined varied between 87 and 93 µg/L and were approximately 5 µg/L higher than the mean values in ten European countries. Paediatric means (under 15 years) were slightly lower (78–83 µg/L). A decreasing trend with age above 60 years was observed, especially in males; no significant difference was observed for sex or geographic area of residence within Italy.
cards.watchOut: Regional means are ranges across sub-populations (87–93 µg/L), not a single pooled Italian mean — printed as the range the abstract gives.

cards.summary: Selenium dataset 3 of 4 (Safaralizadeh 2005, Nutrition Journal — Tehran adults; the study's 184 participants include children and the adult N is not separately documented in the abstract): adult mean serum selenium 100.6 ± 13 µg/L (10.06 µg/dL) — men 102.2 ± 12, women 93.9 ± 14 µg/L
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — serum selenium, Tehran adults (selenium dataset 3 of 4; adult N not documented in the abstract)
cards.people: 184 healthy individuals in Tehran, Iran, divided into children (1–16 years) and adults (over 16) for analysis; the adult subset's own N is not separately documented in the abstract and prints as 'adult N not documented' — no N is imported. Serum selenium by hydride generation and flame atomic absorption spectroscopy.
cards.result: In adults (over 16 years) the mean serum selenium level was 100.6 ± 13 µg/L; among women 93.9 ± 14 µg/L and among men 102.2 ± 12 µg/L, a significant sex difference (P < 0.005). In children the mean was 84.3 ± 11 µg/L with no sex difference. There was a positive correlation between selenium concentration and age in men (P < 0.001). Calculated daily intakes were 67 µg (men) and 62.1 µg (women). The authors note Tehran values resemble other Middle Eastern populations, particularly Saudi Arabia.
cards.watchOut: 'Adult N not documented' labelling applies to this dataset, per the standing rule. The study total (184) includes children and must never be printed as the adult N.

cards.headline: Selenium synthesis — labelled a synthesis, not a dataset (Alfthan 1996, Journal of Trace Elements in Medicine and Biology — TRACY-project critical review: of 291 papers published 1983–1993, 36 were suitable): geographical variation in selenium intake was so large that one universal reference serum selenium value for the world's population was not feasible
cards.summary: Selenium synthesis — labelled a synthesis, not a dataset (Alfthan 1996, Journal of Trace Elements in Medicine and Biology — TRACY-project critical review: of 291 papers published 1983–1993, 36 were suitable): geographical variation in selenium intake was so large that one universal reference serum selenium value for the world's population was not feasible
cards.type: Critical review / synthesis of 36 suitable papers (TRACY protocol) — labelled a synthesis, never counted as a dataset
cards.people: Published reports on serum/plasma selenium concentrations critically reviewed against the international TRACY project's pre-analytical and analytical criteria; only data on healthy adults were retained from the 36 suitable papers. Labelled a synthesis on this shelf — it is not a fifth selenium dataset.
cards.result: Geographical area and time of sampling were the pre-analytical factors of high importance; gender, occupation, diet data and supplement/medication use were also important determinants, while ethnic origin, smoking, fasting, contamination control and storage were of relatively low importance. Analytical accuracy criteria were generally satisfied. Due to the geographical variation of selenium intake, one universal reference serum selenium value for the world's population was not feasible, though the selected data documented concentration levels among populations of different (mostly European) areas.
cards.watchOut: The TRACY conclusion is the shelf's selenium verdict: no universal reference value. Any single dataset's mean printed without its geography contradicts this synthesis.
cards.source: Alfthan G et al. Reference values for serum selenium in various areas-evaluated according to the TRACY protocol. Journal of trace elements in medicine and biology : organ of the Society for Minerals and Trace Elements (GMS). 1996. PMID: 8829130. Registry ID: none in the record. Selenium — 4 datasets + 1 synthesis counted separately (Barcelona N = 150; Italian regions N = 4,201 adults; Tehran, adult N not documented; the Czech whole-blood selenium median counted in neither serum set) plus the TRACY synthesis (36 papers).
cards.result: PHYSIOLOGY framing only — no intervention stamp applies. Diurnal and fasting effects on zinc are large and print beside every mean; soil/dietary geography drives selenium; no universal interval is printed for either analyte.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

(physiology: matrix discipline binds — the czech dataset is whole blood, flagged wherever it appears; µmol/l values carry µg/dl equivalents.) synthesis all reports carded on this shelf, counted separately on the face as the row directs: zinc — 3 datasets (nhanes 2011–2014, n = 4,347 aged ≥6; northern ireland surveys, ≈4,375 adults; czech whole-blood donors, n = 1,216, matrix-flagged). selenium — 4 datasets + 1 synthesis counted separately (barcelona n = 150; italian regions n = 4,201 adults; tehran, adult n not documented; the czech whole-blood selenium median counted in neither serum set) plus the tracy synthesis (36 papers). physiology framing only — no intervention stamp applies. diurnal and fasting effects on zinc are large and print beside every mean; soil/dietary geography drives selenium; no universal interval is printed for either analyte. see the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
